Throughout the twentieth century, the architecture of the house has been a locus for experimentation with ideas about ways of living, individual expression, and social relation and class. It served as a platform of design trialing for materials and forms and was the site where architects have sought to offer new domestic lifestyles. From Kenzo Tange and Kazuo Shinohara to Sou Fujimoto and Atelier Bow-Wow, nearly all architects of the past hundred years have catalyzed their most elaborated ideas through the design of houses. The house is not simply one type within the architectural vast constructed inventory, but arguably the most important medium for the investigation of architectural ideas.

Our window into the field of architecture will be a small, carefully selected group of seminal houses, which were constructed in Japan from the beginning of the 20th Century until the last decade. These works of architecture have an accumulated value. Each of them had the ability to mirror a crystallized image of its social-cultural-political surroundings at the time of construction and carries extraordinary relevance to the study of the field even today. As a group they form a balanced account of architectural traditions in the modern period and an opportunity for acquaintance with the architectural knowledge of that time, drawing from a range of fields that influence how a building is designed, described, constructed, with how it is imagined and with how it is used once build.

The course will be conducted in a form of a studio. Each of the participating students will be assigned to one project/house. The work during the semester will occur along two paths. In the first, students will conduct a study in relation to ‘their’ particular house, gather material for a ‘box of references’, and gain an understanding of its architectural style, its use and structure, its motivation, and contextual power. At the second path of the course, we will study through practice. In this section each student will construct a series of physical, analytical models of his/her assigned house, getting familiar with design ideas, understanding spatial concerns, considering methods and materials, and offering individual interpretations.

The course has no prerequisites. Besides an interest in the course subjects, students are not required to have any prior knowledge of architecture. There will be no writing assignment. The course will conclude in a presentation and in an exhibition of the models.

Objectives:
Acquiring knowledge of central concepts in the field of architecture, and establishing complex connections between those concepts through acts of analysis and representation.

This course provides a concise introduction to Russian Studies, serving both students who wish to broaden their area studies perspective and those intending to specialise in the field. It is designed to cultivate interest in Russian history and culture, enhance understanding of Russia’s contemporary political, social, and economic context, and assist students in defining the focus of their future academic and professional pursuits within area studies.

Objectives:
Course Objectives

This course aims to:

• Introduce students to key historical and cultural references in Russian Studies.

• Emphasise themes of enduring relevance for understanding Russia’s past and present.

• Provide analytical tools for interpreting Russia’s political, social, and economic transformations.

• Situate Russian Studies within the broader field of Area Studies, encouraging comparative and cross-cultural perspectives.

• Develop students’ capacity to critically engage with diverse sources and scholarly debates.

Expected Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

Knowledge and Understanding

• Demonstrate greater knowledge of Russia’s historical development and major turning points.

• Display enhanced familiarity with Russian cultural heritage, traditions, and their role in shaping identity.

• Analyse Russia’s transitional trajectory and contemporary socio-economic dynamics with sharpened critical awareness.

Skills

• Apply comparative analysis by relating Russian experiences to those of other societies in Eurasia and beyond.

• Interpret and evaluate primary and secondary sources, including historical documents, cultural texts, and scholarly literature.

• Communicate informed arguments in written and oral formats, using appropriate academic conventions.

Competence

• Integrate Russian Studies into a broader Area Studies framework, recognising interconnections across regions and disciplines.

• Demonstrate cross-cultural awareness and sensitivity in analysing Russia’s place in global contexts.

• Exhibit readiness to pursue advanced study or research in Russian Studies or related fields.

Iakwe! Kaselehlie mai! Hafa Adai! Alii! Aloha! Aroha! Ia Ora Na! Kia Orana! Welcome to Oceania!

When people in Japan talk about the Pacific Ocean, usually they think about a big, vast sea, with America on the other side. They think of tropical islands and hula dancing, or mysterious military operations, tuna fish and other seafood. Usually we don’t consider that, from a Japanese perspective, the Pacific is what connects us to the United States and the rest of the world. We forget about the Pacific War or about the other ways that the Pacific links Japan to the United States, and instead we just talk about ideas like “the American dream,”“freedom,” fast food, or economic power. Some people have referred to the Pacific Ocean as “an American Lake,” when referring to American military and economic power. In this class, will take this into consideration and take a very different approach to “America," "Japan," and "gender relations" through "international relations," by thinking of how these things are seen from the vast communities of people who live on islands in the Pacific Ocean. .” The great Tongan scholar Epeli Hau’ofa called the Pacific Ocean a “Sea of Islands.” By this, he meant that usually we think of the Pacific as a big, empty ocean, but in fact it is filled with thousands of islands that are all connected to each other and that all connect everyone in the world together. His message was that we should take Oceania seriously and realize our deep ties to this place and to each other. Especially during the times of this new coronavirus pandemic, and amidst the tides of massive climate change that deeply affects the Pacific Islands, this course takes on more urgency and relevance for all of us.

First and foremost, this is a course about appreciating and empathizing with historical narratives on many levels, exploring histories of empire, war, and globalization from the perspectives of indigenous Pacific Islanders. Although this history is not well known by neither Japanese nor Americans, the Pacific history of the islands between these two countries is very important for understanding the history of the 20th century. This will be a very unique opportunity to get a new awareness not only of America but of militarization, nuclear weapons, globalization, climate change, international politics, and historical popular culture--and especially Japan--through the eyes of the Pacific Islanders who have the closest connections to Japan and the United States. Moreover, we take a deeper reading on how gender plays a big part in colonialism, militarization, and power/ How have Pacific Islanders been influenced by Japan and America? How have we in continental nations been influenced by Pacific Islanders? How did World WarⅡconnect and divide Japan and America? What remains of the war in the Pacific, and what is remembered or forgotten? How does this play into nationalism today? Using the metaphor of “coral” and the “reef,” we will talk about how each and every one of us is somehow related to the Pacific Islands, and we will look closely at the Pacific to give us many serious examples about major issues that affect the whole world. Many people say that the Pacific is the most globalized--and also the most American place on earth. Let’s explore why.

Objectives:
This is a large lecture class, taught in person. By the end of this class, you will be expected to have a basic historical understanding of early settlement, navigation, European and Japanese colonialism, and war in Oceania from the perspectives of Pacific Islands, with a particular emphasis on how America and Japan are connected through Oceania. You will be challenged to rethink your assumptions about America and Japan, and to try to creatively think of new ways of approaching globalization and change so that Islander and other indigenous or marginalized perspectives are also taken into consideration. Hopefully you will also have a better understanding of our shared histories and have a better idea of how we can all cooperate to create a better world.

This course is taught from multiple, intersecting perspectives in Gender Studies, International Relations, Area Studies, cultural studies anthropology, and Pacific Islands postcolonial and historical studies. You will cultivate an awareness of all of those fields through your study as well.

【Course Delivery Method】Face-to-Face

This course will be taught in Spanish, and students are expected to participate in class discussions in Spanish and complete all the assignments in Spanish.

In this course, we will examine some of the most important historical, cultural, and socio-political occurrences of the Spanish-speaking world through the critical analyses of the selected cultural, artistic, and literary texts. We will explore current issues and contemporary socio-political, cultural, and artistic forms of expression produced in the Spanish-speaking world, by discussing how historical memories (the past) are related to the contemporary themes and phenomena. The ultimate goal of this course is to acquire the knowledge and skills to critically observe and express how and why important it is to connect the past and the present within the context of the Spanish-speaking world. More details will be given during the first class.

Objectives:
Students will

1. acquire and deepen the knowledge about the Spanish-speaking world.

2. improve their critical thinking skill through reading cultural texts related to the Hispanophone world.

3. reinforce their ability to logically articulate ideas and opinions through writing and aural exercises.

4. improve their Spanish language skills.

As with in the Spring Semester, this advanced seminar provides students the chance to build upon their previous studies of cultural studies, gender studies, and postcolonial studies, particularly in the context of Pacific and Asian regional studies. However, this seminar also has a significant writing component to it, geared toward students in the final stages of completing their graduation theses, and this is why there is an additional period of class built into the schedule for final semester students only. Aside from this, like the spring semester, this zemi also engages with creative representation in film and contemporary art. It is especially an opportunity for mainly students who have already studied with this instructor to apply their knowledge to specialized individual studies around themes of interest in cultural studies. Adding to what has been discussed in previous courses and seminars with this instructor, this course allows students to work toward a senior thesis project in terms of the intersections between gender/identity/sexuality/culture/region/militarism/tourism/race, etc. to further their understanding of cultural studies, gender studies, and Pacific Studies, and to develop their own individualized projects that cater to their particular interests. Since this is a seminar for advanced students, much of the content will revolve around sharing lively discussion that is of mutual interest to all students, and working together on your independent graduation projects.
This seminar is offered in a group discussion-based format, focused primarily around individual student research projects, in which students learn from each other at different levels. All students do shared readings and explore different topics together each semester, and each semester the instructor curates a unique cultural studies/history/gender studies/ethnography theme that we all focus upon. In general, juniors (3rd year students) help to lead the readings about the main theme and work toward writing a general reflective essay on that theme at the end of the semester; whereas seniors (4th year students) present and teach the seminar about the research that they are doing on their respective topics, with the goal of writing chapters toward their senior thesis due at the end of the year. Together, we also will pursue group projects and different outreach activities, as well as possible extracurricular activities, based on the proposals of all participants in the seminar.

Each semester, the collective conversation theme is different, and we cycle through these themes as each cohort passes through the seminar. For example, in previous semesters we have considered "Vulnerable Histories;" "Reading with the Senses;" "Mythologies of the Everyday World," and other themes. In 2020-2021, due to the pandemic, we took on more projects related to global turmoil, vulnerability, trauma, and self-reflexivity as we transitioned to a temporary all online format. In future semesters, we will gradually transition back to in-person classes little by little when it is advisable to do so, but on Zoom we make creative use of breakout rooms to divide students into interesting cohorts based around their biggest interests, to maximize learning. At other points in our seminar, we spend time thinking about urban cultures and communities in Tokyo, sensory learning, contemporary art, indigenous communities in Oceania, queer studies and masculinities, and so on. In the 2020-2021 period, we aimed to welcome guest speakers who were successful contemporary artists in Japan to come and talk with us about the theme of "decolonizing Japan," which gave students unique opportunities to think about how to take action in their own lives and with their own talents. We will continue to pursue such activities in coming semesters as well. We may also connect Greg's students in the Graduate School of International Culture and Communication Studies as well as art students in other parts of Japan that Greg mentors, as a way of expanding our awareness and creativity. As always, incoming new students to the seminar will easily be able to access all of our archived previous readings and discussions and encouraged to learn from their sempai by reading their theses.

Students who have already studied with this instructor are strongly encouraged to join this seminar (especially those who have taken all of the instructor's courses, including first year seminars), while those who have not taken previous courses should first consider taking the instructor’s intermediate seminar and other lecture courses, since there is prerequisite knowledge that you should know in order to make the most of this seminar. This is meant to be a lively but rigorous seminar, but only with a limited number of participants, so that everyone can participate and contribute fully. Because of this, not everyone who applies for the seminar can be admitted, and in principle, some semesters allow more students than others, based on the number of students currently enrolled. Please keep this in mind if you apply.

Objectives:
Throughout this semester, students will expand upon the nuanced understanding of the core themes discussed in previous courses they have taken with this instructor, in terms of how these relate to the Pacific and Asian region and their own interests. They will also cultivate and hone their abilities to do successful and interesting, stimulating, unique research and writing for their senior projects. You will be expected to utilize cultural studies and gender studies-inspired approaches to problems such as conflict, marginalized groups, vulnerable communities, militarism, globalization, and environment, through readings assigned in the first part of the seminar, and later through independent research toward your senior project. This thesis project will be crafted using unique and interesting methodologies which we will also discuss extensively in our seminar, by doing readings in ethnographic and cultural studies techniques, as well as self-reflexive writing, filmmaking, photography, and other creative approaches.

This course will be taught in a Face-to-Face format.

This course will be taught in Spanish.

There is no prerequisite for this course.

Those who have not taken Topics in Spanish America (English) CAN take this course.

Students can take both courses in any order they like. Students must have at least an advanced-intermediate level of Spanish. Reading materials and class discussions will be in Spanish.

In this course, we will analyze the concepts and phenomena of cultural encounters and border-crossings in Spanish American societies, mainly through some of the fundamental works that were produced in the 20th and 21st centuries. We will examine where and how we can observe the phenomena and processes of cultural encounters and border-crossings in the texts and explore the meaning of each aspect of these phenomena within a specific socio-historical and political context. Throughout this course, we will contemplate the following key questions. How a culture travels and encounters with another? How does it change its shape upon encountering with other cultures? Is it possible to have the concept of a return to “the original” point of departure or the concept of “authenticity”?

Objectives:
Students should be able to:

Develop and broaden their knowledge of the concept of cultural encounters and border-crossings within the context of Spanish America:

Develop and improve the ability to critically analyze literary, cultural, and artistic works

Reinforce the ability to articulate ideas and opinions in an oral and written academic from.

Reinforce the ability to listen to and analyze different perspectives and interpretations in a logical and critical way.

This introductory course provides a comprehensive overviewof the history of political ideas, offering students a solid foundation in thesubject to be able to critically analyze political ideas implications in varioussocietal contexts. We will explore the evolution of knowledge surrounding theorganization of societies and the governance of populations. By delving intothe thoughts and theories of prominent political thinkers from ancient times tothe present, with a particular emphasis on French political thinkers, we willuncover the diverse interpretations of fundamental concepts such as justice,equality, nature, freedom, law, and the individual within various historical,social, and economic contexts.

Objectives:
This course provides an introductory exploration of the history of political ideas and political thought, aimed at familiarizing students with key concepts and theories within the field of political science. It aims at cultivating an appreciation for the relevance and impact of political ideas on contemporary society, emphasizing their significance in shaping political systems, institutions, and societal norms. By examining the contributions of French political thinkers, drawing upon the work of influential theorists, this course aims at facilitating a deeper understanding of the dynamics and transformations within French society during significant historical periods.

Thecourse gives an overview of key topics in the linguistics of German such asPhonetics and Phonology, Morphology, Semantics and Pragmatics. Apart from thatit also touches on the sociolinguistic and historical contexts of the Germanlanguage such as its pluricentricity, its contact with other languages incolonial contexts and its historic ancestors. The course is designed as anintroduction to the social contexts and linguistics of German and is supposedto complement the language acquisition during the first semester in the APMGerman Program.

Objectives:
The objective of this course is to give students an overview of central topics of the linguistics of German while providing social and historical context of this language in use.

In this class students will learn about the political system and political cultures of Germany, Switzerland and Austria (as well as the former GDR as a contrasting example). We will get to know political parties, civil society actors, and learn about protest dynamics and different participation forms within these liberal democratic systems as well as the role of labor unions and the other “social partners”. The class will assess the challenges of populism and growing authoritarianism on democratic discourse, and the role of the media systems in political deliberation. Different approaches to direct democracy will be thematized from a comparative point of view. The political system of the former GDR will serve as a historical example of a one-party-state without separation of powers.

Objectives:
The objective of this class is to give students and overview of the core political institutions and electoral systems and political cultures of the German speaking countries (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) as well as a historical note on the former GDR.

In Italy, many monuments and works of art attract our attention. Besides their aesthetic significance, they contain much information about Italian history. Each monument and artifact was created under certain social circumstances, and sometimes, they hold the key to understanding each epoch. As an introduction to Italian studies, this course offers a general description and detailed analysis of some masterpieces to reveal the connection between history, art, and society. The objects of our analyses range from ancient Rome to contemporary Italy, illustrating the transformation and continuity of Italian society. Through the analysis of historical documents, students can develop critical thinking skills and an objective view toward both the past and contemporary society.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to:

- develop an awareness of the Italian culture

- learn fundamental skills for historical study

- acquire knowledge about the relationship between history, art, and society.

- gain the ability of critical and logical thinking

This course will be taught primarily in English, with some materials in French depending on the students’ proficiency in the language. It examines the approaches of France, the European Union, and Japan to environmental and climate change challenges from the post-war period to the present. While France displayed limited proactivity in environmental matters until the 2000s, Japan began implementing anti-pollution laws in the late 1960s, achieving an early convergence of energy and environmental policies by the 1970s. However, this convergence has weakened in recent years. Japan made significant reductions in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions following the oil shocks of the 1970s, but progress plateaued after the 2000s and declined further after the Fukushima disaster in 2011. In contrast, France has become a leading advocate for ecological issues in Europe, particularly following the Grenelle Environment Forum in 2007, which harmonized ecological constraints with innovation. France’s role in climate leadership was further solidified with the adoption of the Paris Agreement in 2015.

This course critically analyzes the environmental and climate change policies of France and Japan, with a specific focus on energy transitions across various sectors, including civil society, businesses and organizations, and local, national, and supranational governments.

Objectives:
This course examines the long-term perspectives of environmental and climate change policies in France and Japan, focusing on historical developments, current challenges, and future prospects. Drawing on sources in French, English, and Japanese, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of the policies, strategies, and frameworks implemented to address environmental and climate change issues. The course also develops students’ analytical skills by comparing the approaches and effectiveness of environmental and climate change policies in France and Japan. Additionally, it enhances communication skills through active participation, discussions, and the exchange of ideas on contemporary environmental and climate change challenges.

This course, a Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) program, is conducted in French and English. It aims to deepen students' understanding of the French language and provide insights into key aspects of French culture and politics. Emphasizing the interconnection between language and content, the course engages students in discussions about the role of public debate in French political processes. Students will analyze French audiovisual and written materials to examine the institutionalization of public debates, focusing on current social and environmental issues like climate change and policy development. The course includes interactive components such as role-playing games to improve public speaking and writing skills. It is designed for students with an intermediate French proficiency (B1-B2) and will be delivered in both French and English, using French instructional materials. This course is particularly beneficial for those preparing for a study-abroad experience in a French-speaking country.

Objectives:
The main objectives of this course are to enable students to:

Enhance understanding and reading proficiency in the French language.

Develop a comprehensive knowledge of contemporary French culture and politics.

Improve public speaking and writing skills, utilizing role-playing games and presentations.

Strengthen French language proficiency through active participation in group discussions.

Acquire insights into the role of public debates in French politics and their contemporary applications.

This course is designed as a preparation for studying abroad in German-speaking countries. Students will get to know and practice a variety of text types and communicative genres that are crucial for everyday life and studying at a University in Germany, Austria or Switzerland. We will practice communicative situations like taking care of administrative requirements, looking for an apartment, communicating with university staff or coordinating group assignments with fellow students. The course also covers intercultural challenges like different ways of communicating politeness and positive and negative emotions or needs.

Objectives:
The objective of this course is to prepare students for their year abroad in a German-speaking country and practice important communicative and social situations.

This course offers an introduction to key questions related to the political system of contemporary France. It examines French political ideas and history from the Enlightenment to the present day, the transformation of political parties from the Fourth to the Fifth Republic, and France’s distinctive place within the European Union. The class will also examine how participation, alongside the evolving roles of the state and citizens, is redefining contemporary democratic norms and reshaping political institutions.

Objectives:
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:

・Understand the meaning and evolution of key political concepts: liberty, equality, fraternity, secularism, liberalism/socialism,

・Be knowledgeable about French political history from the 19th century to nowadays: the Consulate, the Empire, the Bourbon Restoration/ July Monarchy, and the Fourth and Fifth Republic,

・Know France’s key political institutions and contemporary democratic innovations, including the role of the National Assembly, the President and Ministers, the Constitutional Council, as well as the CESE and recent citizens’ conventions,

・Become familiar with contemporary debates in political science, e.g. decentralization versus centralization, the role of countries in shaping EU’s policies, the dynamics of the partisanship and electorate,

・Develop oral and written expression, and reading comprehension in French, through authentic materials,

・Practice French in real-life situations, through debates, simulations, quiz, role-plays.

This course examines the various ways political ideas are expressed within the French and francophone tradition. It explores how the French language shapes political discourse, communicates information and concepts, and as a tool for persuasion and the expression of conflict.

Each class is centered on the close analysis of a short excerpt, selected from a diverse range of materials, such as speeches, reports, podcasts, videos, songs, social science texts, and newspaper articles.

The course includes practical exercises to help students think critically, improve academic writing, and learn methods of analysis that are useful in academic contexts.

Objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

・Improve written and spoken French

・Learn new vocabulary and expressions

・Practice academic writing and text analysis

・Develop critical thinking skills

・Understand key political concepts

・Be familiar with French politics, history, and culture.

Important note: Intermediate knowledge of German is required for this class as material and readings will be (partly) in German.

This seminar examines memory culture and memory politics in Germany after 1945, from early postwar narratives of rupture and responsibility to evolving public debates about remembrance. We study theoretical frameworks of collective and cultural memory, philosophical reflections on “Aufarbeitung,” and the interplay of state policy, civil society, law, education, and media. Topics include memorial practices, museums and commemorative sites, generational change, contested narratives, and the ethics of remembrance. Attention is given to politicization by contemporary actors, transnational influences, and postcolonial critiques. Students engage in critical reading, source analysis, and project work connecting historical interpretation with present day memory discourses.

Objectives:
Students will learn about theories of memory, analyze policies, media discourse, and material form memorial sites. They will engage with political and ethical debates and do analyses, as well as train reflective argumentation skills.

Important note: Knowledge of German is required for this class. Participants should have a Level of A2 or higher (or have finished German 3 or Intensive German 2 at SILS).

In this class student will get an overview of German history of migration since 1945 and the according discourses, policies, conflicts and cultural as well as societal developments. We will discuss the political economy of labor migration (in the FRG as well as the former GDR), the different waves of anti-migration politics, the paradigms of “assimilation”,“integration”, and “post-migration society”, and discourses and imaginaries connected to the demography of the German population. The syllabus will consist of excerpts from literary texts, scholarly publications as well as newspaper articles and political speeches.

Objectives:
Apart from an overview of German migration history, students will practice their reading comprehension in German across different text genres. The class will therefore not only deepen knowledge about German history and society but also teach important reading strategies.

Thisintermediate level seminar explores the dynamic world of youth culture andyouth language in contemporary Germany. Students will examine how young peoplein Germany express identity, resistance, and belonging through language, media,music, fashion, across different historical contexts, including the studentmovements of the 1960s, punk and hip-hop subcultures, post-reunification youth,and contemporary digital communities. Students will engage with authenticmaterials, including video clips, social media content, and interviews,alongside scholarly texts.

Objectives:
To deepen students' understanding of how youth language and culture reflect and shape social change in Germany, while fostering critical and intercultural perspectives on identity and communication.

This course explores key contributions to democratic theory within the twentieth-century Francophone intellectual tradition. It examines how French-speaking thinkers have conceptualized democracy through key themes such as ideology, conflict, representation, recognition, and compromise and how they understood the social contract. The course engages with a wide range of contemporary political philosophers, and considers contemporary critiques and possible future directions of democracy. It encourages a critical examination of competing conceptions of democracy and their relevance for addressing new political challenges.

Requirement: minimum B2 level in French.

Objectives:
By the end of the module, students should be able to:

- Identify and explain the key concepts developed by twentieth-century political French-speaking theorists and philosophers,

- Situate philosophical arguments within their historical and political contexts,

- Analyze complex philosophical texts and arguments in oral and written form,

- Compare competing models of democracy and their assumptions,

- Evaluate the distinct contributions of Francophone democratic thought to political philosophy and political theory,

- Understand a significant portion of the modern continental political philosophy landscape and democratic theory debates.

This class explores the ethics of public office as a central political issue sitting at the intersection of political theory, the history of political thought, democratic practice, and institutional design. The course provides an overview of contemporary debates in political ethics through a comparative analysis of French and American political traditions in order to trace the historical roots of their distinct political-ethical cultures and highlight contrasting conceptions of public responsibility, political representation and democratic legitimacy.

Objectives:
By the end of the course, students will:

- Understand major past and present theories of political ethics, as well as ongoing debates within democratic theory scholarship,

- Draw comparisons between American and French political thought on questions of political ethics,

- Be familiar with key legal and philosophical debates on integrity, accountability, and corruption in democratic institutions,

- Connect the history of political and intellectual thought in France and the United States, with current debates in political ethics and institutional reform,

- Critically analyze normative arguments concerning democracy and its contemporary challenges,

- Develop strong research, analytical and argumentative skills in both oral and written forms.

Democracyis under pressure the world over and Germany is no exception. The rise of thefar-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) has been accompanied by a growingnormalization of anti-migration rhetoric, disregard of democratic norms andgrowing xenophobia. At the same time, conservative and center parties seem totake over politics and rhetoric from the far right. In this class, we willapproach the challenges of growing authoritarianism and populism in Germanyfrom different perspectives, focusing on communicative strategies and languageuse in far-right milieus. We will also discuss options and possibilities ofdemocratic counter speech and democratic action. The class will be taughtmostly in German with English as an auxiliary language.

Objectives:
The objective is to give students an overview of the challenges of authoritarianism and populism for liberal democracies, especially Germany. The course also enables them to think about their own democratic agency.

Important note: This advanced class will be held in German with English as an auxiliary language. Students are expected to participate in the discussion and read in German.

This course will give an overview of the role of language during National Socialism in Germany (1933 – 1945). We will analyze the propagandistic use of language during the Nazi Party’s rise to power, its use of language as a tool to submit the public and its function and perversion during the war and the justification of the holocaust. The class will also deal with the after-life of fascism in the German lexicon and the discourses on education and memory politics after 1945. Due to the current rise of fascist ideology, we will also look into new theories of fascisms and discuss ways to counter fascist ideology.

Objectives:
The class aims at giving students an overview of the historic period of National Socialism and its after-life as well as its current renaissance in far-right ideology and conservative politics. The specific focus is on language use but topics like education and memory politics will also be thematized.

This advanced course offers a comprehensive examination of women's engagement in politics worldwide, with a primary focus on the French context. Through a nuanced and comparative lens, we explore the complex dynamics surrounding women's participation in political spheres. We critically analyze the multifaceted challenges that women encounter in their pursuit of political power and decision-making roles but also in influencing political and intellectual debates. Drawing on extensive research and scholarly works, we investigate the historical, social, and political factors that have shaped women's involvement in politics from a global perspective.

Objectives:
Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of the global landscape of women's political participation, delving into an examination of the barriers and challenges encountered by women in different regions. They will analyze the historical context and societal factors that have contributed to the persistent gender disparities in political leadership, with a first focus on France serving as a case study. Additionally, students will critically evaluate the impact of legal frameworks, electoral systems, and institutional mechanisms on women's political representation, while assessing the effectiveness of various strategies employed to promote gender parity. By examining the experiences and challenges of historical female political figures, and by exploring their contributions to shaping political landscapes, we will compare and contrast the role of appointed versus elected women in political positions, critically assessing the barriers and opportunities for women in both contexts. Moreover, students will investigate international case studies, such as Japan, Middle East, Latin American, and Southeast Asia to gain a broader understanding of diverse approaches to women's political empowerment, exploring the factors contributing to varying levels of women's political representation across different contexts. Students will engage in advanced analysis of theoretical frameworks and scholarly debates surrounding gender and politics and will be encouraged to develop critical thinking and independent research through assigned readings, active participation in class discussions, and the completion of research projects.

This seminar is designed for students with an advanced level in French and interested in deepening their understanding of International Communication in a French perspective.

The seminar revolves around the reading of the book "Savons-nous vraiment parler? Du contrat linguistique comme contrat social" (see Textbook).

The seminar will be conducted in French (the textbook is written in French), but in-class discussions may also be conducted in English when necessary.

Students may choose to write their graduation thesis in French or in English with a long abstract in French.
Former seminar students have written theses about French/Japanese comparative themes such as: Perception of foreigners; University degrees and job-hunting; Religious education and laïcité in primary education; Students, baito and petit boulot; Parisian and Tokyoite stereotypes; Velib and Community cycle; Colour symbolism for web design; Luxury brands; The notion of work and the case of marketing; Convenience stores and supérettes; Descendants of immigrants; Baby-sitting systems; Lipsticks; MacCafé; Tourism and Omotenashi; Fashion and oshare; Perception of happiness; Air France vs JAL commercials; The perception of strikes; Parental leaves; etc.

On a more linguistic level, past themes include: Usage of the adjective "zen" in French; The future of French education in Japan; Linguistic policies in France and Singapore; Study-abroad and linguistic identities; Differences between French and Quebec French, etc.

Former seminar students have pursued their academic studies in MA programmes in prestigious institutions (Sciences Po Paris, Geneva Graduate Institute; ENS Ulm Paris, Aix-Marseille University, HEC Paris, TUFS, Waseda) as well as in PhD programmes (France, Germany) and found work in a variety of companies and institutions in Japan and abroad (some of them requiring French abilities, e.g. Minisitry of Foreign Affairs).

Objectives:
Objectives for students:

1) deepen their understanding of the French language and culture.

2) acquire general skills in terms of academic project planning (general methodology in Human and Social Sciences - in French SHS).

3) develop a sense of internationalization-oriented maturity, academic autonomy, and task-based cooperation around the topic of International (and National) Communication from a French perspective

The ドイツゼミ　is the intellectual hub for all students interested in research on the language, culture, society and history of the German speaking countries and areas. Depending on the research interests of students, we jointly decide on the agenda for each semester.

Among the topics covered in past semesters are:
- Germany's handling of the pandemic and Angela Merkel's communication during the crisis in comparison with other world leaders
- language and society in Nazi Germany
- refugees, migration and challenges for the education system
- gentrification in urban spaces
- framing in political communication
- social inequality in Germany and Japan
- deitary habits, vegetarianism and veganism in Germany and Japan
- the German health system and its digital transformation

We drink handground coffee and enjoy tons of sweets while engaging in scientific discussions. Other activities include out-of-classroom teaching, film screenings, cultural activities and a gasshuku in the summer.

The instructor is aware, that the German level of students, who have not (yet) spent their time abroad in Germany, cannot be at a high level. We will therefore adjust the language policy in the ドイツゼミ to your skills and needs.

Objectives:
This course will deepen not only the knowledge of the German language and society, but also the insight into a variety of features of modern Germany.

This seminar is designed for those students who have an interest in Italy and European history. Besides the historical study, we will discuss various topics in Italy (art, literature, architecture, city planning, language, etc.). This seminar is conducted in the form of a research seminar, the ultimate aim of which is to write a senior thesis. Each student chooses their own topic, gives a presentation, and makes a discussion to improve their studies.

Objectives:
By the end of this seminar, students are expected to:

- develop an awareness of historical or Italian study

- deepen their knowledge about each topic, based on academic research ability

- acquire essential skills for writing a senior paper

This course focuses on how ancient Rome was used and revived in the history of Italy. The Colosseum (originally named the Flavian Amphitheater) was inaugurated in 80 CE, and from this time on, this huge monument stands in the city of Rome and has captured the attention of residents and travelers alike due to its scale. Various individuals have left impressions and opinions about the Colosseum through books, letters, and diaries, allowing us to trace the transformation of its image over time.
To analyze this issue, firstly, we will explore the role and function of the Colosseum in Ancient Rome. This analysis will enable us to deepen our understanding of ancient society. Subsequently, we will examine the diverse images the Colosseum assumed in later periods. In some instances, the Colosseum presents unexpected faces, closely linked to historical assumptions about ancient Rome in each era. Through this process, we will analyze the transformation of the memory of the Colosseum, seeking to understand how Italian society used ancient Rome to solve its problems. This examination prompts us to consider how our current image of the past has evolved.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to:

- develop an awareness of Italian history and culture

- demonstrate a critical awareness of the relationship between the past and contemporary society

- understand how the historical tradition was made and how it was used

In this course, we will study the impact of social movements on the politics and culture of Germany. Social movements are defined as networks of organizations or groups of individuals that advocate for, resist, or aim for undoing political and cultural change. By analyzing the conditions under which social movements occurred in the German contemporary history and their repercussions since World War II, we will gain a deeper understanding of how Germany has developed into a liberal democracy.

Objectives:
At the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Define what a social movement is.

• Explain, with historical examples, when and why social movements occur, how they organize, what movements do, and who participates.

• Understand, how social change and social movements relate.

• Explain, how social movements like the student movement of the 1960s, the women's movement, the lesbian and gay movement, the environmental movement, the alter-globalization movement, but also the neo-Nazi contributed to political and cultural change in the history of Germany.

Islam is currently the world's second-largest religion, following Christianity, with Muslims (adherents of Islam) comprising nearly one-fourth of the global population. Due to its faster growth rate compared to Christianity, Islam is expected to become the world's largest religion in the near future.

Although Islam originated in the seventh-century Arabian Peninsula, the majority of Muslims today live outside the Arab region. The Asia-Pacific region is home to the largest Muslim-majority countries, including Indonesia, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. Even in Japan, where Muslims are a minority, there are around 230,000 adherents, underscoring the importance of understanding Islam in the contemporary world.

The course will cover a broad range of topics, including the geographic distribution of Muslims, the diversity within Islam, the Abrahamic religions, pre-Islamic Arabia, the life of Prophet Muhammad and the origins of Islam, fundamental beliefs and practices, the Quran and Hadith, Islamic celebrations and daily life, Islamic law, religious scholars (ulama) and theological seminaries (madrasas), sectarian differences (Sunni and Shia), and Sufism (Islamic mysticism). While recognizing the rich diversity of Islamic practices, the course will focus on the core beliefs and obligatory practices universally accepted by Muslims across different regions. By exploring these topics, students will gain insights into the common denominators that unite Muslims globally, fostering a deeper understanding of Islam's role in today's world.

As this course will be conducted in person, regular attendance is mandatory for all students. Please note that there will be no online distribution or simultaneous virtual sessions available.

Objectives:
The course aims to achieve the following objectives:

1. Develop an understanding of Islam's core beliefs, practices, and historical foundations.

2. Gain familiarity with key terms commonly used in Islam.

3. Understand the defining features of Islamic culture.

In this course, guided by a native instructor, students will develop practical skills in basic Arabic grammar, conversation, reading, and writing, along with an understanding of cultural contexts.

Grammar study covers the Arabic script and spelling, demonstrative, personal, and relative pronouns, as well as noun gender and singular, dual, and plural forms.

Students will also learn essential vocabulary and expressions for daily communication—such as greetings and thanks—while exploring everyday life, literature, art, traditions, and religious culture in the Arab world.

Through these topics, they will gain a well-rounded understanding of the Arabic language and culture.

Although Arabic is the primary language of instruction, communication with the instructor in English is also possible.

Objectives:
1. Acquisition of the basic knowledge of Arabic （system of grammar, mode and pronunciation）

2. Acquisition of writing, conversation, listening and reading skills and acquaintance with the basic Arabic grammar.

3. Gain familiarity with various elements of Arab culture

This course aims to deepen students' understanding of the Middle East by exploring key concepts and theories that illuminate the formation of states, the unique features of political systems, and the socio-economic challenges faced by the region's inhabitants, particularly the youth, in contemporary times.

The course will cover topics such as state formation, colonialism, authoritarianism, rentier states, clientelism, monarchies, and republics, as well as the Arab uprisings, with the goal of understanding the characteristics of Middle Eastern states. To analyze the complex challenges confronting Middle Eastern societies, we will examine issues like demographic transition, the youth bulge, the expansion of higher education, academic credentialism, graduate unemployment, brain drain, waithood, gender and Islam, marriage and divorce, and the growing discontent among youth. Through the assigned readings, students will develop the skills necessary to analyze these issues from multiple perspectives, leading to a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of the Middle East.

As this course will be conducted in person, regular attendance is mandatory for all students. Please note that there will be no online distribution or simultaneous virtual sessions available.

Objectives:
This course aims to achieve the following goals:

1. Develop an understanding of the historical origins and evolution of modern states in the Middle East.

2. Acquire useful conceptual frameworks for effectively assessing the characteristics of political regimes and comparing the governing systems of Middle Eastern countries.

3. Become familiar with concepts and theories relevant to analyzing the challenges and concerns faced by people in the region, particularly the younger generation, and apply these frameworks to the study of Middle Eastern societies.

This course aims to assist students in comprehending the dynamics of contemporary Islamic movements in the Middle East and South Asia, with a focus on their diverse manifestations. The expansion of Islam across different geographical regions has led to a variety of interpretations among Muslims. However, Muslims in today's globalized world face common challenges, such as navigating modernity and dealing with the overwhelming political, economic, and cultural dominance of the West. As a response to these unprecedented challenges, various types of Islamic resurgence movements have emerged.
Notably, a significant event occurred in Iran, where the Western-oriented dictatorial monarchy was overthrown through the 1979 revolution, leading to the establishment of the “guardianship of the jurist.” The success of the Islamic revolution in Iran not only inspired Shiite populations in Arab countries but also had an impact on South Asia. Additionally, both political and non-political Islamic revivalist activities have garnered considerable support within Sunni Islamic societies. The Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt, for instance, has gained widespread backing from intellectuals and the general populace.
Of particular concern in South Asia are the escalating sectarian conflicts, which have facilitated the establishment of various militant groups in the region. This course provides students with an opportunity to comprehend the complexities surrounding contemporary Islamic societies by exploring a wide range of resurgent movements.

Objectives:
1. Deepen understanding of the distinctive features and dynamics of contemporary Islamic movements.

2. Develop the ability to analyze issues from diverse perspectives.

3. Foster a comprehensive understanding of the intricate and multifaceted nature of the challenges in the Middle East and South Asia.

This seminar is specifically designed for students with a keen interest in contemporary political, social, religious, and cultural issues in the Middle East and South Asia. Its primary objective is to provide participants with a comprehensive understanding of these topics through engaging with relevant literature and various materials. To ensure a solid foundation for active participation, students are required to have successfully completed at least one course on the Middle East or Islam at Waseda University or during their study abroad.
Throughout the seminar, we will explore a wide range of subjects, including the relationship between state and religion, Islamic movements, protest movements, radicalism, ethnoreligious minorities, social change and education, urbanization, secularization, youth and employment, youth culture, gender and Islam, international migration, brain drain, and more.
Students will learn how to conduct research on a topic of their choice and present their findings. They will be encouraged to deepen their understanding through class discussions. Ultimately, students will be required to culminate their research in a graduation thesis. Therefore, students enrolling in the seminar must demonstrate a strong commitment to completing a graduation thesis.
As this course will be conducted in person, students are required to attend every class without exception.

Objectives:
The final goals of this course for third-year students are as follows:

1. Broaden knowledge of contemporary Middle Eastern and South Asian politics and society through extensive reading.

2. Enhance the ability to examine issues from various perspectives.

3. Deepen the students' understanding of the complexity of the issues.

For fourth-year students, the final goals are as follows:

1. Encourage students to develop the ability to think independently.

2. Learn how to select a research topic, identify a problem, and discuss it for their thesis.

3. Master the skills necessary for thesis writing, including conducting a literature review, creating footnotes, as well as employing proper citation and referencing

This course is designed to explore contemporary Korean history at the introductory level. After its liberation from Japan in 1945, Korea sought to build a new modern state, but suffered from division and the Korean War. North and South Korea were at odds with each other even as they sought reunification, and South Korea sought economic growth and modernization but struggled with democratization. To understand South Korea today, it is instructive to look at the historical development of a post-colonial underdeveloped country. Audio-visual and multimedia educational materials will be used to enhance the understanding of Korean history.

Objectives:
The course is designed to help students understand the process and major events of Korea's contemporary history in chronological order. In doing so, it develops their ability to understand contemporary Korean history from a humanistic perspective and promotes sensitivity to the history and culture of other countries as well as multicultural communication skill.

This course is designed to explore contemporary Koreanhistory at the introductory level. Since its liberation from Japan, Korea hasexperienced division, war, military dictatorship, and democratization. Korean society and the people within it haveendured, resisted, and united to overcome suffering and rapid change. To betterunderstand Korea today, this course will focus on the people and societies ofKorea's post-1945 history. Through lectures using video and historical teachingmaterials, students will have the opportunity to present on key topics.

Objectives:
The course is designed to help students understand Korea's contemporary history through some key figures, groups, and their experiences. In doing so, it develops their ability to understand contemporary Korean history from a humanistic perspective and promotes sensitivity to the history and culture of other countries as well as multicultural communication skills.

This course is designed to explore various social and cultural issues in Korea through reading and discussing Korean-language books and articles published in contemporary Korea on a variety of topics and fields, and to improve Korean language skills at the academic level. As in other countries, some articles and books from Korea are translated from other languages, so the course also includes this, and it includes essays, popular and academic texts, and testimonies as well. All course materials are in Korean.

Objectives:
This course is designed to provide undergraduate students with a broad overview of various central problems in the humanities in Korea. It aims to acquaint students with the significance and methodology of various disciplines in the humanities. The goal of this course is to provide students with interdisciplinary learning opportunities through collaborative presentations and discussions of assigned books and texts, and to promote multicultural and multilateral learning.

This course is a Content and Language Integrated Learning course (CLIL) in English and Korean to explore drastic changes and various figures' lives, events and movements from late Joseon, colonial Korea to divided Korea with regional, global, and critical perspectives. Modern and contemporary Korea has been shaped not by temporal and spatial disconnections, but by internal and international relations with its surroundings. Rather than approaching various cases and events in modern/contemporary Korean history solely from an accumulation of knowledge, this lecture is preferred to introduce and discuss various historical perspectives and ideas. This course is based on history textbook written by East Asian scholars with the aim of overcoming historical conflicts in East Asia and promoting integration and peace. Most of the reading material is in English, with a few exceptions.

Objectives:
The purpose of this course is both to improve students’ language skills to communicate academic ideas in Korean and to analyze the topic of international relations regarding East Asia. The instructor leads the students comprehending the topics, approaches, and contentions with critical perspective. Finally, students can improve their ability to express their creative opinions on each topic of the class in Korean.

This course is a Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) course in English and Korean to explore Korean history in the 20th century with a focus on disasters, accidents, and crises. Disasters, accidents, and crises are not just singular, isolated events, but are deeply related to historical, structural issues, and are not just the problems of one country, but are deeply related to changes in world history. In the 20th century, the world, including Korea, experienced imperialism, colonization and war, and after many countries were liberated, they had to go through the Cold War and so on. In this regard, we will cover various disasters, accidents and crises in Korea before achieving rapid capitalist industrialization and democratization. Class lectures and communication will be mostly in Korean, with readings in both English and Korean to achieve the goal of the CLIL course.

Objectives:
The purpose of this course is both to improve students’ language skills to communicate academic ideas in Korean and to analyze the topic of disasters, accidents, and crises regarding Korean history. The instructor leads the students comprehending the topics, approaches, and contentions with a critical perspective. Finally, students can improve their ability to express their creative, detailed opinions on each topic of the class in Korean.

Thiscourse is designed to explore the diverse nature of Korean society and improveacademic-level Korean language skills by reading and discussing contemporaryKorean books and articles on assigned topics. Lectures will include oraltestimonies, essays, and academic papers on topics such as the multiculturalnature of Korean society, various conflicts, social and culturaldiscrimination, and inequality.
The course will be conducted in English and Korean.

Objectives:
This course aims to provide undergraduate students with a broad overview of various key issues in the Korean humanities. It does so by providing students with interdisciplinary learning opportunities through presentations and discussions of assigned books and texts, and by promoting multicultural and multifaceted learning. It also seeks to develop students' academic-level Korean writing skills by requiring them to write a paper in Korean on a specific topic of their choice.

This course is a Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) course in English and Korean to examine how Korean intellectuals and citizens responded to various political, economic, social, and cultural issues after liberation in 1945, and to research and present the thought/practice of selected major figures or groups in Korea and abroad. The intellectual history course deals not only with contemporary Korean history itself, but also with the cultural Cold War, the Korean War, modernization theory, democratic movement ideas etc. in a global context. Most of the readings will be in English, with a few exceptions. Class lectures and communication will be mostly in Korean, with readings in both English and Korean to achieve the goal of the CLIL course.

Objectives:
The purpose of this course is both to improve students’ language skills to communicate academic ideas in Korean and to analyze the topic of contemporary Korean history from the perspective of intellectual history. The instructor leads the students comprehending the topics, approaches, and contentions with critical perspective. Finally, students can improve their ability to express their critical, creative opinions on each topic of the class in Korean.

This course is a Content and Language IntegratedLearning (CLIL) course in English and Korean to explore recent literature inKorean Studies. The scope of Korean Studies is constantly expanding, and wewill cover topics such as the changing functions and roles of universities andintellectuals in the 20th century, discourses and practices surrounding humanrights, Cold War social sciences, and minorities in Korea. This course willallow you to understand the current features of research in Korean Studies aswell as its relevance and uniqueness to the foreign research literature. Classlectures and communication will be mostly in Korean, with readings in bothEnglish and Korean to achieve the goal of a CLIL course.

Objectives:
The purpose of this course is both to improve students’ language skills to communicate academic ideas in Korean and to analyze the selected topic of Korean studies. The instructor leads the students comprehending the topics, approaches, and contentions with a critical perspective. Finally, students can improve their ability to express their creative, detailed opinions on each topic of the class in Korean.

※Face-to-Face Delivery
This advanced seminar is intended for students who have a keen interest in cities, architecture, public spaces and urban life in general. Despite representing only about 2% of the geographic space, cities accommodate currently over 55% of the global population, produce 80% of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, consume 75% of the world's energy and 80% of its resources. On the other hand urban areas also generate 93% of the world's patented inventions. City governments face a wide range of challenges: they need to produce prosperity and innovations but also well-being and sustainability. Cities are to be green and resilient but also culturally vibrant. On top of this, cities are integration machines that integrate growing populations from different ethnic, religious, cultural, and socio-economic backgrounds. To cope with these pressing issues, change makers are not only needed in ministries and city halls but also in the business world, in non-profits, independent consultancies, or in academia. This seminar, will provide you with a first step to become an urban change maker.

This 3-semester long advanced seminar offers students the opportunity to sharpen their understanding about urbanisation issues, urban governance, place-making, and the social production of space. In this course students develop an own, individualised urban studies or urbanism-related research project from an initial research proposal (1rst semester), over an annotated bibliography (2nd semester), a midterm paper (2nd semester), and conclude the course in the 3rd semester with a full graduation thesis.

Possible research subjects may be sustainability transitions, creative neighbourhoods and social innovators, new urban commons, community resilience, participatory place-making, social construction of space, contestations of public space, environmental and economic gentrification among other topics that help us to understand how socio-cultural, historical, economic and political aspects influence the emergence of cities and communities in an era that Neil Brenner and Christian Schmid have identified as "planetary urbanisation". In fact, students are encouraged to approach the subject 'city' from any disciplinary angle, be it social, cultural, historical, environmental, economic, or artistic.
Students are expected to begin the work on their graduation theses at an early stage in this seminar. They will present their own work on a regular basis, and participate actively in the discussion of the work presented by other members of the class. Class room sessions will be supplemented with different urban walks, during which students will learn about different urbanisation issues and different socio-spatial settings. The learning culture of the seminar is similar to that found at graduate school level, with all members, including the instructor, being active co-learners. This seminar will enable students to enter urbanism and urban planning related graduate programs and only highly dedicated students should consider applying.

For students who take this Zemi in the first (of three) semesters the focus will be on exploring different urban settings in Tokyo and familiarise themselves with urban studies research methods. Students will present the impressions of their urban walks as visual essays in class. At the end of the first semester a first draft proposal for their graduation research will be completed.
Students for whom this is the third semester of the Zemi will solely concentrate on the writing of their graduation thesis.
The first period will be reserved for the first semester Zemi students and the following period will be used for presentations and discussions of the graduation research projects of third semester students.

Objectives:
In this seminar students will ...

(1) ... develop an own self-selected research project that culminates in a full-fledged graduation thesis,

(2) ... acquire substantial knowledge about complex, interrelated urban issues through engaged in-class discussions and urban walks,

(3) ... improve their academic writing skills and hone their presentation skills,

(4) ... learn about research methods, and techniques to undertake an own urban research project,

(5) ... build an important stepping stone that will enable students to enter urbanism, urban planning, environmental studies related graduate programs at top international universities.

Culture is very much a combination of lifestyle and art. This course will explore the development and transition of Japanese aesthetic in lifestyle from prehistoric Jomon Period all the way to today, with special emphasis on the crafts and arts of Edo, Meiji, Taisho and Showa eras. In Japan, there are fine arts, fine crafts, Mingei (the people’s arts and crafts) and design. We will examine the trends in art and lifestyle from ancient times, how traditional crafts and arts appeared in art history, and how Japanese arts and lifestyle transformed with the industrial revolution during the Meiji Era with a newly applied idea of “fine arts”, followed by the emergence of the philosophy of Mingei.We will finish by discussing how art and crafts influence our everyday lifestyle, what it means to us today, and what you think will happen in the future.Classes are all face-to-face. Attendance and participation is invaluable. You will get an experience that will last a lifetime.

In an extreme case there is need to hold classes remotely, you will be notified at least one week in advance and it will only be conducted within a maximum of five times.

Objectives:
This course aims to gain an understanding of the transition of Japanese aesthetics and lifestyle throughout history -- from prehistoric times, all the way to today – especially as seen in the Japanese arts and crafts. We will learn about the theory of “Mingei”, and see if the theory of Mingei still thrives today. In order to discuss “beauty”, besides class lectures, students are given a rare opportunity to also see and appreciate real works in museums and galleries. No previous knowledge is required, however commitment and consistent class attendance are imperative. Art is a very physical expression, thus physical attendance in class and at designated venues are invaluable in understanding the course. Come prepared to class. Active participation and class contribution required. You must be on time, no late paper accepted, all conditions equal for every student, individual exceptions not accepted. This is a class where each student is expected to find his or her own universal meaning of art and lifestyle through the study of the past, present and future of art and culture in Japan.

This course introduces selected Japanese masterpieces in the hand-scroll (emaki 絵巻) format from the late-classical and medieval periods, while referencing other types of narrative imagery. The course considers how scholars approach these images from a variety of perspectives, how historical developments shape images and are reshaped by them, and visual storytelling techniques.

Classes will be conducted in person only.

Objectives:
Students will be introduced to masterpieces of Japanese painting and their historical contexts. They will also examine and experiment with strategies for telling stories with images.

This class surveys premodern Japanese art, looking at painting, sculpture, architecture, and material culture--especially that which pertains to Buddhism, kami worship, and Buddha-kami combinatory practices.

Classes will be conducted in person only.

Objectives:
To study Japanese sacred art in its social and historical contexts.

The lectures on this course are basically face-to-face lectures,except for the first and final days. *Course orientation on the first day and the introductory lecture will be conducted via video on demand (VOD) to accommodate late arrivals of third-round registrants.

In addition to regular classroomlectures, there will be two museum tours. And one workshop will be held in the classroom to allow students to see, touch, and experience painting materialssuch as ink, pigments, and special papers (parchment, vellum, and Japanesepaper). If there are many registrants, instead of a　workshop for all registrants, it will be replaced with a lecture on traditional art materials and a petite exhibition of actual art materials. Only those whowish to participate will be able to experience calligraphy using traditional tools and ink.

This course is designed to introduce students to the mutually influential art of the East and the West. This semester will again consist of two parts, the first half of which will focus on Shosoin Treasures and Buddhist Art of Todaiji Temple. The second objective of this part is to interest each student in the origins of traditional designs and symbols in Japanese art.

The second half of the course will cover a different topic each time. For example, we will focus on the visualization of the "Arabian Nights" and consider Orientalism andJaponisme in art. We will also examine manuscript illustrations from the Islamic world and Japanese picture scrolls. This semester, we will hold one discussion session focused on mountain landscape paintings.

** The schedule of classroom lectures and museum visits will be explained in detail in the first section.

Objectives:
In the first half of this course, students will understand the basic framework of traditional Japanese designs and craft techniques seen in the Shosoin treasures and acquire basic knowledge of Japanese Buddhist art associated with Todaiji Temple, thereby examining the exchange of ancient art via the Silk Road.

The latter half focuses on manuscript illustrations. However, the objective extends beyond book illustrations to utilize familiar iconographic expressions, such as ceramic decorations, to understand the mutual influence between Western, Eastern, and Middle Eastern painting.

Throughout the course, the objective is to cultivate the habit of carefully observing works of art from a global perspective and to develop an interest in the techniques used in works of art and the historical background of their design.

The course aims to introduce what is arguably the most complex product of society and Japanese society in particular — the city, and to concentrate on the city of Tokyo.

Our study will encompass a range of issues concerning the city, and the complex consequences of urban developments under modern and contemporary conditions. We will observe how the city has defined, and was in itself defined by, a particular reality at a particular time, beginning in Edo period and concluding in the present. Such an approach emphasizes a need to examine the external relations of the city with context, and particularly relate to its social, cultural and political circumstances. Thus, we will look at the creation and recreation of the city’s physical texture, at architecture, urban landscape, infrastructure and technology, and at the same time observe the city as a social product determined by everyday life and habitual practices, organization of the immediate surrounding, personal rites and the micro-politics of life in the city. In the same manner, we will look at buildings and neighborhoods per se, as a material construct guided by geometry and legal code, but at the same time recognize how the pragmatics of this built environment interrelate with cultural systems such as literature and film, and thus examine the mechanisms that relate the city to culture. Also, we will see how the city is not merely a reflection or expression of politics, but rather an intricate political apparatus in and of itself, influencing relationships and encouraging change.

There are two consecutive class sessions every week. Usually, there will be a lecture at the first session, and the second lecture period will be used for class discussions, screening of films and videos, visiting lectures, or field trips. In taking the classroom outside the campus, we will use the benefit of the Tokyo locality to be in and see the subjects of our study. These activities are equally important to the class lectures and should be used to further practice critical thinking and develop skills for analyzing the built city.

The course has no prerequisites. Besides an interest in the course’s subjects, students are not required to have any prior knowledge of Tokyo, architecture, art and/or other disciplines of urban studies.

Objectives:
As a whole, the course aims to discuss central themes emerging from the city of Tokyo. It aims to acquaint students with detailed knowledge about the modern and contemporary histories of the city, and an ability to position this knowledge in a range of discursive and theoretical frameworks.

This class offers an introduction to film studieswith particular emphasis on film analysis. It covers major aspects of cinematicform such as mise-en-scène, cinematography,editing, and sound. By examining films ranging from Classical Hollywood torecent anime smash hits with key concepts in film studies, we consider howfilms organize cinematic form both in classical narrative films and alternativestyles.

Objectives:
Students will acquire basic knowledge of key concepts in film studies, become able to analyze films by using terms in film studies, and learn how to engage with the current discussion in film studies.

This is an introductory astronomy course to study general principles and fundamental facts of astronomy. The main topics covered in the course are the universe, galaxies, stars and planets.

This course will train students for studies in U.S. politics, law and history. The textbook provides a concise but sophisticated view of U.S. history as seen from the perspective of constitutional politics. The same forces and institutions reappear in its historical evolution up to today. As such, close reading and discussion of this text will deepen students’ analytical skills—their ability to recognize dynamics and patterns behind a given phenomenon.Also, since this will be the first seminar students will be taking at SILS, the instructor will from time-to-time set aside time to provide general advising to prepare students for their academic enrichment at the program, including towards their study abroad year.

Objectives:
Students will:

1) Be able to analyze U.S. society through the perspective of constitutional politics.

2) Be able to identify key ideas, perspectives and patterns from a sophisticated academic text.

3) Be able to articulate their own views; deepen their discussion and ask relevant questions over key issues in U.S. constitutional politics, with the knowledge and understanding of the social, political, and historical context of such issues.

4) Acquire key skills, as discussed above, that will prepare them for their academic enrichment at SILS, including the study abroad program.
