This seminar provides an opportunity for students to think about current issues in the society they live in and also to practice basic academic skills.

Students are expected and required to have read and understood the assigned reading before class, and, if necessary, obtain information from other sources (e.g. books, magazine, newspaper articles and websites). They are required to participate in discussion and are expected to give oral presentations in class, demonstrating their understanding of written texts, finding supporting data and developing ideas through further reading, and produce a short essay at the end of the semester.

Class will be conducted in Japanese, though students may be required to read texts in English.

Objectives:
The main purpose of First Year Seminar A is to improve students' reading comprehension and oral communication skills. Through close readings of the text, their abilities to express their opinions convincingly in writing and speech should be improved.

Students are expected to be capable of presenting their own opinions clearly in both writing and speech and support them convincingly with statistical and other kinds of objective evidence. In particular, they should be able to create a PowerPoint file that includes their own argument and objective supporting materials. They should also be capable of evaluating their fellow students' presentations.

In this seminar, students will explore a wide range of questions about language, such as “Do animals use language?”, “Will there ever be perfect machine translation?”, and “Why are Japanese people not good at English?”, as a broad and accessible introduction to the study of language, or linguistics. The textbook is a collection of essays in which the author, Professor Emeritus Ken Machida, addresses common and intriguing questions about language, with each chapter focusing on a single topic.
In each class, we will read and discuss a few chapters, with students taking turns reading passages aloud and participating in small-group discussions related to the themes of the readings. No prior knowledge of linguistics is required. The seminar will be conducted in Japanese.

For the final assessment, students will complete two assignments—a presentation and an essay—in which they will formulate and explore their own question about language.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

・Demonstrate familiarity with basic concepts in linguistics.

・Develop oral communication and presentation skills in Japanese.

・Develop logical and critical writing skills in Japanese.

This seminar is an introductory course designed to help students understand what it means to study at a university and how university learning differs from secondary education. While providing guidance on how to make the most of four years of academic life at Waseda University, the course encourages students to reflect on the nature of academic inquiry itself.

Rather than passively memorizing knowledge, students will experience the fundamental practices of academic learning at the university level: formulating questions, reading academic texts, organizing ideas in their own words, and deepening understanding through discussion.

In this semester, the course uses The Economics of Democracy as its primary textbook. Through this text, students will examine the scope of issues addressed by economics in democratic societies and explore how institutional arrangements and public policies can be analyzed using introductory economic models. The course also introduces basic mathematical models employed in economics, enabling students to gain a concrete understanding of what it means to “model” society.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

•　Understand the basic structure and interpretation of introductory economic models and use simple models to explain social phenomena

•　Comprehend the scope of issues addressed by economics and analyze the relationships among institutions and policies in democratic societies from an economic perspective

•　Read academic texts, summarize key arguments in their own words, and present reasoned opinions based on evidence

•　Acquire fundamental academic learning skills—such as autonomous study, question formulation, and active participation in discussion—that will serve as a foundation for future specialized study

This seminar aims to develop students' basic academic skills, including bibliographic survey, logical thinking, convincing presentation, and writing. The main theme of this seminar is the relationship between art and society in Europe from antiquity to the present day. Each art and monument has its own background and history, closely tied to contemporary events, revealing intricate details of past societies.
To acquire the skills of critical and logical analysis of past objects, we will carefully read the assigned text book on the Romanesque Art, which is chronologically located between Classical and Renaissance arts, to understand the difficulty of interpretation and meaning of academic study.
In the second part of this seminar, each student will choose their topic of interest freely and present a final paper on it. Throughout this process, students will conduct a bibliographic survey, read relevant academic papers, and write a short research essay, to foster the skills of critical reading and writing.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to:

- Develop an awareness of the connection between history and art.

- Acquire basic history study skills.

- Develop critical and logical thinking skills.

This seminar aims to provide students with some basic knowledge about Japanese ways of thinking, Japanese culture and tradition, etc. in relation with politics and internataional relations (IR). They will acquire a historic view-point of the current situation of Japan and its people through the classics carefully chosen by the teacher of this course.
The course will discuss the relationship between war and peace in Japanese history, the Japanese way of thinking with respect to the Japanese Constitution, war and peace, and what the current younger generation should think in their university life, among others.

They are also strongly encouraged to have read through all the textbooks indicated below before they attend the first session of this class.
This course will be held in a classroom (face2face), if the COVID-19 situation allows. Please wait for further notices.

Objectives:
The course will hopefully give some important points that the students should learn before they study abroad in their second year at SILS.

Discover how classical plays come alive through voice — revealing new narratives through performance

Experience masterpieces from Shakespeare to Beckett and Mishima Yukio, not through silent reading alone, but through vocal performance and dramatic reading. By embodying the emotions, struggles, and joys of characters through voice, participants will discover new dimensions of dramatic works that remain hidden in text alone.

Experience masterpieces from Shakespeare to Beckett and Mishima Yukio, not through silent reading alone, but through vocal performance and dramatic reading. By embodying the emotions, struggles, and joys of characters through voice, participants will discover new dimensions of dramatic works that remain hidden in text alone.

Our post-reading discussions will explore the deeper layers of each work that become apparent only through performance, and we'll examine the unique expressive possibilities that theatre offers. Objectives:

2. Comprehend the universality and diversity of theatre through exposure to plays from various periods and cultures

3. Develop new perspectives on textual interpretation through reading aloud and discussion

4. Cultivate analytical and critical thinking skills for dramatic works

This course aims to cultivate students’abilities to critically think, concisely write and orally present an analytical and logical argument. We will read masterpieces of science and discuss the logic of authors’ claims in the class.

Face to Face. In the so-called era of globalization, information, money and things cross the borders easier and faster than before. However, people’s cross border movements, especially from the global south to the global north, are often controlled heavily except highly skilled and/or wealthy persons. Under the current nation-state system, people are treated differently according to their labels, for example, the refugee, the labour migrant, the stateless person, and a person with a certain nationality or nationalities. Further, some ambiguities often exist between such labels and actual persons. In this class, you will first learn why the existing labels were made, what they are and how they have been applied. Through readings and discussions, you would examine to what extent those labels differ from the realities, and how those who are labelled, think about his/her label a how they behave and why. It’s important for you as a young adult, who can vote,, to understand the issues concerning refugees, labour migrants and stateless persons. You are required to conduct your own research, read a lot, raise questions and participate in the discussions. The instructor will share her experiences gained at UNICEF, UNHCR and UNTAC in a total of eight countries, and during her research in India and Japan when appropriate.

Objectives:
１．You would gain the basic knowledge on (1) refugees, labour migrants, stateless people and nationals, (2) The roles of the UN/international/regional organizations including UNHCR, UNICEF, IOM, EU, OAU, OECD, WB, etc and (3) impacts of new technologies on such labels.

２．You would improve your critical thinking through your group works, presentations, the class discussions, and you will demonstrate your progress in your final report.

3 You would gain basic academic skills including research, presentation including citation, asking questions and make constructive criticisms.

This course provides students with a basic knowledge of multilingualism and provides an introduction to the key social issues in the study of multilingualism.

The students will learn to think critically about important social issues such as the following:
“What is a language?”, “Language variation and the spread of global languages”, “Revitalization of endangered languages”, “Societal multilingualism”, “Language and identities”.

The students will be required to read texts in English and participate actively in class discussions.

They will also be required to conduct a short research project.

This seminar will be conducted face-to-face.
Active participation will be highly evaluated.

Objectives:
The purpose of this class is to become aware of language use in society.

After learning the key terms, concepts, and theories of sociolinguistics, students will understand the language situation in various ethnic groups around the world and consider the political, social, historical, and ethnic factors behind the language situation.

In addition, students will also gain a deeper insight into their own linguistic situation through their own research and class-wide discussions.

In today’s global world, Englishhas become the main Lingua Franca. Yet, English is not the only “international”language: Spanish and French, for example, are spoken across several continentsand are used as official languages in many international organizations. In SILS,students are given the opportunity to become plurilingual speakers beyond Englishand Japanese, to get a better grasp not only of linguistic but also ofsociocultural diversity in different countries. In this Seminar, students will learnhow to study French: it is essential to understand specific key linguisticconcepts which differ from the ones found in Japanese (e.g. grammatical gender,articles, moods, etc.) envisaged in their historical evolution. Students whoattend this seminar will build their academic foundations to study not only theFrench language, but also the method used to describe, analyze and comparelanguages in general, both from a linguistic and historical viewpoints.Ultimately, students will learn how to read and discuss academic issues onrelated topics.

Objectives:
The objective of the Seminar is for students to be able to understand the core structure of French from a linguistic viewpoint (i.e., theoretical and contrastive methods for the analysis of French), and also some important aspects of the formation of French. By the end of the term, students should be able to understand the essential systems of French : (i) vowel and consonant systems, (ii) number and gender, (iii) adjectives, adverbs, prepositions (iv) verbal conjugation, (v) aspect and mood of French verbs, (vi) sentence structures, i.e. passive, conditional, subjunctive, (vii) evolution of French especially from 16th to 20th centuries. Students should be able to find and use academic references on the topic, and write academic comments on related issues.

In liberal arts and international communication education, understanding languages and their diversity is essential, not only for students who are interested in linguistics or literature, but also for students who are interested in history, sociology, law and marketing, for example. Now, in our multilingual world, understanding the connections between different languages can help to learn these different languages (e.g., Italian and French, or Spanish and Portuguese, or even English and Latin!). In fact, Latin is a key language to understand the roots and branches of many European languages, which belong to what is called “Romance languages”. Therefore, in the Seminar, students will receive an introduction to Romance Linguistics, which will help them in many ways in their liberal studies, especially if they are interested in developing their linguistic skills not only in English but also in other European languages. They will learn how to read about and discuss issues concerning the evolution from Spoken Latin to Romance Languages, their characteristics and formation with a specific case study around the French Language as a rich illustration.

Objectives:
The objective of the Seminar is for students to be able to understand how all romance languages are connected and how this knowledge can help them learn different languages, starting with English. By the end of the term, students should be able to (i) understand the core of the formation of Romance Languages, starting from spoken Latin to the contemporary situation of Romanian, Italian, French, Occitan, Spanish and Portuguese, etc., and (ii) have some knowledge about their typical features in terms of phonological systems, tense or aspect systems, and syntactic structures. Students should be able to find and use academic references on the topic, and write academic comments on related issues.

In this seminar, students are invited to discuss various philosophical questions. In the first class, each student should choose one philosophical subject to focus on (see examples of the subjects below). Throughout the semester, students will work on the subject they have chosen.

Examples of subjects:
1. What is a lie? Is a lie justifiable?
2. How should human beings treat the pigs they eat?
3. Is a medical experiment on human beings justifiable under certain conditions?
4. Is the death penalty justifiable?
5. What is beauty? What does it mean to find something beautiful?
6. What is scepticism? How can a sceptic avoid self-contradiction?

This list of examples is not exhaustive, and students are free to choose any subject they prefer after consultation with the instructor.

Students should develop philosophical thinking skills and the capacity to argue their thoughts and discuss with others in Japanese. At the end of the semester, students are expected to write one philosophical essay in Japanese concerning the subject they chose.

Determining ethical standards poses significant challenges. For instance, while lying is generally considered immoral, it may be viewed as necessary when saving others. This raises a fundamental question: Is morality objective, or does it rely on subjective value judgments? Furthermore, is individual moral determination compatible with living in a community?

Each seminar session is organized around a specific agenda or question, such as the Trolley Problem ('Is it right to kill one to save ten?') or intergenerational ethics ('Are we responsible for the future?'). These topics correspond to assigned textbook chapters.(approx. 10–15 pages).

Students are required to prepare a one-page position paper for each class. The sessions will be facilitated by student moderators. Please note: A Japanese syllabus will be distributed during the first session.

The aim of this course is to develop academic Japanese skills in consideration of language related problems and issues in learning English and current English education in Japan. The characteristic of this seminar is to adopting a specific learning process, called 4 round system, in which students will address the same topics four times from different perspective. The system simplifies and deforms a research process which many SLA researchers go through when they conduct research. This is designed to deepen students’ understanding of the selected topics. In this course, we will examine the history of American popular music in order to understand how music shaped the American mindset in the twentieth century, particularly in its second half.

The course will begin with an examination of the origins of so-called root music—such as Native American music, minstrel music, and the songs of Stephen Foster—in early American history. We will then explore how blues and jazz emerged and developed into popular musical styles in the early twentieth century. The primary focus of the course, however, will be on the expansion of popular music genres such as rock and roll and rhythm and blues in the latter half of the twentieth century, especially from the 1960s to the 1980s, when American popular music became increasingly industrialized and commercialized.

James M. Vardaman’s Hajimete no Amerika Ongakushi (『はじめてのアメリカ音楽史』) will be used as the main textbook, while additional materials—including musical recordings—will also be introduced. The course will be conducted in Japanese.

Objectives:
To understand the history of American music; to learn how American society has been constructed culturally.

This seminar will delve into one of the challenges facing Japan today — the economic and cultural coexistence with people from diverse cultural backgrounds. Among them are foreign Muslims, whose numbers have been increasing in recent years. They arrive from various countries in Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. While they have their own distinct culture and language, they share common challenges as 'Muslims living in Japan.' Many Muslims come to Japan alone and establish families after securing an economic base. Foreign-born Muslims and their families confront numerous challenges in Japan’s non-Islamic society, including the difficulty of gaining an understanding of Islamic religious practices in workplaces and schools, transmitting the Islamic faith to their children, and obtaining a cemetery for burial—a necessity for their journey as Muslims into the next life.
In this seminar, students will gain basic knowledge about the current situation and issues faced by immigrants in contemporary Japan. We will explore the historical background of immigration, the characteristics of their countries of origin, and the problems encountered by Muslim immigrants and their families living in Japan. Students are encouraged to search for literature and newspaper articles, collect information, organize issues, prepare reports, and present and discuss their findings in the classroom.
All classes will be conducted face-to-face, providing a platform for students to actively engage in discussions, share findings, and collaborate on understanding the multifaceted issues.

1. Acquire the skills to search for relevant books and articles to collect necessary information.

2. Cultivate the ability to consider issues from various angles.

3. Develop the ability to organize and present issues clearly and effectively.

4. Acquire the skills to actively participate in class discussions.

授業は、原則として対面式で実施する。授業では、受講生が指導教員とともに教科書A）上杉勇司『どうすれば争いを止められるのか』（WAVE出版、2023年）、B）上杉勇司『紛争地の歩き方』（ちくま新書、2023年）、C) 上杉勇司・長谷川晋・高木綾『アクティブ・ラーニングで学ぶ国際関係』（有斐閣、2026年）が提示する知識を深めていくことを目的とする。毎週、今日の知（Think）、今日の技（Work）、今日の心（Review）、今日の身体（Action）、今日の目標 （Personal Goal)、今日の学び（Take Away) という6ステップで学びを深めていく。授業では、受講生たちが、ともに考え、気づき、共有することで「創発」が生み出される環境を整えることで、受講生の平和についての思考をほぐし、その視野を広げていく。

本演習の目的は、大学で必要なアカデミックスキルを身につけることです。日本における外国語教育・外国語学習をテーマに、新書などの文献講読を通して、アカデミックスキルの向上を目指します。具体的には、以下のようなテーマを扱います。

大学外国語教育：日本の大学で英語のみの講義を必修化することの問題点は何か。英語以外の外国語を学ぶ意義は何か。

バイリンガリズム：幼少期に2つの言語を同時に学ぶことのメリットとデメリットは何か。母語習得と第二言語習得は何が違うのか。

自然科学における仮説(理論)を批判的に考察し理解することは現在社会において重要なスキルです。
とくに、進化生物学の理論は、今日の地球環境問題や人類社会を理解するうえでの基礎的な知識です。
この授業の目的は、生物進化に関係した研究成果（従来の仮説とそれを批判する新しい仮説）を自らが検討することによって、その理解力・批判力を修得することです。
具体的なテーマは、古生物学：恐竜などの現在は生存しない絶滅生物の進化の研究、です。
これらの生態や形態を科学的にどのように復元するか？は、まさに、過去を探る自然科学の特徴的な例と言えるでしょう。
これらの研究成果についての普及的な文献を受講者全員での講読、それについてのプレゼンテーション、そして受講者による議論で授業は進められます。
静止画および動画を含むスライドを使っての講義や議論もおこなわれます。
さらに、科学理論が一般に提示されて理解される場としての博物館展示(恐竜を始めとする自然史についての展示)の見学を行い、その方法論について受講者全員で分析・検討します(これまでの通常の授業の場合：この方法は、社会状況によって変化します)。
授業に必要な文献は必要に応じて提供します。
この授業は、対面で行われます。必要な場合には、オンラインで一部実施されることもあります。

Objectives:
- 科学仮説を批判的に理解する能力を習得する。

- 普及を目的とした自然科学分野の文献を読解できる能力を習得する。

- 科学仮説を理解し、それについての自分自身の意見を他に対して論理的にプレゼンテーションする能力を習得する。

- 科学理論の提示手段とその効果について、博物館展示などを例として多角的に学ぶ。

- 科学研究についての方法論を理解し、その応用の可能性を自分自身の経験のなかで探る力を身につける。

In his executive order 14253 titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" issued in March 2025, President Donald Trump argues that teaching of American slavery is "driven by ideology rather than the truth" and it "fosters a sense of national shame" in such a great nation as the United States. It is true that nothing better illustrates American irony than the existence of slavery in a land of freedom. Since the founding of the nation, freedom for white people in the United States depended upon the enslavement of black people, and the nation’s growth owed much to global economy based on the Atlantic slavery. The fact that the United States alone required a civil war to abolish the institution testifies to the strength of its slaveholding class and the weakness of American democracy. The official end of slavery in 1865, however, failed to solve the problem of race in the United States, as seen in the recent Black Lives Matter throughout the world. it is, therefore, essential to understand slavery if one wishes to understand both US history and American society of today. Contrary to what President Trump wishes, we have to face this "negative" (in his word) side of history because there is so much to learn from it. It is rather inspiring to learn how people continue to struggle for their rights.

This course will first give us an overview of American slavery by reading Peter Kolchin’s American Slavery, 1619-1877 and then enhance our understanding of the day-to-day practice of slavery through the eyes of a fugitive slave, Frederick Douglass (My Bondage and My Freedom). Together, they will help us understand the workings of human bondage as well as the impact of slavery upon people, both black and white.

Objectives:
1) Since the subject of slavery and racism is a requisite for understanding American society, those who intend to study in the United States will benefit from a number of important historical writings and theories that are familiar to American intellectuals.

2) Students’responsibilities explained below will help develop skills to critically view and logically evaluate the assigned material as well as to lead the discussion where no one should feel inhibited in expressing views contrary to other students. Those responsibilities are: each student will have at least one opportunity to make an oral presentation and serve as discussion leader; oral presentations should provide an analytical summary of the week’s reading and set forth questions for further discussion by the class. The student leader will chair the ensuing discussion.

3) While there is no midterm examination, students are required to submit an essay at the end of the seminar drawing from the books and what transpires in the class.

Did you ever wonder why urban Japanese looks so different from Western cities in Europe or the Americas, or its Asian counterparts? What makes Tokyo look and feel so special? Do you think this is merely an aesthetic difference, or that we can learn more from it? Are there useful lessons we can draw from the Japanese city, for example, to pressing issues of today like climate change, social polarisation, or post-disaster planning? And if yes, what are they?

Japanese urbanism has been seen as an important test case for our thinking about the planning, making, and governing of cities. Although also Western cities grew immensely during the 19th and early 20th century, the rapid and sudden transformation of Japan from a primarily agrarian country into one of the world's most highly urbanised ones was unparalleled until recently. The frantic socio-economic change and urban growth that Japanese cities witnessed during the 1950s and 60s anticipated much of the contemporary urban expansion in rapidly developing countries like China, India, or Brazil. In this context Japan’s experience offers valuable lessons. While Japanese governments and planners borrowed carefully from planning ideas and methods of other advanced countries to respond to swift social and urban change, urban planning, urban governance and cities developed distinctly different in Japan from those of other developed countries.

Based on a critical reading of André Sorensen’s book ‘The Making of Urban Japan’ (2001), this beginners seminar explores how Japan's distinctive patterns of urbanisation emerged over time, how pre-modern urban forms, traditional urban practices, and a blend of established institutions and newly imported foreign ideas contributed to this. The course will critically challenge established assumptions about urban Japan and students from other late developing countries will have the chance to reflect about important lessons from the Japanese case.

What looks unorganised & chaotic on the surface and has been often unjustly criticised on purely aesthetic grounds is in reality dense in population and experience, walkable, bike friendly, economically diverse, socially mixed, and highly adaptable to future challenges. We will also examine the critical role of civil society and its relationship to government and the market economy. One of André Sorensen's central arguments is that in the case of Japan, central government dominated urban affairs, while at the same time the weakly developed civil society, and comparatively powerless local governments could do little to advance alternative visions and models for land development and planning.

This seminar is not only useful for aficionados of cities and urban life. The course book also offers a broad and rich survey of Japan's modern history from the late Edo Period to the year 2000 and provides an important historical, political, social, cultural and environmental context for the development of Japan's cities and civil society. Although already 20 years have passed since 'The Making of Urban Japan' have passed, this is to date the most comprehensive, most-cited text about Japanese urbanism.

Objectives:
In this course, you will ...

(1)... engage in a critical reading of the most central English language text on the history and development of urban Japan from the pre-modern Edo Period to the present,

(2)... develop a first understanding of how urban form, social practice, civil society, governance and planning are related, and how this led to the particular heterogeneous appearance of cities in Japan as we know them,

(3)... explore and discuss why and how urban life in a non-western context has changed over time, and how the city and the knowledge about cities emerged between vernacular and foreign, ‘travelling’ ideas,

(4)... learn to summarise longer text sections in series of short writing assignments and practice academic writing,

(5)... hone your presentation skills, present your chapter summaries along with own ideas in class.

Frantz Fanon (1925 Martinique-1961 Algeria) was trained as a medical doctor in France. He served in the French military medical services as psychiatrist to both oppressors and victims of torture in French prisons in Algeria at the time of its occupation. Fanon would eventually join the ranks of Algerian nationalists fighting against French oppression. Fanon wrote extensively and his seminal critique of colonialism laid the foundations for much that would follow on the subject. In this course we will examine his two major works: "The Wretched of the Earth" and "Black Skin White Masks". The first book argues for colonial struggle, while the latter criticizes the psychological dimensions of colonial subjugation, characterized by oppression and self-hate. In our seminar we will unpack and contextualize Fanon's ideas and will also examine the impact they have had on political and liberation movements (for example on Nelson Mandela) as well as on social theory.

Objectives:
The goal of our seminar is to have students learn to read critically so as to discern theoretical issues of interest, and to learn to communicate ideas in open and free discussion.

We often use the words “mainstream,” “normal,” or “everyday,” without considering the inherent violence behind the idea of privileging some people as normal and considering some as “different,” “other,” or otherwise marginal. What are the dynamics of this process of othering, who benefits, and who suffers? Whole populations of people have been marginalized by war, colonialism, and militarism. Whole groups of people have been marginalized by ideas about what is considered an “abnormal” identity. How can one better appreciate the diversity and complexity of humanity by taking historical account of this violence and inequality?

This first-year seminar is part of a series of seminars that applies cultural studies and gender studies approaches to the postcolonial history and present-day of the Asia and Pacific region, challenging students to think about colonized, displaced, and marginalized communities and subjects in different societies. Considering ideas about citizenship/borders, immigration, indigenous communities (like Ainu or Okinawan), Disney movies and popular cultural ideas about gender, sexual orientation and human rights, race, and other keywords, we think about how all these different themes intersect. We also give some consideration to how those keywords relate to marginalized, colonized regions like Hawai'i, Okinawa, and the colonized Pacific Islands, with a particular emphasis of the place where we are doing this study-- the place we call "Japan."

Objectives:
By taking an assertive, participant, self-reflexive approach, students in this seminar shall develop a basic understanding of problems of nationalism, ethnicity, gender, and popular culture, with a particular emphasis on how these issues relate to the Asia and Pacific region between Japan and the United States. Students will conduct group presentations and each write a short analytic piece related to how these themes intersect a subject of their choosing. They will also be encouraged to cultivate a nuanced awareness of this region, the societies in which they live, and the complexity of their own lives.

By the end of the semester, students will increase their awareness of contemporary problems of inequality in the world, especially in relation to Japanese and American histories in the Pacific, and you will also gain some basic skills in feminist inquiry. Additionally, you will be expected to push beyond your “comfort zone” to think more about how we all marginalize others in some way, and how we are all in some ways marginal as well.

This raises the question of, however, whether the computer being used to its maximum potential for language learning. In this subject, students will learn how the computer can be used in teaching foreign languages, investigating what should be kept in mind when using new technologies.

Few books have been more influential on how we think today about liveable, lively cities, than Jane Jacobs’ seminal text ‘The Death and Life of Great American Cities’ (1961). Despite it's age, the book is significant in many ways. In a lucid language, Jacobs (1916-2006) systematically dissects the inner workings and failings of cities and urban communities, and thus she inspired generations of urbanists and citizen activists alike. Although she didn’t hold a formal college degree in architecture or urban planning, the self-taught urban thinker, influential community organiser and social activist relied on her precise observations and common sense to show why and how certain places flourish, and what can be done to improve those that do not.

Even though Jacobs wrote ‘Death and Life’ over six decades ago, many of her ideas and conceptions of how to make cities liveable, safe and economically viable are as relevant today as they were in the 1960s. Just like in Jacobs's days, in many contemporary cities around the world large-scale urban redevelopment and infrastructure projects are still replacing integrated, tight-knit, vernacular urban communities with function micro-economies and a diverse social life. Now as then, often the results of such scrap-and-build development have been devastating. Jane Jacobs' ideas offer many timely insights into what are the ingredients of resilient, adaptable, and sustainable cities and neighbourhoods.

Despite the unbroken relevance of ‘Death and Life of Great American Cities’, the text is also profoundly a product of 1960s America. In this course students engage therefore in a critical re-reading of the 'text as a historical artefact' and interrogate it from a perspective of their own (often non-Western) urban culture and in a 21st century context. What is the impact of new technologies such as social media and other technological inventions that emerged since the book was published and that have a profound impact on urban life today? Through the work with one of the most central and widely-read treatises in urban studies, student will also understand how the urban planning of the past has led to much-debated issues such as structural racism and socio-economic segregation in American cities.

Objectives:
In this seminar students will ...

(1) ... engage in a critical re-reading of one of the most seminal texts on urban life and city making,

(2) ... develop a first understanding about the different ‘ingredients’ that make a vibrant public life, lively neighbourhoods and liveable cities,

(3) ... explore the different forces that shape our cities, and how they can be controlled,

(4) ... learn to summarise longer text sections in series of short writing assignments and practice academic writing,

(5) ... hone your presentation skills and present your chapter summaries along with own ideas in class.

The aim of this course is to develop academic English skills in consideration of language related issues in Second Language Acquisition (SLA). The characteristic of this seminar is to adopting a specific learning process, called 4 round system, in which students will address the same topics four times from different perspective. The system simplifies and deforms a research process which many SLA researchers go through when they conduct research. This is designed to deepen students’ understanding of the selected topics. Through the system, students are expected to go through a “research process” from expanding their interest in this field to presenting their research project.

Topics the seminar are going to focus on are issues related to issues in Second Language Acquisition (SLA). As you can see in SILS, almost all students and faculties are bilingual speakers, who use their first language and concurrently learn their second (third, fourth and more) language to communicate each other. How can we learn the language other than the first language? Are there any effective way(s) to do so? The field of SLA seeks to understand and explain the development of proficiency in additional languages as a cognitive and social process. However, as second language learning becomes more common, there has been emerging many “myths”- the ideas that many people consider to be true but they don’t know where they came from. In this seminar, students will learn some common ideas about second language learning and compare what people tend to think about and what researchers say about.

Objectives:
The primary objectives of this seminar are for students to engage in research processes such as analyzing data, evaluating texts, and applying knowledge to practice (which is called academic skills in university). By doing so, students are expected to become a more informed and thoughtful thinker of academic research. Since this course choose SLA as a topic, students can also build a knowledge base about those topics. By the end of the semester, students should be able to show the ability of the following skills:

1. To understand general topics in the field of SLA.

2. To relate the topics in the textbook to own experience and knowledge.

3. To grasp and explain a selected topic in the textbook (e.g., question, claim, and evidence).

4. To read the textbook critically

5. To construct own argument (claim and evidence) based on the selected topic in the textbook.

6. To collect data and arrange own argument logically with the data.

7. To raise questions about others’ claims and comments.

Shinto 神道 refers to symbolic, aesthetic, religious and ritual practices and performances in Japan that are associated with local, regional and/or national identities, as well as with the imperial institution. This course will examine various aspects of 'Shinto' from the lenses of Anthropology, History, and Legal Studies. We begin with historiographical debates and sociopolitical contextualization of Shinto. In this course we will examine on both micro- and macro-levels the language, concepts and ritual practices found in Shinto shrines and associated ceremonies and performances. Attention will be drawn to the diversity of practices (despite modern streamlining since Meiji); the place of imperial ritual (Daijosai etc.) in the imagination of Shinto before and since 1945; the legal background of Shinto in ancient and modern times; as well as recent changes in the popular imagination of 'Shinto' religious practice within Japan and beyond. Some comparative examples will be drawn, especially with East Asian, Southeast Asian, Indian and European contexts.

Objectives:
This Freshman seminar aims to introduce students to the fields of Anthropology, History, and Legal Studies as tools to observe, analyze and interpret phenomena and practices that are referred as 'Shinto' in contemporary Japan.

Students will take turns making short 10-15 minute presentations of readings. Although these will not be graded as such for course evaluation, they will form the basis for discussion by the group as a whole, and will be essential to the acquisition of substantive knowledge as well as analytical method by individual students.

Although this is not a language course, acquisition of a limited vocabulary (30 words/compounds or so) of Shinto terms will be expected of all students in Japanese and in their usual English translation.

The seminar will take place as an active seminar with meetings in-class. In addition, there may be two or three sessions planned as observation of Shinto ritual activity. Among these is an optional field trip to Nagoya to observe a ritual on May 5th, during Golden Week holidays. Additionally, there will be a film showing on religious art on the evening of April 29th on campus, in period 6.

After examining various competing theories of ethnic identity, national identity and nationalism, the last 6 weeks of the semester are set aside for discussion, preparation and delivery of student presentations. These presentations of approximately 15-minutes duration may be done in teams of two or three students, or as an individual project. Students will be required to make a presentation on the contemporary symbols and meaning of national identity in a location of their own choosing, and to analyze the evolution of that identity in terms of the ideas we discuss during the course.

Objectives:
This course is designed to be part II of a two-part course in conjunction with my first semester IIB seminar. Students may choose to take just one or both of the courses. The second semester will focus on issues associated with group identities, such as ethnicity and national identity.

[IN-PERSON COURSE]

The Civil War (1861-65) was one of the most decisive turning points of American history, for it not only freed four million slaves, which amounted two-thirds of the world's entire slave population at that time, but also transformed the union of separate states into a more consolidated nation-state. It is not too much to say that but for the Civil War, the United States might not have become the world's superpower. As the failure of a Republican candidate for the 2024 election to answer the question about the cause of the Civil War became widely reported, the knowledge about the Civil War is regarded as essential for the understanding of US history. Moreover, recent controversies over the Confederate statues and monuments revived the public interest in slavery and the Civil War in the United States, while the Black Lives Matter has regularly brought up the subject of inequality in American life to the center of the public discourse. This course attempts to understand why what happened more than 160 years ago matters to Americans of today, by examining why the United States became disintegrated after eighty-five years of existence, how the war was fought, and what replaced the slaveholding nation. It might be also meaningful to look back the history of the United States because this year commemorates the 250th anniversary of its independence.
We will be reading the masterpiece of political history: Eric Foner, The Fiery Trial: Abraham Lincoln and American Slavery. This Pulitzer-winning history makes us understand that the abolition of slavery was not the primary purpose of the Northern army, but a war strategy to defeat the South. It also sheds new light on Lincoln, whose greatness lies in his capacity to grow from a racist politician to the great emancipator. By reading his work along with other primary sources, the course ultimately aims to help us better understand current issues of the United States, such as the threat to democracy by Trump supporters in Jan. 6, 2021 and the glaring inequalities between races, both of which continue to divide American society today.

Objectives:
1) Since the era under study is the key moment in American history, the issues discussed in this course will enhance both the knowledge about and understanding of American society as it is now.

2) Students’responsibilities explained below will help develop skills to critically view and logically evaluate the assigned material s well as to lead the discussion where no one should feel inhibited in expressing views contrary to other students. Those responsibilities are: each student will have at least one opportunity to make an oral presentation and serve as discussion leader; oral presentations should provide an analytical summary of the week’s reading and set forth questions for further discussion by the class. The student leader will chair the ensuing discussion.

3) While there is no midterm examination, students are required to write an essay at the end of the seminar drawing from the books and what transpires in the class.

The method of course delivery will be Face-to-Face (F2F) (*Please note that if a sufficient number of students are unable to attend in-person because of travel restrictions, it may be necessary to move to Live Stream via Zoom).
This course offers an introduction to the European Union(EU), including its history, institutions and decision-making processes. We also consider some of the key aspects of the EU’s international relations. An honest appraisal of the strengths and weaknesses of the EU is offered. The EU has been referred to as the most successful peace experiment in history, and the most successful international organization in history. The bases for both of these claims are examined.

However the EU is also experiencing several interlocking and enduring crises which some claim are a threat to the very future of the organization. These crisis include; the Ukraine crisis, accusations that the EU has a ‘democratic deficit’, and Brexit. Each of these crises will be considered in some detail.

We will also look in some detail at the relationship between the EU and Japan, who recently signed a path-breaking Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) and a Strategic Partnership Agreement (SPA). The EPA is one of the largest trade deal ever signed, and was a direct and deliberate attempt to counter the effects of Brexit and the Presidency of Donald Trump.

Objectives:
This seminar class has two main aims. The first is to foster independent study skills; it is important for students to become familiar with the academic culture of seminar study. Students will develop their ability to conceptualize a problem, and utilize academic resources (books, teachers, the Internet) to learn more about it. Students will be encouraged to think critically, and to organize their thoughts clearly in writing. It is also important that students develop the ability to express their ideas clearly and confidently in public, through presentations and discussion.

The second objective of the seminar is to learn about the European Union as an example of global governance.

Students will gain an understanding of:

- the history of the EU

- the political institutions of the EU

- the decision-making processes of the EU

- whether it is fair to claim that the EU suffers from a ‘democratic deficit’

- the extent and nature of the EU migration ‘crisis’

- the strengths and limitations of the EU as an international actor

- the EU’s self-image as a unique type of international actor, ‘normative’ or ‘transformative’

- the successes and failures of EU enlargement

- the EU’s attempts to promote abolition of the death penalty in Japan

- the significance of the EPA and SPA that have just been signed by the EU and Japan

※in-person ONLY
This seminar is an introductory seminar on International Relations. We will further examine some of the essential ideas and issues that are fundamental to an understanding of contemporary international relations. We will also seek to identify how these issues affect global governance and global business practices. Based on readings given on Waseda Net throughout this course, it will be a practical discussion-based seminar that seeks to develop an understanding about the complexities of IR by using contemporary examples. Previous exposure to IR theories might be an advantage.
By the end of the course you should be able to discuss and critique IR issues. You should expect to work individually and in groups with people of other cultural identities.

Objectives:
By the end of this course you should be able to discuss contemporary international relations issues objectively. You should be able to recognize the fallacies, debate and defend positions and consider possible outcomes of contemporary IR events. You will be expected to demonstrate theoretical knowledge by application to scenarios or situations throughout the course. My goal is to apply the theoretical understanding you develop in your studies.

This course offers a broad introduction to topics in the natural sciences for liberal arts students. The content of the course will serve as a basic introduction to various topics in specific sciences (e.g. biology, biomedical science, physics, astronomy, geology, environmental science, data science and artificial intelligence), as well as an introduction to various standard scientific methods such as data collection and analysis, hypothesis construction and testing and mathematical modeling. The class will be conducted in an omnibus format, featuring lectures from various faculty members specializing in the sciences and related disciplines.

[Note: This course will be conducted in person.]

Objectives:
The objective of this course is to offer a broad introduction to topics in the natural sciences for liberal arts students.

The environment impacts our life in many aspects. Adverse impacts to this environment affect our life and other living organisms. Thus, it is important to understand natural environmental systems, physical and social causes of environmental problems, and strategies to manage these issues.

Objectives:
The goal of the course is to learn

-the scientific method is a deliberate way of asking and answering questions about natural world

-the basics of life science and evolution

-organisms interact with one another and with the environment, shaping ecological systems that sustain life.

course will be conducted face-to-face
What are the fundamental features of living systems? This course introduces basic essence about life and covers a wide range of topics from DNA to our body and human life. Intended for non-science majors, and those who desire an understanding of fundamental life processes, or who intend to pursue higher biology courses.

Objectives:
Students will be more familiar with scientific thinking and approaches and will be able to explain the basic concepts about life.

This course focuses on biology relevant to the behavioral sciences. Introduces basic principles of evolutionary biology, genetic/hormonal/neural systems and ecology that illuminate the behavior and social organization of humans and other animals. Topics include human variation/adaptations, sex differences, emotion/cognition, and life history traits. Discussions highlight nature versus nurture issues.

Objectives:
Major goals:

1) to learn basic biological principles, approaches and theories

2) to appreciate/evaluate scientific studies of human behavior

3) to consider human prospects

Traditional biology is the study of the rules of morphology, classification, evolution, behavior, and genetics of living organisms. However, when the molecular structure of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) was proposed by Watson and Crick in 1953, biologists for the first time recognized the possibility of understanding living organisms at the molecular level, and here molecular biology was born. The fields of medicine, pharmacology, agriculture, and chemistry have included biochemistry, which studies the structure and function of molecules comprising living organisms from the perspective of chemistry. Biochemistry and molecular biology are closely associated with each other, and together they continue to provide important insights for the development of the biotechnologies. The achievements of this research form the basis for various applied technologies in the fields of medicine, pharmacology, and agriculture.

Objectives:
This lecture covers the molecules that constitute living organisms and their control mechanisms, as well as biotechnologies and the principles of aging and disease. Students are expected to acquire the abilities to understand and explore biological system at the molecular and cellular level.

This course 1) introduces principles of evolution and the major events in the history of life, and 2) provides a basic understanding of how scientific methods are used in the field of evolutionary biology, and how evolutionary thinking is applied to issues in biological diversity, animal behavior and modern human biology. The main goal is to develop a scientific way of thinking about the facts of life, including human beings.

“There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.” (Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859)

Objectives:
Upon completion of this course, students should demonstrate basic knowledge in the followings:

1) evolution and its mechanisms

2) history of life on earth

3) evolution of sex and sex differences

4) evolution of social behavior/communication

5) modern human mind/body/society from evolutionary and comparative perspectives

course will be in person.
Human life is a fight against disease. In this course, we study important discoveries in Medicine and learn the basics of diseases which threatened human in the past and present.

Objectives:
The goal of the course is to learn how modern Medicine has been developed and gain deeper insights into the cause and cure for major diseases.

This is an advanced seminar course in Life scienceand Biomedicine. We will read and discuss recent discovery and breakthrough inbiotechnology and medicine.

Objectives:
Students will learn broad knowledge in recent progress in life science and develop critical thinking skill.
