In this course, we introduce and discuss some key issues and problems in the cognitive neurosciences.

Objectives:
After completing the course, the student will be able to pursue his or her own lines of interest in this field more or less independently.

This is an introductorycourse in the basic principles of chemistry. Chemistry is one of thefundamental sciences and essential to understanding the world around us. It isalso necessary for a range of other disciplines, from biochemistry to materialscience. The course will focus on the basic building blocks, such as thestructure of atoms and molecules and interpretation of spectra; chemical bonds;kinetic theory of gases and the gas laws; the periodic table; chemicalreactions and equilibria; and acids and bases.

Objectives:
This course aims to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of chemistry. By the end of the course, they will be in a position to solve problems and take more advanced lecture and laboratory courses in areas such as physics, chemistry and biology.

Business plays a fundamental role in all societies through promoting prosperity and innovation. This course will first examine the basic nature of market systems, firms, and their governance. The foundations of business entrepreneurship and creativity are then explored; followed by an examination of uncertainty, risk and information problems as pervasive features of all economies. Key functional and strategic challenges in business are then studied: finance, marketing and branding, pricing, incentive design, negotiation, and managing people and operations. The course will feature a range of contemporary and historical examples and students will work together on a business proposal. It will also offer some practical early-career advice.

Objectives:
The course will equip students with an understanding of key business principles and issues that will be valuable in any career. In addition, it aims to foster broader SILS learning outcomes such as

+ a participatory mindset through active and collegial engagement with class activities.

+ enhanced analytical reasoning, research and presentation skills.

+ further ability to work independently, through proactive study of video-on-demand (VOD) and written class materials - tested through class quizzes - and collaboratively, through the group project.

+ further appreciation for a diversity of perspectives through class discussions and problem-solving in the group project.

Strong design cultures have proven to be a source of resilience and prosperity for nations, cities and enterprises. As recent Ai developments portend disruption of industries, work, and familiar career paths, this course aims to equip students with a solid understanding of design principles and practice. Once primarily associated with the built environment, physical products, and corporate illustration, design principles have come to be widely applied to experiences, systems and processes, places and identities. The course demonstrates how design thinking represents a distinctive way of seeing and thinking, in contrast to those of the familiar humanities and sciences, yet complements and strengthens a liberal arts education. Design is optimistic, aims to make a difference through problem-finding and solving, and is inherently multi-disciplinary. By exploring the evolution of design practice through historical and contemporary examples, and a group project of design inquiry, students will begin to cultivate a design mindset.

Objectives:
It is anticipated that students will

+ demonstrate sound foundational knowledge of the history of design practice, principles and education, and familiarity with major debates over the scope and purposes of design.

+ show active engagement with illuminative historical and contemporary examples of design-centred enterprises.

+ be alert to examples of poor design experienced in daily life, sharing insights with classmates to foster a design mindset that is always alert to the potential for better solutions.

+ engage positively with an introduction to the common ‘critique’ practice in design education; complementing the key SILS learning objective of a participatory mindset - engaged, incisive and collegial.

+ through active collaboration with class colleagues in a group project, conduct an effective design inquiry; demonstrating research and observational skills, effective refining of the design problem, judgment in evaluating viable solutions, and persuasive presentation of findings and propositions.

+ reflect upon, and articulate understanding of, the distinctiveness of design as a field of knowledge, mindset and practice and its relationship to the liberal arts.

The goal of this advanced seminar series is to foster students’ creative confidence, design and visual literacy, and understanding of the distinct business challenges in industries in which creativity, sensibility, the consumer experience and cultural resonance are key. The transformation of enterprises and work is accelerating with digitisation and Ai, disrupting industries and once-stable career paths. This seminar’s premise is that we can learn valuable lessons from the creative and cultural industries; notable for managing uncertainty, producing original and meaningful experiences, aesthetic regard, and problem discovery and resolution through design.

Under the general rubric of ‘Creative Industries’, it has the following three semester sub-themes, in this order: Creative by Design (Fall I), Selling Sensibility (Spring I), and The Design Enterprise (Fall III).

The seminar is complemented by my new intermediate course in the Fall, Design and Enterprise.

Students therefore are expected to take that course or ‘audit’ it informally through periodic lecture attendance and through active engagement with the course materials made available on Moodle (access will be arranged if not enrolled.) Students accepted to the seminar are urged to use the priority registration option to secure a place in the Design and Enterprise class. Please note that for students who have previously taken my Designing Corporate Communications course you will be unable to enrol in the new course because it shares the same course code with the old course. About one-third of the course content will overlap and I will arrange for auditing the new content.

Objectives:
+ enhanced creative confidence and visual literacy.

+ further aptitude for reflective learning and practice.

+ insight into design as a distinctive way of seeing and thinking.

+ becoming comfortable with the critique process of one’s own works in a class context.

+ understanding of creativity and debates around its importance and scope for fostering it.

+ increased ease of active participation in conversations around enterprise, creativity, design and sensibilities.

+ familiarity with business aspects of the uncertainty-prone creative industries, such as managing costs, incentive design and assigning decision rights, rights to rents, the role of gatekeepers and the impacts of digital transformation.

In the second semester of our Creative Industries zemi series we will explore the increasing importance of ‘sensibility’in modern economies: how the ‘enterprise of taste’has come to shape our cities, our public culture, identities and our economic prospects. We will explore the ecologies of sensibility in various national and sub-national contexts through weekly exploration of industry case-studies. We will examine cuisine, including ‘coffee culture’and beverages such wine and cocktails, hairdressing, fashion, ‘select’lifestyle retail and media, product design, architecture, event design, photography, and the academy. A key organizational premise is that the boundaries of these industries are not merely fluid, but are routinely and deliberately spanned in profoundly important ways by creative entrepreneurs and arbiters of taste, in processes of sensibility-shaping for commercial gain. Spatial co-location has become a new norm as urban sites compete to attract consumers in an era when mobility, virtual connectivity and online-retailing of goods and services has become the norm. In all of these industries there is a shared regard for creativity, and the discourse of design has increased influence, but there is also a regard for ‘authenticity’ that is in part a regard for contemporary ‘authentic’ sincere, authorial-like, acts of creativity. It also often more or less explicitly entails a custodial component: carrying forth of traditions of good practice in a field, a respect for origins, forebears in the field, and a ‘mindful’ regard for process and inputs. In an increasingly digitally-enabled world there is a renewed regard for materiality, for the artisanal; at least in spirit.

Objectives:
Through exploration of contemporary and historical case studies students will gain a deeper insight into the analytics of the creative industries, encompassing business, design and aesthetic perspectives. In addition, the seminar will cultivate further core SILS learning objectives, such as:

+ insight into the plurality of ways of thinking and seeing.

+ appreciation of the multi-disciplinary nature of creative problems and their resolution.

+ the powerful creative resource that diversity can be.

The course examines principles necessary for developing marketing strategy for customers, consumers, and public, with attention to delineating strategic plans and identifying target markets. Multiple elements of the marketing mix (e.g., product development and management, pricing, distribution, and communication) are surveyed.

Objectives:
In this course, students will:

1) understand the role of marketing within society and within an economic system

2) learn the vital role of marketing within a firm and the necessary relationships between marketing and the other functional areas of business

3) consider the various decision areas within marketing and the tools and methods used by marketing managers for making decisions

4)learn key marketing principles and terminology

5) appreciate how a marketing perspective is important in your own personal and professional development

We live in a society where questions of difference and diversity play an increasingly central role in debates over cultural values, public policy, and the shape of our daily lives. This course is an introduction to studying the diversity of contemporary human culture, both within and outside of Japan and issues concerning globalization and interconnectedness. This course introduces various theories of difference, with particular attention paid to race, ethnicity, and nationality. It will provide students with an understanding of the cultural diversity of our changing society by examining and discussing the values and characteristics of different communities and the dynamics of power. We will explore issues of equality, prejudice, and discrimination by engaging with theories of difference that set up categories of difference and how these are discussed inside and outside of Japan, as well as the work of people who attempt to disrupt these categories. Please remember that you will be reading material from multiple viewpoints, engaging in difficult conversations with people you may or may not know, and, hopefully, “trying on” many different ways of seeing the world.

Objectives:
• Explain such concepts as race/ethnicity, nationalism, minority, and diversity

• Think cross-culturally, critically, and collaboratively about the cultures and practices of “Japan” in specific and changing sociocultural contexts.

• Analyze, apply, and extend conceptual material both informally and formally through discussion and writing.

• Think critically about the relationship between cultural differences, personal experiences, and power dynamics.

• Understand and analyze a complex set of privileges we live with and how differently we are situated in society accordingly

• Converse civilly with people whose backgrounds, social positions, and beliefs are different from yours.

• Envision different ways to realize equality and equity

Thiscourse is designed to familiarize you with some of the basic terms and conceptsin the field of communication studies, to enhance your understanding of therole of communication in your everyday life, and to give you opportunities toimprove your skills in interacting with others. Over the course of thesemester, we will examine key themes in the discipline involving the social,political, economic, cultural, and technological contexts of many forms ofcommunication, from interpersonal to public communication. As a result of taking this class, you shouldhave a more sophisticated understanding of what is involved in many forms ofcommunication.

Objectives:
• Develop an understanding of communication as a dynamic process that occurs in a variety of contexts to inform our understanding of self and other, and the world we live in

• Think critically about identity, difference, language, culture, and power as constructed through communication

• Reflect on our communicative behaviors and practices, as well as those of others in everyday practice

• Analyze, apply, and extend conceptual material in class discussion, research, and writing

• Increase our competence as communicators

This intermediate course is an introduction to the idea of "intersectionality" in gender studies— in which we take as our starting point the idea that gender itself is largely a cultural construction and a phenomenon that intersects with other cultural constructs that societies have about race, age, nationality, body, sexuality, desire, ability, privilege, power, science and many other discourses. Indeed, gender is embedded so deeply in nearly everything we do and think that it is quite difficult to become conscious of the ways in which we literally gender our world and create hierarchies that empower some people and marginalize others. The way we think about gender literally creates insiders and outcasts in our social systems and also can cut us off from seeing the larger fluidities and connections between people, societies, and ways of being in the world. This course thus aims to equip each student with an awareness of how studying gender is essential to understanding society and making meaningful change in the world, and to offer tools and language that can help each student analyze and critique gender and power in everyday life. "Gender Studies" itself is a very broad field—the approach we take is built on feminism, masculinities studies, and queer studies, and thus our focus is especially on equality and being inclusive.
Throughout the course, we will examine themes of bias, equality, hegemony, marginalization and minorities, social justice and human rights. We will also look especially at how gender studies is useful in thinking about Japanese history and histories of the larger Pacific and Asia region. In so doing, we will examine how understanding gender helps us to think critically about power and the institutionalization of inequality. At the same time, we will engage in our study and discussion in a spirit of self-reflexivity, creativity, and open-mindedness, attempting to go beyond binaries and overly fixed categories.

A core part of this course will be making a distinction between labels and lived experience, to truly examine what gender is and why we gender the world, each other, and ourselves as we do, as well as what implications this has for each of us. The methodological considerations of gender studies and feminist inquiry, as well as some contextual discussions of how those methodologies emerged, will be complemented with examples of how gender intersects with a wide range of topics historically in Japan, other parts of Asia, Oceania, and the United States. Through lectures and discussions of historical examples drawn mainly from a Pacific and Asian context, students will be encouraged to observe the intersectionality between race, ethnicity, region, sexual orientation, class, age, health, and many other backgrounds, such as colonization and globalization. Through occasional films, Zoom discussions, and extra-credit field activities in Tokyo, discussions, surveys, and reflective projects, students will also be given an opportunity to apply the concepts learned in class to their own lived experiences to enrich their learning.

*NOTE-- during the pandemic, this course was redesigned supplementarily with comprehensive online modules. Owing to the new 100 minute class period time, this course schedule will thus combine two back-to-back periods on campus, but at other times, there will be plenty of on-demand content to make it easier for your to learn, review, and to compensate for situations when we cannot meet in person. 200 minutes weekly equates to 3.5 hours of study time, which is better spread out if you have some regularly scheduled class time combined with some online learning you can do at your own pace. A clear schedule will be provided at the beginning of the semester.

Objectives:
Upon completion of this semester, you will be expected to have a working knowledge of the basics of gender studies methodologies, concepts, and historical contexts. You will also cultivate an appreciation for the rich diversity of genders, sexualities, identities, and cultural practices in Japan, the Pacific, the United States, and many other parts of the world. You will also be challenged to reflect on the ways in which you personally “do” gender to construct your own identities and participate in society, and thus to consider problems of your own engagement with power, privilege, and inequality. Ideally, students should be able to reflexively use gender studies as a tool to critique power in society in their future studies and careers.

※in-person ONLY
This interactive lecture-based course seeks to identify what it is people mean when they invoke the term ‘culture’. Throughout, we will critique the term “culture” in different contexts to examine whether it is a defensible position to justify the activities of different actors. To achieve this, we will need to examine our own position, critique it, then develop a defensible stance that defines and understands culture (and cultures). To do this we will consider how culture is transmitted, how it evolves, the different values it promotes, whether culture has boundaries, and critique the concepts of gender and nationality in culture. Particular focus will be placed upon five topics. (1) Identity, through which we consider how culture/s use tools to create and maintain individual and group identity. (2) Cultural Legitimacy, where the ideas of cultural relativism, consumerism (Pop v Mass) are addressed. (3) Language, through which we consider semiotic values and examine how cultures utilize the media to reinforce values. This will then lead us to (4) Taboo, wherein we will critique real world contemporary examples to consider our values, ethics and morality. And (5) we will reflect on the way our brains process and make sense of the information in the worlds we create.

Objectives:
By the end of this course you should be able to recognize how the term culture is applied to sustain “values”. As this course blends practical components to demonstrate culture in context, you should be able to critique your own values and understand how you process information and identify with the world around you. You will be expected to demonstrate both theoretical and applied knowledge by the end of the course.

This is a unique culture cluster course which focuses on advancing students’ framework for investigating fundamental questions in culture, language, and law. Class discussion will focus on how cultural values are reflected in language, reasoning, and in legal communication. This course includes students’ participation in reading core texts selected for enhancing analytical and logical reasoning from the critical perspective. Readings includes critical cultural theories covering themes related to rights, coercion, equality, justice, diversity, and ethical responsibilities.

The course is divided into three sections. First two sections are devoted to learning various cultural theories in relation to private and public law. The remaining weeks focus on the issue analysis. Students will select issues and will engage in interactive discussions. This course is also writing intensive. Upon the completion of the course, students will gain confidence in academic writing in English, issue spotting, and will acquire communication skills for carrying out a coherent argument.

Objectives:
The purpose of the course is to help students build strategic thinking skills for conflict resolution. The course attempts to unveil multi-layered cultural assumptions by identifying cultural particulars and socio-political issues via hypothetical examples and court cases.

This course explores the ways in which Japanese Occidentalism and Western Orientalism (Japonism) are interrelated in their representations of Japan.
In historical and cultural encounters between Japan and the West, Western countries have often conceived stereotyped images of Japan regardless of its social and historical realities. Cultural stereotypes such as the “salaryman” and images of high-tech industries—let alone more traditional icons such as “geisha,” “Mount Fuji,” and “kabuki”—are among the most familiar examples. These are culturally biased and distorted representations that do not necessarily correspond to the lived realities of Japan and its people.

However, it is not only Western countries that have produced distorted images of Japan. More interestingly, Japan itself has actively constructed its own self-image in response to equally distorted images of Europeans and Americans. Through Japanese perceptions of the Western “Other,” Western nations have often been idealized as “white” and therefore imagined as “beautiful,” “intelligent,” and “strong.” At the same time, Japan has frequently portrayed itself as a nation continually oppressed or “bashed” by Western powers, struggling to recover from this condition (cf. the Meiji Restoration and the economic recovery following the Second World War).

By reading a wide range of texts and media representing Western Orientalism and Japanese Occidentalism, this course aims to analyze these constructed images of Japan and to explore the possibility of proposing alternative representations.

Objectives:
1): To analyze East–West relations in terms of power, gender, and race; 2) To investigate the ways in which the East and the West have negotiated with each other culturally and politically.

What is material about communication and media? While these two concepts seem to be referring to immaterial symbolic exchange, what enables communication and media are constructed material objects and artifacts. This course focuses on the materiality of communication and media technologies. We situate this materiality within historical contexts and definitions of history themselves bound up within the social diffusion of different media forms. We understand the study of the materiality of communication/media technology as a form of critical practice, without which a robust understanding of the relationships between and among gender and technologies, labor and technologies,mediation and mobility, ways that space is conceived, produced, and maintained would not be possible in communication or media studies.

Objectives:
- Understand a set of influential theories within media, communication, and cultural studies

- Read texts within these fields and reflect on their arguments

- Reflect on the materialities of algorithmic media such as the Internet from a critical and historicizing perspective

- Perform analytical thinking (within theoretical, abstract categories) as well as synthetic, integrative thinking (relating theories to concrete cases and applying theoretical categories responsibly)

- Reflect on your own media environment and its material construction

- Make concise, convincing arguments in discussions.

Thiscourse approaches media and popular culture as a dynamic field of production,consumption, and contestation. After an initial phase of understanding forms ofpopular culture, the semester will focus primarily on case studies from Japan,along with some comparative examples. We will learn to examine historical andcontemporary meaning-making processes in context. Lectures will expose studentsto academic vocabulary and approaches and provide tools to examine popularculture and media. Students will bring personal experiences and observations tobear on class discussions and presentations. There will also be in-classscreenings. By the end of the term, students will be able to think cross-culturally,critically, and collaboratively about not only media and popular culture butalso everyday life and the world in which we live.

Objectives:
• Think cross-culturally, critically, and collaboratively about media and popular culture in specific and changing sociocultural contexts.

• Understand and explain a variety of academic positions that inform the study of popular culture and media.

• Make connections between popular culture and larger patterns of social change.

• Apply the theoretical perspectives we have studied to specific cultural texts (i.e. be able to relate theoretical arguments to specific examples drawn from popular culture).

• Be able to engage in a sophisticated and respectful class discussion of topics relevant to media and popular culture.

• Refine critical thinking skills and oral and written communication in English.

This seminar examines major issue of diasporas and migrants in Asia. Theory of multiculturalism, globalization and contemporary dynamics of race and ethnicity will studied. Topics to be covered will include Japanese diaspora, Filipino diaspora, Chinese diaspora, Korean diaspora, Indian diaspora, statelessness etc. Various issued as education, identity, citizenship, passport, language inheritance and cultural transformation of different diaspora and migrants groups in Japan will be discussed as well.

Objectives:
Expect every participant to write individual report related on migrants and diaspora based on fieldwork.

The objective of this course is to help students understand Korea and Asia as a region by analyzing universal and particular features unique to Korea different from other East Asian nations. This course is designed to help students enhance their research writing skill. This seminar also focuses on conducting individual research projects. A student is to write a graduation thesis based on his or her research theme. The seminar puts an emphasis on writing. Students in this culture seminar will have opportunities to participate in academic conferences. Since writing is a difficult and challenging task, the instructor and students will interactively engage in discussion sessions. Themes do not necessarily have to be confined to one region. Comparative studies are welcome. For your reference, refer to a sample list of prior research themes: Patriarchy in Korean Conglomerate Firms, Urban Planning Projects in Japan, A Comparative Analysis of Gender in Korean Proverbs, Glocal Concepts in the Disney Resort, Kafka and Existential Literature, Power Structure in Media, Contradictions in the Kawai culture, Semiotic Analysis on Zainichi Kankokujin, Representation of Zainichi Chosenjin, Higher Education in Japan and in Korea, Language of Accounting Frauds, Rhetoric in Kana and Hangul, Oriental Discourse in FTA and in Korea and Japan, Ideology in Medieval Education for Women in Japan and Korea, The Notion of Oppa and the Korean Wave, and Entropy and Business: Nissan and Alibaba.

Objectives:
This course is comprised of two parts: the first half of the course focuses on theories and the latter half concentrates on the application of theories to social, political, and cultural issues. The theory part will explore theories from social sciences and humanistic subjects and the application part will focus on how these theories can be applied to the historical and contemporary issues in Asia.

Chinese migrants are spread all over the world therefore we can encounter Chinatowns everywhere. Chinese migrants are often referred as cosmopolitan or global citizens. On the other hand, it is also true that Chinese migrants are an ethnic group that has often been tossed up by the turbulent situation in international politics and the volatility of national regimes.
This course will study Chinese migrants in the world as different case studies. Also will analyze Chinese migrants from political, economical, legal, and cultural angles to understand their relationship with global issues. Comparative studies with other diasporas are recommended.

Objectives:
Understand issues of migration from global perspective as well as local perspective.

This course is designed to help students to understand the United States in terms of race and ethnic relations. In particular we will focus on pop music and films from the 1960s to the present: the 1960s, because it was the decade when racial and ethnic minorities as well as sexual minorities were getting more and more active socially and politically, and the 1970s and after, because more people started to pay attention what is today known as "DEI," that is, "diversity, equality, and inclusion."
Our purpose in the class is to understand historical settings in which people's awareness of these issues are raised and also to think about where we are heading in the future.

Objectives:
To understand the United States in terms of race and ethnic relations.

This semester will continue our discussion of Anthropology and Sociology of Law. Our focus this semester will be the Legal Anthropology of Sex and Marriage. The interpretation and application (or evasion) of family law, and the imagination of law as it applies to the regulation of sex will be explored in three geographical contexts: Japan, Iran, and southern Spain among Roma (Gypsy) communities. The course will also deal with the role of judges and the courts in the adjudication of cases and the production of jurisprudence.

Objectives:
To acquire an anthropological perspective for application to the analysis of law and social and cultural phenomena.

This semester will continue our discussion of Anthropology and Sociology of Law. Our focus this semester will be the Legal and Social Anthropology of Modern practices of Witchcraft, Sorcery and Magic. Main questions to consider include: How do modern discourses about Modernity, Science and Rationality oppose themselves to Witchcraft, Sorcery and Magic and to other seemingly 'imaginary' or 'irrational' practices? How, conversely, are Witchcraft, Sorcery, and Magic opposed to, or how do they exist in parallel with, Scientific or Rational understandings of the physical and spiritual worlds? How are Witchcraft, Sorcery and Magic used by people to act, sometimes with extreme violence, against other members of their societies, oftentimes women? How have modern legal systems legislated or handled cases of violence by Witchcraft or Sorcery? How have Social Anthropologists apprehended Witchcraft and Magic differently than governing bodies and their legal systems, and how can anthropological and historical perspectives be used to promote understanding of articulations of modern witchcraft and magic practices in post-colonial contexts?

Objectives:
This course aims to make students familiar with the main body of literature in the Anthropology and Sociology of law. Short introductory lectures will be complemented by class discussion and group discussion, presentations and activities.

Generally this class will meet in the classroom for our sessions. There may be one guest lecture. Students intending to attend graduate school in the social sciences, or those who intend to attend law school may benefit from taking this seminar.

All students must read all materials and be willing to be discussion leader for specific dates and assigned readings.

Human lives have been embedded in art or technē—part of the etymological origin of “technology”—that makes the material world legible and workable for us, through which we create our culture. “Technology” and “culture,” however, are deceptively common terms. We participate in culture and are constantly surrounded by technology but seldom pause and reflect on them. What is culture? What is technology? How are the two related? What is our relationship with each or both? How do we live in a culture surrounded by technological objects, artifacts, structures, and institutions? How does technology change culture, and vice versa? The answers to these questions are complicated and open-ended. This course is designed to provide students with theoretical tools to begin asking questions for themselves and seeking better answers. Whether one applies these questions and answers to their job, life, or personal interests, the knowledge gained in this class facilitates the creation of a description of the world that is far more complicated and fascinating. Over the course of the semester, we will examine key themes in technology studies that involve the social, political, economic, and cultural contexts in which technological artifacts, services, and platforms are produced, distributed, networked, and used.

Objectives:
- Understand and explain a variety of academic positions that inform the study of technology and culture.

- Make connections between technological artifacts and larger patterns of sociocultural change.

- Apply the theoretical perspectives we have studied to specific objects (i.e., be able to relate theoretical arguments to specific examples).

- Be able to engage in a sophisticated and respectful class discussion of topics relevant to technology and culture.

The purpose of this course is to study anime movies and serials by focusing on their stylistic details and thematic motifs on the one hand, and the socio-historical context of their production and consumption on the other. In addition to such central themes and motifs as urban space,war, violence, ruins, environment, magic, curse, the non-human, and the post-human, the students will be also introduced to the history of anime/Japanese animation. We will analyze the formal and stylistic specificity of each anime(narrative structure, world-setting, audio-visual form, etc.) by linking them to a wide range of issues and questions pertaining to aesthetics, subculture, history,and politics. The tentative list of anime movies and serials to be examined include, but not limited to, Ghost in the Shell:Stand Alone Complex, Spirited Away, Howl’s Moving Castle, Puella Magi Madoka Magica, Violet Evergarden, The Tale of the Princess Kaguya, Jujutsu Kaisen 0: The Movie, etc. We’ll also watch and study short animation films by Tezuka Osamu and others.

Objectives:
--Students will learn why anime is an important cultural text, and what socio-political, historical, and philosophical issues they often raise for further critical thinking.

--Students are expected to acquire analytical skills to discuss anime as a complex text from thematic and formal perspectives.

Whilethe study of communication historically has had a diverse focus, spanning fromspeech and theater to film, journalism, and public relations, the importance ofcritical social science approaches is ever-increasing in today’s world, wheretechnological objects and platforms exert a profound influence on communitiesand communication in all cultural contexts. The goal of this advanced seminaris to introduce students to social science research methodology employed in thefield of critical communication studies and cultural studies. It is designed toexpose students to ethnographic research methods. Students will learn not onlyto analyze and evaluate qualitative data but also to develop research questionsand produce preliminary field notes on the issues of their interest.

Objectives:
• Familiarize with the methodological approaches in communication and cultural studies.

• Develop an orientation to central subjects, methodological tools, and epistemological questions in communication and cultural studies through reading ethnographic works

• Develop an elementary experience of fieldwork through participant observation and interpretation of data

• Be able to engage in a sophisticated and respectful class discussion.

• Apply critical thinking and develop a research proposal of one’s own interest.

Photography has become a part of our everyday lives. In fact, few of us leave home without a camera, but how much do we really understand about the history, processes, and power of the photographic image?
This course is designed to give students a firm foundational understanding of the development and history of photography, themes and genres in modern and contemporary photography, and some first-hand experience of the challenges involved in producing a deliberate and considered photograph.
Although this is not a practical class, there will be some introduction to the fundamentals of shooting photography. There will also be some opportunities to share your own photographs through assignments for this class.

Objectives:
To develop a deeper understanding of the photographic medium—its relationship to technological development, and aesthetic, cultural and political relevance.

This course offers an introduction to the history of Japanese film. We examine diverse media ecologies and topics ranging from masterpieces by great directors such as Ozu Yasujiro, Mizoguchi Kenji, and Kurosawa Akira, to the history of industrial genres and industrial structures. Acquiring knowledge of the history of Japanese cinema, students are expected to develop a historical and critical perspective on today’s media environment.

Objectives:
Students will acquire basic knowledge of Japanese cinema, become able to analyze films with the knowledge of Japanese visual culture, and improve critical reading skills for visual texts.

This seminar is designed to support students in conducting their own research and writing their graduation thesis relating to cinema and media studies. Research topics can be varied according to students’ interests including but not limited to East Asian cinema, Hollywood cinema, global art cinema, documentary films, anime, and so on. Since the goal is to complete a graduation thesis, our focus is students’ output. Throughout three semesters, students are expected to present their progress to receive feedback from members of the seminar.

As for the first semester, students will study the basics of cinema and media studies using some introductory texts. Through discussing the texts together, students will find their research topics and explore possible research frameworks.

Objectives:
Students will find and deepen understanding of their topics (1st semester), conduct research (2nd semester), and write a graduation thesis (3rd semester).

This course combines weekly lectures with student-led discussions and presentations exploring the translation, production, and reception of Japanese literature in the Anglosphere in the twenty-first century.

As the course focuses on a specialized topic, it is best suited to students with some prior knowledge of Japanese and/or international literature, as well as an interest in literary translation, cross-cultural exchange, publishing, and the historical and sociological dimensions of literary production.

The course will be conducted in both Japanese and English. Students should be able to (1) follow lectures in both languages and (2) complete substantial reading assignments in Japanese and English, although most theoretical readings will be provided in English. Students are welcome to participate in either Japanese or English, whichever they feel best enables them to express their ideas. They should also be comfortable engaging in discussions in which classmates may use either language.

Those interested in an interactive, workshop-based class focusing on the practice of literary translation may find that my course Translation as Creative Writing is a better fit. Other students may be interested in pairing the two classes so that they have both a content-focused class and a more interactive practice-focused class. SILS also offers a range of compelling literature/translation courses by other instructors on topics ranging from Modern Japanese Literature, postcolonial literature and the theory of translation.

Objectives:
By the end of the course, you will have:

- become familiar with key concepts related to literary translation and the international production and circulation of literature;

- become familiar with the principal actors, structures, and processes involved in literary production in the Japanese and Anglophone literary spheres, including the roles of authors, editors,

- publishers, literary agents, translators, reviewers, critics, book designers, festival directors, and government and non-profit organizations; and

- developed a comprehensive understanding of the English translation, production, and reception of Japanese literature in the twenty-first century.

Creative nonfiction is one of the most prevalent modes of discourse in the 21st century. It is everywhere from literary magazines to newspapers, books, blogs and websites. In this course, students will read, write, and investigate an array of creative nonfiction writing such as personal narrative/memoir, profile, essays on popular culture, and the lyric essay. Students will read a diverse range of works from various national traditions for their craft and technique. This course will expose students to read and write in forms ranging from popular, literary, and experimental. Some of the authors we will read are: Zadie Smith, Maggie Nelson, Rebecca Brown, Eula Biss, Hanif Abdurraqib, Jenny Zhang, Virginia Woolf and others. Students will learn the core elements of prose writing: voice, scene, description, and structure. The final portfolio will consist of three original revised essays or a video essay.

This is an advanced course where students will be required to engage in combination of writing exercises (including collaborative exercises),
class discussions (of assigned readings) and workshops. The writing workshop--where you will be asked to provide detailed and constructive feedback on peer work--will be a central component of the course.

By the end of the course you will have produced a significant body of writing in the form of:
1) three revised essays of around 2,500 words
2) various drafts of the following essays: personal narrative, pop culture, and lyric essay
3) written responses to weekly assignments. Approx. 500 words
4) written responses to peer work: Approx. 800 words
5) other writing generated through exercises assigned in-class

The average length of weekly reading assignments (essays) will be between 10,000 to 20,000 words and there will be an additional 3,000 to 6,000 words of peer work to read on workshop weeks. This means that on a busy week you may have more than 25,000 words of reading and 3,000 words of writing (essays, peer feed-back,reading responses, etc.).

While there is no prerequisite for this course, given the workload and strict emphasis on attendance/participation, this advanced course is recommended for students who:
1) have previously taken creative writing and/or literature courses at the university level
2) are capable of handling reading assignments of significant length in English
3) enjoy actively participating in and leading group work and class discussions
4) are able to work in an organized manner (including submitting weekly assignments beforehand via Moodle)
5) enjoy thinking/writing both creatively and analytically) and already have ideas about writing that they would like to pursue as part of the course
6) students will be required to work collaboratively and critically with classmates on a weekly basis

The expectation is that students will attend every class and submit all assignments.
Course Delivery Method:
Face-to-Face (F2F)

Please also note that:

1) Students will be asked to submit assignments via Moodle.
2) Late registration of attendance/submission of assignments will not be accepted.
3) This class will be taught in-person on campus.

Objectives:
By the end of the course you will have:

- been exposed to (and hopefully inspired by) works of various contemporary writers

- learned to read a text closely and analyze a piece of writing critically

- learned how to read and revise your own work (not only for language but also for ideas)

- become better equipped to provide constructive feedback to peer work

This course will center around literary translation workshops in which students will be asked to provide constructive feedback to peer work as well as take turns facilitating the workshops. Students will be asked to work with peers to create joint translations as part of their class work. The emphasis of the course is to provide a space for participants to explore literary translation in its many forms (and not to train professional literary translators).

By the end of the course you will have produced:
1) a dozen or so translations of selected excerpts (approx. 400 words) from reading assignments (short stories, essays, graphic novels, etc.):
2) written responses to class assignments:

Given the workload, emphasis on attendance/participation, and class format, this advanced course is recommended for students who:
1) have previously taken writing and/or literature courses at the university level
2) are capable of handling reading assignments of significant length in English and Japanese
3) enjoy actively participating in and leading group work and class discussions
4) are able to work in an organized manner (including submitting weekly assignments beforehand online)

English will be the primary language of instruction/communication in the classroom. However, students will be expected to be able to handle literary texts in both English and Japanese. Please note that this course requires you to work as part of a group to create a joint translation every week, and it is essential that participants are able/willing to provide/receive peer feedback in a professional, respectful and collegial manner as they work in groups.

Objectives:
Objectives:

By the end of the course you will have:

- become familiar with some of the key elements/techniques of literary translation

- been exposed to various literary texts (with a focus on contemporary Japanese and Anglophone literature)

- learned how to read a text closely and analyze a piece of writing critically

- learned how to read and revise your own work

- become better readers of translations

- become better equipped to provide constructive feedback to peer work

* The plan as of January 2022 is for this course to be taught during the Spring 2022 semester through a combination of in-person and online classes. Students need to be able to attend classes both on campus and online in order to register for the course. (Hi-flex option will not be available for this course). Please contact the SILS office with any questions you may have regarding the format of the course.

This advanced creative writing/translation/literature seminar will be organized around workshop discussions of student writing and assigned readings by a range of writers.

By the end of the course, students will have completed:
- several 1) short works of prose fiction or 2) translations of prose fiction or 3) essays on contemporary literature (each around 2,500-3,000 words)
- written responses to weekly reading assignments and peer work

This course will also prepare students write their undergraduate theses comprising a portfolio of 1) short fiction or translation and 2) critical analysis. (Students are also welcome to write theses on topics related to translation studies and contemporary literature).

Given that 1. This course is an ‘advanced’ seminar in creative writing/translation/literature and 2. the course is designed around a series of workshops it is best suited for those:

a) who have taken a number of other creative writing and/or literature courses (whether at SILS or during their study abroad year).
b) are capable of handling reading assignments of significant length
c) enjoy actively participating in and leading group work and class discussions (including leading discussions as a moderator)
d) are able to work in an organized manner (including submitting weekly assignments beforehand online).
e) enjoy thinking/writing both creatively and analytically

Although not a prerequisite, it is recommended that you take one of the other creative writing or translation courses at SILS before registering for/committing to this advanced seminar.

Objectives:
In this course students will:

- complete a short story of around 2,500-3,000 words (as well as several drafts), translation of around 2500-3000 words (as well as several drafts), or translation studies/contemporary literature paper of around 2500-3000 words.

- generate written responses to weekly reading assignments and peer work

- become better equipped with the key tools and techniques of creative writing and translation

- be exposed to (and hopefully inspired by) works of various contemporary writer

- learn to read a text closely and analyze a piece of writing critically

- learn how to read and revise their own work (not only for language but also for ideas)

- learn to provide constructive feedback to their peers

- make progress on their undergraduate thesis

[授業実施方法:Face-to-Face]
The focus of the seminar is media and visual culture. Students will work on research with an eye toward their senior thesis, which can be focused on a wide range of subjects including movies, photography, television, digital media, anime, comics, visual art, architecture, performing arts, etc. The seminar is organized around students’ bi-weekly research presentations, bi-weekly discussions on critical or theoretical texts relevant to their research interests and topics, and individual tutorials and research consultations. We may take a field trip depending on the students' research interest.

Objectives:
--Students will further develop their analytical skill by closely reading theoretical texts.

--Students are expected to finalize a research plan and produce a preliminary version of one thesis chapter.

The focus of the seminar is media and visual culture. Students will work on research with an eye toward their graduation thesis, which can be focused on a wide range of subjects including movies, photography, television, digital media, anime, comics, visual art, architecture, performing arts, etc. This semester, the seminar will not be divided into two sections—one for 3rd and another for 4th year students. At the first meeting, we’ll discuss how to organize weekly classes so that both 3rd and 4th year students can get the most out of the seminar.

Objectives:
--By the end of the semester, 3rd year students are expected to learn how to analyze and discuss media, film, and visual culture critically.

--The goal for 4th year students is to finish a graduation thesis and graduate!

In this class we meet in the classroom regularly. In this seminar, we will learn various cultural expressions such as literature, film, fine arts and other forms of arts; one third of the classes will be used to deepen awareness of those who are going to write graduation thesis; one third of the classes are for lectures of cultural and literary theories to explore various expressions; by using these theories, students are encouraged to deepen their approaches to their own topics of graduation thesis. The last one third of the classes are open for various topics which will be explored based on students’ necessities. Discussion will be introduced based on Socrates method; therefore, each one should finish indicated reading material(s) before each class. Besides lecture-style class contents, graduation thesis proceedings should be shown at the beginning and at the end of the semester by each student; student should prepare power-point material and explain the proceedings orally. When the proceedings are not ideal, it is each student's responsibility to make an appointment with professor to find out necessary materials at library.

Objectives:
The final goal of this seminar is to understand the relations between specific forms of arts and our society; students are expected to understand multiple layers of society composed of various cultural elements through critical ways of thinking.

The major theme of the seminar is to explore various kinds of cultural expressions; in order to feel authentic elements of each expression style or method, we will read various short stories along with visiting nearby museums to broaden our experiences in cultural expressions; since museums are cultural icons in any society, students are assigned to visit at least one museum in Kanto area and make a presentation on each visit. The purpose of this seminar is to enhance students’ knowledge on culture through active learning method of doing fieldworks. Students are expected to do at least one field work project and do presentations based on their research work. Class instruction will be given mainly in Japanese, and students can use either English or Japanese, in presentations and final paper, according to their language abilities and challenges; therefore, participants are requested to be cooperative when other students use the language of your preference. （言語は発表・レポートともに日英使用可。） Discussions and reports can be done either in English or Japanese according to each student’s preference, abilities, challenges. From time to time, to understand several sociological and historical phenomena according to the directions of the discussions in the course, students may broaden the borders of the themes treated in the seminar and extend the research areas to other parts of the world. Particularly in this semester, students are required to explore their own research interests for graduation thesis. Further instructions are given in the classes. Class schedule is tentative and will be adjusted according to the number of seminar students and their research preferences.

Objectives:
The final goal of this seminar is to understand multiple layers of expressions and society composed of cultural elements through critical ways of thinking. Junior students are supposed to decide their graduation thesis topic during this fall semester. To finalize their topic, students should submit summary paper of the topic and each one should be approved by the end of January.

Designed to teach introductory earth and planetary sciences for both science and nonscience majors, encompassing the major disciplines of Geology, Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geobiology, and Astronomy. "Face-to-Face" style.

Objectives:
Students will learn how the universe began and evolved, how the earth was formed and evolved, how life was originated and evolved, and how the earth’s environments evolved through geologic time and will evolve in the future.

Global warming is perhaps the greatest challenge of our era. To meet it requires both a multidisciplinary perspective as well as a solid understanding of fundamental principles. This course aims to introduce students to the basic scientific principles governing Earth’s climate system. It will cover the fundamental physical, chemical and biological concepts relevant to understanding how the climate system works and how humans are perturbing it. Topics to be covered include: physics of blackbody radiation; radiative balance and radiative transfer; circulation of the ocean and atmosphere; the carbon cycle; physics of clouds and aerosols; basic thermodynamics and the water cycle; climate variability over geological history; sea level change; monsoons and El Niño; anthropogenic climate change.

Objectives:
This course aims to introduce students to the fundamentals of Climate Science. By the end of the course, they will have a solid, quantitative understanding of the basic physical and chemical ideas involved, and be prepared to take more advanced courses on topics ranging from environmental modeling to sustainability.

Designed to teach introductory “Earth System Science” for both science and nonscience majors.

In the class, important issues involved in global environmental changes are covered and the system approach is introduced. It will resonate with many students, since the system thinking has been used in virtually every area of inquiry, including branches of both the natural and social sciences.

Active participation in the class as well as discussion, an essential part of this class, is expected. Homework assignments involving some mathematical calculations will be given to students almost every week.

Prerequisite: none, but experience of classes related to environmental sciences would help.

Objectives:
The anticipated goals of this class include the following:

To become familiar with the essence of “system approach”

To be able to use “system approach” for quantitative analysis.

To obtain deeper and wider knowledge of Earth System Science.

To learn ways of critical thinking for various global environmental problems.

Computer modeling is a key tool in science and engineering. This advanced-level course concerns the use of such modeling in understanding and simulating the Earth’s environment. You will learn how to construct simple, yet insightful, mathematical models of various phenomena using basic physical and chemical principles. You will then learn how to formulate the problem in a manner that can be solved on a computer. i.e., as an algorithm. And, finally, you will translate the algorithm into computer code to simulate the phenomenon in question. We will use concrete examples to work through these different generic steps involved in computer modeling. We will also cover fundamental numerical methods such as interpolation, finite difference approximations, time stepping schemes for ordinary differential equations, and methods for solving linear and nonlinear equations. Lastly, we will also touch upon some of the latest developments in the field, for example the use of AI in weather forecasting. The course will be relatively agnostic when it comes to programming language. You can use python or even Excel in many cases.

Objectives:
In this course students will:

1) Learn how to formulate a physical problem as a mathematical one (“mathematical modeling”)

2) Learn how computers deal with numbers and arithmetic (concepts such as floating point, round off error, etc)

3) Learn fundamental numerical methods widely applicable in science, engineering, finance and other fields

4) Learn how to formulate a mathematical model as a computer algorithm

5) Work through a number of practical examples involving environmental phenomena

IMPORTANT: This course willbe taught Face-To-Face.
The broad theme of this seminar is the interdependencybetween human society and the environment. Through readings and discussions, wewill cover the underlying science and explore many different aspects of thistheme. Topics include: natural climate phenomena such as El Niño; air and waterpollution; disease; economic development (why some countries are richer thanothers); global warming; sustainability; challenges and economic opportunitiesof the so-called “Energy Transition”; socioeconomic,political and geopolitical implications of climate change.

Objectives:
By the end of this seminar students should get an appreciation for the many ways in which humans interact with the environment, as well as the many challenges (and economic opportunities) of tackling climate change.

All classes of this course will be conducted in the classroom on the face-to-face basis.
This course is a two-unit lesson designed primarily for non-business majors to offer basic knowledge both on international business practices, and the theory behind them. The course covers a large area of business practices for both exporters and importers. Current topics relating to international trade and business are also picked up in this course. As a quiz (multiple-choice and true/false questions) will be assigned to the students in each class, the students are required to submit answers of the quiz within three (3) days of each class. The class is a mixture of a lecture and participation by the students.

This course will be performed by the lecturer who possesses working experiences and will be taught based on such lecturer's working experiences.

Objectives:
This class aims to attain to help students understand the basic logics why cross-border business exists and also the significance behind the documents or procedures for trade practices. In addition, this course intends to provide students with an opportunity to learn about international business situation from actual business perspective.

In recent years, increasing importance of private sector as a major architect of social and public goals. More private investments and lending are promoting public ivesteement projets, from transportation infrastructure to Moon rocket these days. We would like to partner with private investors to achieve a common well-being for the world. Public-private-partnership (PPP) is becoming a default for most Developing Financial Institutions (DFIs) such as the World Bank, Asian Development Bank (ADB), and Japan Bank for International Cooperation or Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) or Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).

This course is intended to provide analytical tools to quantitatively evaluate the impact of policy interventions initiated by these public and private agencies and investors. We will critically review existing projects in order to feedback innovative ideas for improvements. Wherever possible, examples are used to aid the exposition. Certainly, this is not a course on pure microeconomics or welfare economics exclusively.

Microeconomics and welfare concepts that are relevant in impact evaluation will be discussed. Particular attention will be given to practical analysis with emphasis on the use of shadow prices, the use of consumers’ surplus and the problems of valuing goods that do not have market prices. Students are encouraged to participate effectively in class discussions.

This course uses STATA Ver 18 (to be installed invidually to your PC or MAC) every week. Students are expected to bring PC or Mac with EXCEL and STATA installed, available free for enrolled students.

Objectives:
Ability to evaluate impacts of public projects using panel data

This course is an introduction to finance. The objective is to familiarize students with financial concepts and tools used in an international business setting. The course covers the basic principles of financial management and applies them to the decisions faced by financial managers in global firms. Topics include standard financial decision-making tools, the role of stock and bond markets, and the risk & return tradeoff. Whenever relevant, we will refer to the academic literature in finance for deeper insight on particular topics.

This is an intermediate level course at SILS. While one course in economics, business, or accounting is highly recommended before enrolling in this class - it is not a requirement. However, the instructor will assume students have a sincere interest in learning finance, have enrolled in the SILS required "introductory statistics" course, and have an appreciation for quantitative methods.

Objectives:
After taking this class, the student should be:

1) be familiar with financial securities such as stocks and bonds (Japan context).

2) be able to explain and critique a net present value and internal rate of return analysis for a project (financial decision making).

3) be able to explain the risk-return trade-off as discussed in finance (Sharpe ratio, CAPM).

4) acquire working knowledge (familiar with) of EXCEL for discounting exercises and other finance related functions.

5) develop a solid understanding of the link between topics covered in finance and international business (and other areas/fields in business).

6) acquire the basic skills and knowledge to undertake intermediate and advanced course work in the area of finance (including first year MBA finance)

This course covers the fundamental concepts of finance, including financial transactions, related financial instruments, and risk assessment. It also examines monetary policy aimed at maintaining financial market stability and the role of central banks in implementing such policies.

Finance is a discipline grounded in mathematical modeling. Although this is an intermediate-level course, it is structured around these analytical methods. The level of mathematical rigor is comparable to that of the required Statistics course. Students who are less familiar with mathematical expressions are encouraged to deepen their understanding through careful study of the textbook and consistent practice with problem sets.

Objectives:
The objectives of this course are to enable students to develop a solid understanding of:

(i) the roles and functions of financial systems;

(ii) how contemporary theories in finance and banking analyze financial crises; and

(iii) how new financial regimes aimed at preventing such crises can be designed from a theoretical perspective.

In addition, the course will be taught with reference to the Certified Member Analyst (CMA) examinations administered by the Securities Analysts Association of Japan (SAAJ), particularly the subjects “Securities Analysis and Portfolio Management” and “Analysis of Markets and the Economy.”

We will apply core micro and macro development theories to diagnose why development succeeds or fails in specific country or sectoral contexts. In particular, we will use quantitative tools for measuring poverty, vulnerability, inequality and basic needs outcomes, and interpret these indicators for policy analysis.

Students should be able to formulate evidence-based policy recommendations for governments, donors, and NGOs that align with the analytical tools and case-study evidence presented in the textbook and handouts.

Fiscal issuse on social security is a very important topic in modern society. Why do we need the social securities? Will the private sector be able to provide them? This lecture aims to learn the roles of government concerning the topics on social security and its policies. We emphasize the criteria of efficiency and equity. Government plays an import role in performing the function of income redistribution through the social securities. We study the theories and practices of social securities related to income distribution and redistribution. The social security directly relates to the topics on welfare economics. Hence, this course also tries to analyze the social security at the viewpoints of welfare economics. In Japan, the social securities are composed of social insurance and social welfare. You will find out the huge increase at the expenditures of social security in Japan with the aging of society following the drastic increase of issuances of national bonds after the burst of bubbles in early 1990s. .We discuss Japanese current systems of social securities including annuity pensions, health care, and other social welfare programs.
This class will be conducted by face-to-face. I will provide lecture notes and lecture materials through the [Announcement] on the class of [Fiscal Issues on Social Security　01] in advance (maybe early April).

Objectives:
The course aims to lead students to understand both theory and practice of social securities. Three import functions of government are resource allocation, income redistribution, and macroeconomic stabilization. Among those functions, the social security is mainly concerned with the function of income redistribution. To implement the income redistribution function the government is required to finance social security expenditures. Students need to get familiar with the proper understanding on the relations between social security system and income redistribution, and to evaluate public policies or expenditure programs.

Our class aims to understand the theory and practice of taxation and well-being. We highly emphasize the criteria of efficiency and equity. Considering these two criteria, the course consists of three parts after explaining the features of tax systems in Japan.
Part one presents the construction of a theoretical framework for taxation and income distribution, which is closely related to equity criterion. We analyze tax incidence on commodities and production factors, and discuss commodity taxation without competition.
Part two deals with the topics on taxation and efficiency. Main issues in Part two include tax incidence, excess burden with indifference curves and demand curves. These issues can be revisited as welfare costs of taxation at partial and general equilibrium analysis.
Part three constructs a basic economic model for analyzing efficient and equitable taxation. Two important topics in Part three are optimal commodity taxation and optimal income taxation. We study some rules on commodity tax design such as the Ramsey rule and the Corlett-Hague rule covering optimal commodity taxation. Optimal income taxation can be classified as optimal linear and nonlinear income tax. We also mention a critique of normative optimal taxation and empirical evidence of positive optimal taxation.
Thisclass will be conducted by face-to-face. I will provide lecture notes andlecture materials through the [Announcement] on the class of [Fiscal Issueson Social Security　01] inadvance (maybe late September or early October).

Objectives:
This course focuses on making students understand theory and practice related to the criteria of efficiency and equity. We recommend that students grasp the main features of Japanese tax systems in in practical side, and that they study how taxes distort the market, how government intervenes market failures and it designs commodity and income taxes.

This course offers a comprehensive examination ofthe Russian economy across historical and contemporary contexts. Beginning withthe foundations of Tsarist and Soviet economic development, it traces thetransition to a market economy after 1991, explores centre–region dynamics, andanalyses Russia’s economic model prior to 2022. The course concludes with anin‑depth study of the impact of sanctions imposed after 2014 and 2022,highlighting structural adaptation, financial isolation, and Russia’s geoeconomicreorientation. Students will engage in written and oral assignments, combininghistorical analysis with contemporary policy evaluation.

Objectives:
The objectives of the course are:

• To provide students with a structured understanding of Russia’s economic development from the Tsarist period to the present.

• To analyse the political economy of Soviet industrialisation, post‑Soviet transition reforms, and regional economic specialisation.

• To evaluate Russia’s foreign economic relations and the challenges of diversification prior to 2022.

• To critically assess the scope, intent, and consequences of sanctions regimes and Russia’s adaptive strategies.

• To develop skills in academic writing, comparative analysis, and oral presentation within the field of international political economy.

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

• Explain the historical trajectory of Russia’s economic development, including Soviet and post‑Soviet phases.

•Analyse the institutional and policy frameworks shaping Russia’s transition to a market economy.

• Evaluate the role of regional economic specialisation and policy in shaping centre–region relations.

• Assess Russia’s pre‑2022 economic model, including resource dependence and diversification attempts.

• Critically compare the sanctions regimes of 2014 and 2022, identifying their economic and geopolitical implications.

• Apply academic writing conventions in short essays supported by references and bibliographies.

• Present research findings clearly and persuasively in both individual and group formats.

• Reflect on the long‑term outlook for Russia’s economy under sanctions within a global comparative perspective.

This seminar brings together students interested in exploring critical issues at the intersection of global decarbonisation efforts and sustainable development research. Adopting a “selected topics” approach, the course invites students to engage with contemporary challenges, innovative solutions, policy frameworks, and the socio‑economic dimensions of the transition to a low‑carbon and sustainable future. Emphasis is placed on critical analysis, interdisciplinary perspectives, and the integration of theoretical and empirical scholarship.

Schematically, the keyareas for individual research in this Seminar can be introduced as follows:

1. Decarbonisation inSpecific Sectors

1.1 Energy

• Renewable energyintegration: Examines the incorporation of solar, wind, and geothermaltechnologies into existing power grids, alongside energy storage solutions andsmart grid systems.

• Decarbonising heat andelectricity: Explores the electrification of heating systems, the developmentof efficient heating technologies, and optimisation of energy consumption inbuildings.

• Fossil fuel transition:Investigates pathways for phasing out fossil fuels, including carbon captureand storage (CCS) technologies and the development of alternative fuels.

• Smart energy systems:Focuses on optimising energy production, distribution, and consumption throughintelligent technologies and data analytics.

1.2 Transportation

• Electrification ofvehicles: Studies the development of electric vehicles, charginginfrastructure, and integration into the power grid.

• Alternative fuels:Explores the use of biofuels, hydrogen, and other sustainable fuel sources fortransportation.

• Sustainable urbanmobility: Investigates strategies for promoting public transport, cycling, andwalking, as well as optimising logistics and freight systems.

1.3 Buildings andConstruction

• Energy efficiency inbuildings: Focuses on improving insulation, optimising heating and coolingsystems, and promoting energy‑efficient appliances.

• Sustainable buildingmaterials: Examines the use of recycled and renewable materials in constructionand strategies to reduce the carbon footprint of building materials.

• Retrofitting andrenovation: Investigates approaches to improving the energy efficiency ofexisting buildings through retrofitting and renovation.

1.4 Industry

• Industrialelectrification: Explores the use of electricity to power industrial processes,replacing fossil fuel‑based technologies.

• Carbon capture,storage, and utilisation (CCSU): Focuses on capturing carbon dioxide emissionsfrom industrial processes and utilising them in products such as chemicals orfuels.

• Process optimisation:Examines methods for reducing energy consumption and emissions through improvedindustrial processes.

2. Sustainable EconomicDevelopment

• Circular economy:Explores principles of waste reduction, resource efficiency, and materialsrecovery across sectors.

• Sustainable consumptionand production: Promotes sustainable consumption patterns, reduced waste, andoptimised resource use.

• Ecosystem restoration:Focuses on restoring degraded ecosystems, protecting biodiversity, andenhancing ecosystem services.

• Environmental policyand governance: Examines policies and regulations supporting decarbonisationand sustainable development, including carbon pricing, emissions tradingsystems (ETS), and green finance.

• Social equity andjustice: Considers climate litigation and activism, the social implications ofdecarbonisation, and strategies to ensure a just and equitable transition to alow‑carbon economy.

3. Policy and Governance

• Climate changemitigation and adaptation: Studies international climate agreements (e.g. ParisAgreement mechanisms), climate impacts, and strategies for reducing greenhousegas emissions and adapting to climate change.

• Place‑baseddecarbonisation: Explores the role of sub‑national and local governance, withstrategies tailored to specific geographic locations and industrial clusters.

• Geopolitics ofdecarbonisation: Analyses the geopolitical consequences of transitioning to alow‑carbon economy.

Objectives:
Course Objectives

By the end of the course, students will:

• Gain familiarity with contemporary English‑language scholarship on key themes in decarbonisation studies and sustainable development research.

• Develop the ability to critically engage with diverse academic and policy debates.

• Explore in depth a selected theme of personal interest within the broader field.

Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

• Contextual Understanding: Demonstrate knowledge of the historical, socio‑economic, and geopolitical dimensions of decarbonisation.

• Critical Analysis: Interpret and evaluate academic accounts, and discuss scholarly and media discourse on pathways to decarbonisation across sectors such as energy, transportation, and industry.

• Policy and Technology Evaluation: Assess the role of policy frameworks, technological innovation, and societal factors in shaping sustainable development trajectories.

• Argumentation: Develop and present well‑structured, evidence‑based arguments for sustainable solutions.

• Research Skills: Apply relevant research methods to investigate specific challenges in decarbonisation and sustainable development.

• Academic Writing: Produce critical essays, course papers, and ultimately a graduation thesis on a chosen theme within decarbonisation or sustainable development.
