This course provides an intermediate-level introduction to game theory. Game theory studies rational decision-making in interactive situations, where the outcome for each individual depends not only on their own choices but also on the choices of others. Students will learn what constitutes an interactive situation and how rationality can be understood and evaluated in such contexts.

In particular, the course introduces a novel approach to analyzing experimental data on decision-making in economic and strategic environments. Unlike standard game theory and economic theory, which often assume perfectly rational (or “super-rational”) decision-makers, this approach quantifies the degree of rationality exhibited by actual participants.

Various criteria of rationality are introduced and used to analyze experimental decision data. Students will also study behavioral models in game theory that explain observed decision patterns in light of these rationality criteria. Since the criteria are formulated in mathematical terms, students are expected to engage with some mathematical analysis.

In addition, students will participate in in-class experiments involving strategic decision-making in game-theoretic settings.

Objectives:
In this course, we deepen our understanding of human reasoning and situational awareness in decision-making by comparing deductively derived equilibria based on rationality hypotheses with deviations from equilibrium observed in in-class experiments.

To carry out such comparisons, it is essential to construct mathematical models that formalize institutions and social environments. Students are therefore expected to develop the ability to derive deductive equilibria within these models. In addition, they must be able to design, plan, and implement experiments, and to anticipate what kinds of hypotheses can be empirically tested through those experiments.

To facilitate this learning process, the course incorporates a relatively large number of exercises, allowing students to enhance their understanding through an iterative engagement with both theory and empirical analysis.

This seminar aims to provide students with the knowledge and background necessary to understand cutting-edge research in theoretical economics, particularly in game theory and mechanism design. In recent years, game theory and mechanism design have been increasingly applied in various societal contexts, including recommendation systems, auction design, school choice mechanisms, and so on.

For successful social implementation, it is essential to have a solid theoretical foundation that enables a precise understanding of these mechanisms. In particular, without a rigorous mathematical approach, such theories cannot adequately address the risks and complexities that arise in real-world applications. Consequently, all papers read in the seminar will be mathematically formulated literature only. Students are expected to approach the seminar with sufficient motivation to engage with such an approach.

This seminar focuses on developing students’ ability to understand the mathematical models underlying these social implementations, as well as their capacity to apply these models to create new theoretical frameworks, through systematic study of the mathematical foundations of game theory and mechanism design.

Objectives:
The seminar aims to equip students with the fundamental knowledge required to read cutting-edge research papers in game theory and mechanism design, as well as with the ability to understand how to approach academic papers and develop their own ideas based on them. In particular, students who write their graduation theses within this seminar are required to conduct surveys of specialized academic literature. Accordingly, the seminar places strong emphasis on cultivating the ability to independently carry out rigorous literature surveys and synthesize existing research.

Recent seminar topics include reading and discussing foundational literature on mechanism design for trust formation using repeated games, the theory of recommendation systems through problems of information design, and organizational design based on blockchain technologies. Accordingly, the seminar aims to provide students with the foundational knowledge necessary to read and understand specialized academic literature in these fields.

In this lecture, students explore “Mechanism Design” which is an active research field in economic theory. Mechanism design is an emerging economic theory focused on designing institutions to effectively influence people's behavior.It serves as the foundation for social implementation by addressing social issues through design of social rules (Note that it is different from “Design thinking”).
This lecture focuses on the challenges and innovations in social implementation based on this theory. Moreover, by applying mechanism design theory, students will gain insights into generating collective Intelligence through the aggregation of people’s decentralized evaluations.
Such social implementation is facilitated by a rigorously examined theoretical methodology. Hence, students should recognize that some math (like calculus) in this course is required while the necessary math is explained during the lectures. Consequently, it is crucial to attentively follow these rigorous discussions.

Objectives:
The goal of this lecture is to help students identify people's incentive behavior toward institutions and rules, enabling them to modify or conceive of appropriate institutions and develop such viewpoints.

After this lecture, students will realize that many institutions in our society ignore people's incentive structures. To address such problems,

1. Cultivate the ability to think about how they should be modified.

2. Develop a viewpoint to reduce inconsistency among peoples’ incentives.

A classic example is the King Solomon dilemma. The problem is that King Solomon (who is believed to be the king of Israel around the 10th century B.C.) discerns the correct mother from two women who claim to be the mother of one baby. The anecdote claims that he found the real mother by threatening to cut the baby in half and give it to both, but this is incorrect from a mechanism design perspective. How on earth should this be resolved? After the class, students are expected to resolve this kind of problem.

This course is intended to explain and find out the clues to major environmental issues that we face today. First, we study the basic process and mechanism of the natural environment and how living organisms adapt to the environment. Secondly, we learn about the role of semi-natural disturbances on biodiversity conservation. Traditional agricultural practices in Japanese Satoyama and agro-forestry in Indonesia provide some good examples of where people receive natural resources and ecosystem services locally and how energy is flowing in cycle, as well as providing habitat for native species. Such balanced interaction in turn can function as a resilient ecosystem. This concept is called the Ecosystem-Based Disaster Risk Reduction (Eco-DRR). Thirdly, we study the impacts of recent human activities such as over-exploitation of natural resources, industrialization, intensive agriculture and globalization, on ecosystems, wildlife and as well as on our health and safety. Topics will include environmental carrying capacity, chemical pollution and bioaccumulation, soil erosion, global warming, climate change, endangered species, aging society and under-use of local resources problem, impacts of invasive species and genetically modified organisms (GMO), and learn how they are complexly interrelated. Lastly, we find the clue and issues on alternative power/renewable energy usage, such as biomass and geothermal power generation. This course consists of lectures, discussions and assignments.

This course is designed to learn the cause and mechanisms of environmental pollution that human beings have experienced and are still going on today. First, we focus on environmental laws, regulations and international agreements to prevent further destruction of the Earth's environment. Secondly, we learn about chemical pollution and its effect on ecosystems and on human beings. Areas include greenhouse gas emission and acid rain from fossil fuel combustion, synthetic chemical usage in intensive agriculture causing bioaccumulation and eutrophication, cyanobacterial bloom and intoxication of drinking water, and DNA pollution examples in horticulture and in fisheries will also be discussed. Thirdly, we go through the pollution control measures, focusing on waste water treatment, groundwater protection, and bioremediation technologies, and look at some measurement and modelling examples developed under environmental regulations and the Environmental Impact Assessment Law. Lastly, we find the solution to prevent further pollution, by applying alternative energy sources/renewable energy usage, and notice the importance of watershed basin/ catchment-level point of view to manage and solve complex problems. This course consists of lectures, discussions and assignments.　※The class will be taught by On-Demand format, but each class's video is available until the next week.

Objectives:
To understand the cause of environmental pollution, and be able to explain our present situation and how human activities degrade our environment. Become aware of the prevention measures and acquire watershed/basin point of view to solve such complex environmental problems.

There is hardly anything more fundamental to human life than the perpetual negotiation of the balance between states of public and private in relation to others and our environments. The categories of public and private are a key principle for organising social life and play a central role not only in urban studies but in our every day use of cities, neighbourhoods and other places that encourage public interaction. This course offers therefore to explore the dynamic, culturally and historically contingent ways in which architecture and urban space are structured along the distinction between what belongs to the protected realm of the private and what is to ‘take place’ in the interpersonal sphere of the public. As the physical and experiential form of the city, it’s buildings and the character of its urban life are deeply influenced by the private/public distinction, it is important to understand these implications not only in theory, but also it implications for urban politics, the practices of urban design and place-making as well as for everyday appropriation.
This course will go beyond the theoretical discussion of public space by exploring it across various spatial scales in direct connection with its ‘other’: private space. Beyond conceptual and theoretical discussions, the course seeks to explore the concrete and very real ramifications of the private/public distinction for urban planners, architects, public administrators, urban activists, businesses operating urban spaces, or simply for you as an active citizens as daily users of urban space and your spatial practices. Discourse offers to discuss crucial urban theories (post-structuralism, social constructionism, neoliberalism, critical theory, gender studies, etc.) along with very concrete examples from your everyday experiences and provides a solid basis for anybody with an interest in cities and urban studies.

Objectives:
In this course, students will ...

(1) ... study theories and concepts of delineating private and public realms in different historical and cultural contexts, as well as on various spatial scales,

(2) ... develop the sensitivity and analytical skills for understanding the complex implications of the private-public distinction for it’s manifestation on human behaviour and the built urban form,

(3) ... learn how urban designers and architects seek to translate the private/public distinction in ‘real’ planning and project situations, and how these spaces in turn dialectically impact on social life.

(4) ... undertake a small piece of original research, observation, or experiment of a topic of public interest.

(5) ... learn to think through more complex theoretical ideas in classroom discussions.

Cities are rarely built from scratch. When we aim at creating more liveable, sustainable and resilient cities as response to climate change, resource depletion, more frequent natural disasters, terror, or increasing inequality and social tensions, this usually has to happen by reconfiguring existing cities. It is therefore essential to know more about the people, institutions, practices and ideas that sought to form cities so far.

This course begins from the recent developments in city making that have emerged with the aim of creating more convivial places through pluralistic, democratic practices. These are seen to have positive impacts on streets, neighbourhoods, communities, and cities. Such new participatory place making ideas are rapidly dispersing world-wide. In this course, we ask the question, what are the reasons that city making, urban planning, urban design, urban governance or place making have become more participatory? From here, we will look back in order to understand which other ideas and ideologies of place-making and planning have been influential before and why have they been replaced and altered by newer ideas? The course examines the historical, cultural, economic, political, environmental, and other influences that determine how places form and how planners sought to control their development. Sustainability is one of the most important objectives of place-making and urban planning today. Questions of sustainability are ultimately questions about scarce resources, how we use them, and how they are distributed. Sustainability also involves social and cultural considerations and equity questions. This means that there are often winners and losers, risks and rewards.

Throughout this course we will explore the dynamic and contingent nature of place making practices and theories from four perspectives:

a) the specific activities associated with planning, place-making, and urban governance,

b) the different, often competing perspectives of people who plan, control, manage, and make our cities;

c) the relationship between state agencies, place-makers & civil society, and

d) plans, policies and projects as historical artefacts.

The class examines how and why urban plans and places are created, shaped, and reshaped by market, state and civil society influences as well as technologies at a variety of spatial scales - ranging from the neighbourhood and community level to the whole city and the region. At the same time we discuss the different approaches and strategies that place-making and governance professionals have been using to accomplish specific goals and objectives and how this in turn is informed by specific institutional, historical and spatial contexts.

The course is thus designed to provide students with a broad survey of the history of place-making and urban governance practices, a large number of practical, everyday examples that illustrate central topics to students, as well as a review of the important issues in planning and place-making theory. It focuses on the historical development of place-making ideas, the various roles planners and place-makers play in practice and theory, and the complex ethical dilemmas they face. Emphasis is thus placed on making sense out of theory and practice of how cities are conceptualised, planned, managed, governed, lived-in, appropriated, or contested.

Every lecture begins with an outline of larger social, political, or philosophical theories (e.g. system theory, marxism, neoliberalism, pragmatism, post-structuralism, post-modernism, post-colonialism etc.) and then details their implications for the making of cities and its relevance for the everyday lifeworlds of urban residents.

We will not only explore how larger social and political theories informed the making of cities but we will also discuss how these concepts ultimately impacted the everyday lives and urban practices of the residents of cities.

Objectives:
In this course, students will ...

(1) ... undertake a piece of original research and analysis on a place-making and planning related case study,

(2) ... showcase for each participant the range of skills and interests that they have developed at SILS, The final paper each participant completes will be an important part of the portfolio that they present to an employer or graduate school,

(3) ... develop a self-critical view on those professionals who are planning, making, controlling and governing cities vis-a-vis actors of the market and civil society and provide an understanding of the political, organisational and personality variables that contribute to effective place-making;

(4) ... be prepared to think about the political and ethical ramifications of possible decisions as professional planners, makers of spatial policies, or simply as active citizens, or social activists;

(5) ... learn about the policy/ planning tools with which planners, local governments, civil society actors, social activists, or policy makers seek to control growth & management of cities and develop analytical skills to evaluate outcomes.

For the first time in human history, more than half of the world’s population is living in towns and cities and this figure will grow to 80 percent by the end of this century. This unprecedented, unbroken push towards urbanisation that has ushered in a so-called ‘New Urban Century’ has brought the emergence of gigantic cities, or megacities, which present major new challenges to a planet with limited resources and growing environmental, economic, political, cultural, social as well as health challenges. Global and local urban development are not only shaped through conscious planning, design and governance strategies, but driven by broader processes of political and economic restructuring associated with the logics of capitalism, state power as well as diverse forms of socio-political mobilisation. This course provides students with a broad introduction to key topics in contemporary urban studies.

It surveys a wide variety of methodological approaches through which scholars are attempting to understand urban change and to decipher the forces that are fostering planetary urbanisation, shaping contemporary cities and city-regions under conditions of heightened economic and political volatility, deterritorialisation, widespread adoption of entrepreneurial politics and resulting resistance from popular movements.

The objective of this course is to provide a wide overview of urbanisation issues around the world and stress the interconnected, relational nature of these phenomena.

(4) ... develop a stronger understanding of the interconnections between a variety of urban policy issues and how these are informing the transformation of cities in the ‘global age’ and under conditions of 'planetary urbanisation',

(5) ... appreciate the geographical, historical, and cultural contingency of urban change in a globalising, urbanising world.

Global environmental problems such as climate change, rapid loss of biodiversity and resource depletion are accelerating and have gained prominence on political agendas worldwide, while man-made infrastructure systems and cities have grown more complex and ever more vulnerable. Not least the COVID19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine and recent disasters have revealed the vulnerability of a highly interdependent, globalised economy. Today’s pervasive, interrelated wicked problems differ significantly in scale and complexity from those of the past that could be addressed, for example, with incremental clean technologies and local policy responses. Today’s new socio-environmental problems require more substantive ‘transitions’ in the coming decades such as major changes in energy, transport, community, housing or agri-food systems to name a few.

These system changes are ‘socio-technical’ in nature because they not only entail the mere development and implementation of new technologies, but also changes in markets, mindsets, user practices, policy and cultural meanings. The emergent domain of Transition Design acknowledges the fact that we live in ‘transitional times’ with permanent change now increasingly seen as ‘the new normal’. Accordingly, transition design takes as its central premise the need for perpetual, socio-environmental and socio-technical transitions to more sustainable future system states and argues that design thinking has a key role to play in these transitions. Transition Design applies an understanding of the interconnectedness of social, economic, political & natural systems to address problems at all levels of spatio-temporal scale in ways that directly improve the quality of life and safeguard human-centred development. It advocates the re-conception of entire lifestyles, with the aim of making them more place-based, convivial & participatory and harmonising them with natural environment.

In this course we will first learn to see and appreciate the complexity of so-called wicked problems —problems that are difficult or impossible to solve because of their complex and interconnected nature. We will then think about a system of metrics that helps us assessing the appropriateness of transition design and social design interventions. In the second part of the course, we will explore the transition design framework as it was proposed by scholars of at The School of Design at Carnegie Mellon University. It is one of many useful frameworks that helps us understanding how positive socio-ecological change can be constructed. Lastly, the course will conclude with a discussion of concepts like cosmopolitan localism and inter-localisation that promise a positive way forward towards forming more empowered, resilient communities in an age of intensifying planetary crises.

This course is recommended for students who can imagine themselves as change makers in the future and provides them with a critical language, some initial tools and conceptual ideas to move in that direction.

The teaching methodology of this class is F2F style. The principal aim of this course is to provide for the students an overview of the role of the Japan in the political sphere for International Cooperation.
This course will be divided by two parts. The first part of the course analyses the history, theory, practice and evaluation of what the United Nations (UN) is calling “peace operations.” These encompass post-conflict peacekeeping, peace enforcement, and those elements of peace building integral to organized international support for the implementation of cease-fires and settlements of interstate and intrastate wars.
The second part of the course brings these functional issues together and analyzes security problems on the Japan’s specific area. We will try to discuss on the Japan’s role for the International cooperation, especially PKO area.
What is the role of Japan in the International society in the security field?
What has the UN done for the resolving of the conflicts?
What are the characteristics of the Japan’s security cooperation policy? What is a principal contradiction between the Japan’s PKO law and the international reality?
How to overcome the Japanese judicial problem on the individual and collective right of self-defence?
What is the Japanese security policy?
Other topics include the notion of the collective security, problem of use of force in the modern world.
The explanation on the Japan’s security policy and some specific issues on Japan will be conducted in Japanese.

Enrich the knowledge of students about the security issues.

Are you fascinated by how people learn and use multiple languages? Have you ever wondered what makes someone "bilingual" or how children can grow up speaking two or more languages? This course explores the fascinating world of bilingual first and second language acquisition.

This course introduces students to key questions, debates, and research findings in bilingual/multilingual acquisition across the lifespan, from birth through adulthood. Based on research in bilingualism and language acquisition, we explore topics including:

- Is the earlier the better in acquiring languages?

- How do children acquire multiple languages, and how does their learning process differ from monolingual children?

- What can parents do to support their children's bilingual development?

- Who are bilingual/multilingual users?

2. Analyze the process of simultaneous acquisition of two or more languages in early childhood

3. Evaluate common myths and misconceptions about bilingualism

4. Design evidence-based recommendations for supporting multilingual development

In this class we will cover developments with regard to ‘Brexit’ (the process whereby the UK left the European Union, and negotiated a future relationship). The UK vote to leave the EU was a landmark, deeply controversial and divisive issue which is predicted by many to have significant implications for the UK, the EU, and perhaps even the liberal international order itself. Although the UK has left the EU, and a Trade and Cooperation Agreement has been signed, there are still many important problems in the new relationship that have not been resolved, such as issues with regard to Northern Ireland, and trade problems. It is strongly expected that there will be significant developments in the future relations between the EU and UK between April and July, when this class will run. This class will have a strong current affairs orientation, and we will follow political developments and media reflection on Brexit developments on a weekly basis, and in some detail.

The first half of each class will be given over to a more conventional academic analysis of why Brexit happened, using an influential text on populism written by Matthew Goodwin. In the second half of each class, we will discuss latest developments, and students will be given media materials from the previous week to analyse, present and discuss. We will look at the formal television media that have historically framed UK political debate, including Prime Minister’s Question Time, and BBC political programming such as Question Time, Newsnight, and the Andrew Marr Show. We will draw on well-known UK political satire, such as Have I Got News For You, Yes Minister, The Thick of It, and House of Cards (the original, British version). We will look at a range of UK newspapers and news publications with very different political views, target audiences, and means of influencing debate. This will include broadsheets such as The Guardian, The Times, The Telegraph, and The Financial Times, political magazines such as The Economist and the Spectator, and tabloids such as The Sun, The Daily Mail, and The Daily Express. Students will also be expected to follow several important political influencers on Twitter, and deconstruct their output on a weekly basis.

Objectives:
Students will receive a detailed and nuanced exposure to the political media landscape of the UK.

Most obviously, students will gain a detailed and highly contemporary insight into the answers to three questions: why did voters support Brexit, were they wise to do so, and what is the most likely form that future EU-UK relations will take?.

This intermediate seminar will serve as an introduction to the theories taken up in critical communication and media studies. Seminar participants will be introduced to some of the basic terms and concepts in the intersection of critical theory, communication and media studies, and technology studies. It will address key themes in the discipline by examining the social, political, economic, cultural, and technological contexts in which communication and media/mediation are understood and how media objects, devices, and platforms are produced and consumed. This is a demanding course in reading, discussion, and writing. In essence, it is designed to help students understand the process of (1) reading theoretical texts, (2) critically evaluating and connecting them to real-life cases, and (3) writing a final paper that wrestles with these theories. Each class is spent with active discussion among students. Students are expected to ask questions not only to the professor but to each other with open-ended ones. At all times, we will refer to the specific pages and passages of the reading.

Objectives:
- Engage in active, close reading practice with peers through a collective annotation platform.

- Explain the basic terms and concepts in communication and media studies.

- Explain the social, economic, and cultural implications of communication, media, and mediation, as well as their related practices and texts.

- Explain how media environments and objects produce a relation to the world one inhabits.

- Apply the various perspectives on media and communication discussed in class to your own daily practices in communication and engagement with media.

- Write a succinct essay that brings together ideas from the readings, lectures, and discussions.

This is an intermediate seminar designed to generate conversations around how themes of environment, gender, identity, and resistance intersect in the Pacific and Asia. Structured around the idea of how places and people often presumed to be "marginal" and "living in the middle of nowhere" are in fact at the center of NOW and HERE--contemporary issues that matter to all of us, this seminar is an interdisciplinary approach based on anthropology, human geography, history, political science, literature, art, and gender studies. Broken into three broad themes, the course will facilitate conversation and active learning on three different "scapes" (1) nuclearscapes: cultures of militarism and colonialism, especially as related to nuclear testing in Oceania and the impact this has had on local communities (2) climatescapes; the interplay of bodies, massive human-induced climate changes, and environments in relation to culture (3) genderscapes: gender and identity in relation to colonialism/militarization/globalization—how different gender and sexual minorities respond to pressure from beyond their borders. With each of these themes, our focus will be especially on local creativity and resistance to these problems.
Although these may seem like "heavy" themes, the course will engage with playful and ironic critical approaches by contemporary artists, activists, and writers, to provide a rich and inspiring conversation about issues that are of the greatest concern to seminar participants. We will look at films, pieces of art, short stories, poems, interactive new media, and particularly work done by indigenous, queer, or other marginal community members. At the end of the semester, all students will be required to create a creative portfolio project, not only writing but also using images, art, video, and other media to communicate a reflective response to the themes in the course that were of the most interest to them.

Objectives:
Throughout this semester, students will be expected to develop a nuanced understanding of the core themes discussed in the seminar and how these relate to the Pacific and Asian region. You will be expected to acquire a grasp of cultural studies and gender studies-inspired approaches to ethnicity and colonialism, through reading assigned course texts and additional research related to the subjects that interest you most. Students will develop skills in analyzing popular culture and history, active discussion and presentation, and formulating research ideas. At the end of the semester, you will produce a creative portfolio project, which will be based on course readings and lectures plus your own independent research and critically-informed reflections.

The countries in the Middle East share a strong historical and cultural connection through their predominant religion, Islam. However, it is important to acknowledge that the Middle East is not a homogenous entity. In reality, the region is characterized by a diverse range of ethnic and religious groups. This diversity brings richness to the culture, but it also presents challenges to the process of nation-building.
This course takes a historical and comparative approach to delve into the political and cultural complexities of the Middle East. It addresses topics such as national integration and ethnic/religious minorities, the fragmentation of ethnic groups due to the demarcation of national borders, and cultural strategies employed by various countries to integrate the diverse historical experiences of various ethnic groups into a single national history.
By engaging with insightful readings, participating in discussions, and analyzing case studies, students will develop a comprehensive understanding of the historical, political, and socio-cultural factors that have influenced state formation and shaped the experiences of minority groups in the Middle East. Through this exploration, students will gain valuable insights into the complexities and challenges associated with managing ethnic diversity and ensuring minority rights in the Middle East.

The class will introduce students to the basic elements of interpreting which consists of listening accurately and understanding correctly what the speaker is saying in various contexts, and then reproducing the spoken text in the listener’s language and cultural context. This intermediate seminar introduces students to a sub-field of political science (PS) and international relations (IR).

In the academic year of 2026, the seminar examines the regional dynamics of international relations in historical East Asia. Based on a recently published book on this topic, we will conduct in-depth case studies of eleven consequential events in East Asian history, More specifically, the course will look into the two major regional wars in the 7th and 16th centuries, the founding of the Choson and Qing dynasties in the 14th and 17th centuries, China and Japan's encounter with the West in the 19th century, as well as the hijacked independent movement in the Philippines at the turn of the 20th century.

Focusing on these unique historical experiences, the course sheds light on the regional construction of hierarchical legitimacy, the strategic maneuver of less powerful states, the long-lasting impact of non-state actors, and the divergent paths of modernization in historical East Asia.

Objectives:
This seminar aims to provide an overview of international relations in historical East Asia. Students are expected to develop a sophisticated understanding of the regional context of premodern East Asia beyond the oft-conflicting narratives of national histories.

In this class, we will think about the technological revolution of writing and the impact that it has had and continues to have on the development of human civilization. We’ll read about the history of various writing systems (hieroglyphics, alphabets, syllabaries, etc.) learning about how they were developed and how they work, using as our textbook “The Writing Revolution: Cuneiform to the Internet.” Students will also work on an extended research project on a related topic, such as one of the following:

(1) Linguistic landscape of Tokyo: which languages are used in official and unofficial written messages (street signs, government offices, trains station, etc.) in Tokyo?

(2) A comparison of the information density of different types of scripts: for example, how many characters are needed to convey the same message in Chinese, Japanese, and English?

(3) Writing in text messages and SNS: how are scripts being modified as they are used in online environments?

(4) Universal symbols: What systems are being developed to convey messages for thousands of years into the future (for example, to mark nuclear waste storage sites as dangerous)?

(5) Writing for the visually-impaired: How are braille and read-aloud text technologies being used to make writing accessible to people who cannot see text?

(6) Invented scripts: These include new scripts for languages which already have established scripts, as well as some which are intended to be universal. How do these work, and why haven’t they been successful?

Objectives:
In this class, students will strengthen their ability to read critically, and to apply theoretical knowledge to their daily lives. They will also further develop their abilities to do research and to present their findings both in writing and orally in front of a group.

The term "coloniality"suggests how the violence and domination of colonialism continues even after the formal structures of colonialism have ended. We witness this today in the extreme inequality separating the global north from global south, and within nations. Juxtaposing coloniality with modernity to create"coloniality-modernity" is a way of reminding us of how the sometimes thrilling benefits of modernity depend on the violent domination of 'others,' however much their suffering is hidden from us. Abiding with the complexity and paradoxes of modernity-in the world at large and in our individual ways ofthinking, knowing and being-- without retreating into denial is no simple task for anyone.

Do you still have faith in the promises of modernity to deliver wellbeing to you in the future?. Many of us have begun to realize that large areas in the world already are in collapse as coloniality-modernity pushes us further into lives of competition, domination, extraction, consumption, isolation and obedience to corporate and state authority. We lack opportunities to feel that we belong to caring, egalitarian communities where the voice of each member is heard and valued. We are frustrated by the refusal of universities to declare that students are now facing an unprecedented climate and ecological emergency, or to create spaces where young people can come together and speak honestly about their concerns for their future.

As the American government continues to rely on bombing, military raids and drone strikes as tools in never-ending wars, andJapanese consider reinterpreting the constitution for“collectivedefense,” questions about the legacies of WWⅡand our complicity with violence seem ever more important. While citizenry often appear allergic to discussion of“empire” with its connotations of invasion, oppression and exploitation, this very aversion renders it attractive as a concept forexploration in the multicultural classroom that SILS makes possible. Why is the anger of Japanese nationalists focused on Chinese, Koreans (or Zainichi Chineseand Koreans) and Okinawan protesters rather than on US military bases and American domination? What ethical issues arise when American scholars censure Japan for the denial of wartime atrocities committed against Asians while overlooking the indiscriminate bombing of civilians by the US from WW II to the present? To what extent has violence against women remained invisible within patriarchal nations? Finally, how should we understand our own relationships with violence, domination and suffering?

This course relies on literary texts to unleash our capacities for imagination and empathy, important tools in the creation of what is often called "epistemic justice, a means of resisting the use ofstatistics or abstraction to sterilize violence and make the suffering of others invisible. We will also make use of historical, indigenous, anthropological, feminist, sociological and theoretical readings to complicate our analyses, and meet with activists in Japan to see first-hand how examplesof how new knowledge and ways of understanding can lead to empowerment of self and others.

Objectives:
This course is premised on the notion that (1) unlearning much of what we have been taught in high school and through corporate media, (2) acquiring familiarity with concepts such as positionality, intersectionality and the subaltern (introduced in class) and (3) redoubling our efforts to listen to those who appear as “other” to us are instrumental steps in gaining the ability to act ethically and democratically, to work to extend social justice and to gain the confidence necessary for speaking to power. For us to achieve personal transformations, the classroom itself must be transformed from a place of autocratic instruction and passive student resistance to a more challenging, honest and democratic space of student empowerment.

Learning Outcomes

Students should:

・achieve a greater understanding of Japanese cultural and social history

・gain better understanding of violence enacted by America and Japan

・understand better the structure of empires

・gain awareness of movements in Okinawa dedicated to resisting violence and oppression

・gain critical awareness of the modern nation-state

・become aware of mechanisms of denial and justifications for violence

・understand basic post-colonial theory and become familiar with some basic terms

・understand better the power, pleasure and challenges of literary texts

・gain experience in organizing, preparing and carrying out workshops

・recognize the ethical component of knowledge, communication and action and consider the personal responsibility that accompanies it

・learn how to accurately summarize theoretical, academic texts, personalize the information and communicate effectively to others

・write with conviction and clarity of purpose

・understand the value of editing and rewriting

For many critical thinkers such as Silke Helfrich, David Bollier, David Harvey, to name but a few, the contemporary world is caught between an old socio-economic and political order that no longer works and a new one struggling to be born. Surrounded by out-dated systems of centralised, inflexible bureaucratic hierarchies on the one hand and and what many characterise as predatory, globalised markets on the other, presided over by states and super-national corporations committed to planet-destroying economic growth, people around the world are intensively searching for alternative political and economic models and more sustainable modes of Being in the world.

In response to the recurring and accelerating environmental, economic and political crises, the long-forgotten concept of the commons has gained popularity over the last decade, with its promises of more democratic participatory self-governance, concern for shared natural and man-made resources as well as more equity in addressing fundamental human needs. Originally the concept of the commons emerged in rural contexts in the form of shared natural resources such as pastures, fishing grounds, irrigation or woods but has now come to be applied also to commoning processes in cities.

Beyond these classical conceptions, "new commons" as Charlotte Hess calls them, have been identified such as scientific knowledge, climate, wikipedias, etc. With the subsequent expansion of the commons concept over ever new domains, and along with the rapid urbanisation of the world in an age of "planetary urbanisation" (Neil Brenner & Christian Schmid) urban commons like community gardens, co-housing, or area management arrangements have come into focus.

The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the social innovation of new urban commons and more importantly their normative implications. Key to the course then, is an understanding of how these shape a landscape of inclusion and exclusion. Concurrent with the global shift from a Keynesian welfare state to a more radically marked-centred neoliberal order and against the background of approaching planetary boundaries, community groups, NPOs and a range of institutions are exploring different mechanisms for collective and collaborative management of shared resources.

This course applies a dynamic, emergent understanding of commons that focuses on the practice of “commoning” as historian Peter Linebaugh calls it, or perpetually reproducing the commons. Once thought to be restricted to forms of common land such as community land trusts, the new urban commons cover everything from public infrastructures such as libraries and water, tool and toy sharing, open source formats of information technologies to community gardens.

Objectives:
In this seminar students will …

(1) ... develop an own self-selected research project of one specific urban commons and its commoning mechanisms,

(2) ... explore the philosophies and practices around the emergence of new urban commons and learn to distinguish them from other forms of collective distribution of goods such as “public goods,” “collective consumption” and “collaborative consumption”,

(3) ... explore the limits and possibilities of a commons for social transformation or cooptation, the challenges of scaling a “commons” at the local level,

(4) ... familiarise themselves with competing concepts and technologies of commoning,

(5) ... investigate the limits and possibilities of commoning and some cautionary tales – how commoning can at times rehearse colonial practices, act as a limiting fix to crises of capitalism, or alternately form the basis of a new cooperativism.

Recent scholarship offers a perspective that diverges significantly from traditional history textbooks. The field has expanded and diversified, increasingly adopting interdisciplinary methods. This course serves as an introduction to the current state of historical studies. While students may be accustomed to a passive learning environment, they will be expected to approach history as an active subject of critical inquiry.

The class is structured around three core components:

Historiography and Theory: We will examine how history is written and how our understanding of the past has evolved.

Methodology and Practice: By analyzing a wide range of materials—from government records to films and popular music—lectures will demonstrate the primary methods used to practice history.

Conceptual Frameworks: Key historical concepts, such as colonialism, memory, and nationalism, will be reinterpreted through the lens of other scholarly disciplines. Through these discussions, we will trace the shifting landscape of modern historical studies.

Objectives:
The goals of this course are:

1) to understand what history is as a scholarly discipline.

2) to analyze past and current events in a historical context.

3) to have personal acquaintance with how to use basic historical materials.

This course aims to introduce students to the discipline of history. To do this we will consider a number of basic but important questions such as: what is history? why should we care about it? what does good history look like? what is the role of the individual in history? is history just opinion, or does it offer reliable knowledge about the past? what does it mean to "think historically"? To answer these questions we will consider the nature historical evidence and look at how historians can evaluate and interpret it in different ways, sometimes in ways that provoke public controversy. Several of the lectures will present different types of history (history of science, intellectual history, social history, etc.) by drawing on examples from the history of the city of London (a topic also addressed in the course textbook). We will also examine the surprising ways in which history is constantly interpreted and debated in the world around us in places like newspapers, films, songs, and the physical environment. If you decide to pursue further study in history this class will serve as a useful introduction to the subject. But, even if you do not pursue further study in history, this class will develop your historical awareness and help make you aware of how history continues to shape the present.

Objectives:
By the end of this course students should have a basic understanding of what the discipline of history is, how historians produce history, and some of the main varieties of history. Students will also understand what it means to think historically and will begin to develop their own historical awareness. Students should also be able to explain why the study of history is relevant to contemporary concerns.

In the year 600, Christianity was the dominant religion of both the Middle East and Europe. By the year 750, this had all changed. Instead, Islam was the main religion in the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of southern Europe. So began relations and interactions between the two religions that would last throughout the medieval period, and on up to today, and see periods of both intense, fanatical violence and close scientific and political collaboration. This course will explore the history of relations between members of the two religions over the period of 900 years, from the rise of Islam in the early seventh century to the final defeat of the Muslims of Spain in 1492. In particular, it will examine perceptions between the two sides in writings produced in a variety of languages, cultures, times and places. In so doing, students will not only learn about relations in the medieval period but they will also uncover the roots of many of the tensions in the world today.
This is face to face only.

Objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be expected to:

- Know the outline history of Christian-Muslim relations in the medieval period.

- Have knowledge of the main areas of research into the subject.

- Understand how to use different types of primary evidence, who they were written for, and why.

- Understand the different interpretations of events and ideas put forward by modern scholars.

- Be able to research, create, and give class presentations.

- Understand how relations between Christians and Muslims in the medieval period are still relevant today.

The last two centuries of Japanese history have been defined by alternating eras of war and peace. Because the modern world was shaped by global interactions, Japan’s recent past cannot be understood through a national lens alone. Therefore, an analysis of international history is vital to understanding modern Japan.

This course offers an international history of war and peace, with a primary focus on modern Japan. Spanning from the Opium War and World War II to the 'War on Terror,' lectures and discussions will address the causes and consequences of major conflicts. Primary documents in English will be a core component of the weekly reading assignments.

Objectives:
The goal of this course is to enable students to situate contemporary events and issues within their broader historical context by leveraging a deep understanding of Japan’s recent past.

This seminar is designed for students planning to specialize in historical studies during their senior year. Particularly for students in their first semester of the seminar, the fall term is designated as a foundational period for developing their senior theses. To facilitate this, the curriculum begins in a colloquium style—focusing on broad academic exchange—before transitioning into a research seminar format tailored to individual projects.

Whether you already have a specific thesis topic or only a general interest in history, this seminar will help you acquire the necessary research skills, theories, and methodologies. We will refine these skills by discussing various issues aligned with the participants' individual interests.

Although the instructor’s primary expertise is in modern Japan and international history, this seminar is open to anyone interested in history, regardless of their specific geographic or chronological focus.

Objectives:
To complete student’s senior paper, students should work according to the “road map” distributed at the first session of the seminar. Through this process, they are expected to acquire the skill of profound analysis as well as independent research.

This advanced seminar is for students who have a keen interest in history, want to sharpen their ability to think historically, and intend to write a graduation thesis on an historical topic. The seminar has three main goals: 1) to equip students with a a deeper understanding of the theories and methods (also known as historiography) that underlie historical research, 2) to help students develop a deeper appreciation of what historical research can “do,” that is, the kinds of questions it can answer and the sort of insights it can offer; and 3) to help students choose a viable thesis topic, conduct substantial research on it, and shape that research into a persuasive graduation thesis. How we accomplish these goals will vary from semester to semester depending on enrollment and student interests, but the essential format of the seminar is discussion of assigned readings. What will we read? Typically, we will begin the semester by reading essays and excerpts that relate to Goal #1 above. These readings address questions such as: what is history? how do historians evaluate evidence? what counts as a good historical explanation of an event? Is there such a thing as historical truth?
After a few weeks of this we will usually transition to considering Goal #2 above, and this means reading an exemplary historical monograph. Based on the instructor’s suggestions, together we will choose a book that addresses an important and relevant topic, that is interesting and well-written, and that reveals what historical research can do in the hands of a master practitioner. (Usually these books are in the field of modern British, European, or transatlantic history. Recent choices have included Hyperactive: The Controversial History of ADHD by Matthew Smith, Return from the Natives: How Margaret Mead Won the Second World War and Lost the Cold War by Peter Mandler, and Family Secrets: Shame and Privacy in Modern Britain by Deborah Cohen.)
Parallel to all of this we will be addressing Goal #3, which means that we will have regular consultations about how to choose and research a thesis topic, how your research is progressing, and how to transform that research into a finished thesis.
Believe it or not, while learning all of this we can and will have some fun along the way. We’ll be reading fascinating documents and thinking about important questions. Consequently, this course will include an ample amount of debate and discussion. I want to hear what you think and how you think about the issues we cover.

Objectives:
By the end of this seminar students will have substantial knowledge of the issues and debates that have shaped, and continue to shape, the historical profession. In addition they will have improved their ability to think historically and developed skills in historical research and writing that will allow them to pursue graduate study in history if they so choose.

This advanced seminar is designed for students who are interested in history and/or historical fictions and have decided to write a senior thesis on topics related to history, cultural history, or historical fictions. The instructor specializes in premodern Japanese history, cultural history, and history of clothing, with an educational background in comparative literature and comparative culture. The seminar readings will be mainly taken from these areas but any students interested in history or the intricacy of the relationship between fact/fiction are welcome to join.

The seminar sessions will have two main components: 1) discussions based on assigned readings (and ideally field trips) and 2) a workshop for writing the thesis.

1) For the discussions, we will read academic works that will help us examine our understanding of history, roaming over various issues, including historical fiction and drama, collective memory, and public history. While acknowledging the significance that the modern discipline of history has attached to facts and the process of substantiating them, we will experience together the pains and problems of writing histories and sharing memories.

2) For the writing workshop, the participants will work together in developing their research and writing skills, and share their progress in their individual project.

Objectives:
1) Students acquire substantial knowledge about scholarly discussions on what is history and contemporary issues related to history and memory.

2) Students improve research and writing skills.

3) Students make progress in their thesis project.

This course will offer a whirlwind survey of European history from the French Revolution to the present. Moving at breakneck speed, we will consider the political, economic, social, and cultural transformation of the continent during this 250-year period of dramatic change. At the beginning of our period most Europeans were illiterate, impoverished farm laborers; by the end of our period most had become well-educated, prosperous democratic citizens. As we seek to understand this transformation－which was by no means inevitable－our overarching theme will be revolutions－political, economic, and intellectual－and their attendant ideologies. This means that much of our focus will be on the various “isms” that shaped Europe in this period, such as liberalism, nationalism, imperialism, communism, fascism, and feminism. The course will be built around three tensions that can help us make sense of the proliferation of revolutions and ideologies during this period. These tensions are: liberalism vs. illiberalism, universality vs. particularity, and modernity vs. tradition. These three tensions will provide the overall structure for the course and will act as the “engine” that drives it forward. We will conclude the course by reflecting on the challenges that face Europe today and on what its future may hold.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students should be able to grasp and articulate the main themes of European history from the Enlightenment to the present. They will be able to understand present conditions in Europe as the result of contingent historical developments that shaped not only Europe itself but the rest of the world as well.

This course will offer a rapid survey of ancient and medieval Europe, from ancient Greece to the Reformation. The ancient and medieval world might seem like a remote and different society, but there are many connections with and influences on the contemporary world. Thinking about democracy, politics, religion, liberty, and sciences, the past society gives us clues to see our contemporary world from different perspectives. During the class, students will examine and analyze various primary sources, such as the texts of Herodotus and Thucydides, Res Gestae Divi Augusti (The Deeds of Deified Augustus), Suetonius' Life of Roman Emperors, Pliny the Younger's Letters, Eusebius' Life of Constantine, the forged document of the Donation of Constantine, and the Travels of Ibn Jubayr, to understand how history has been made and interpreted. This process will develop students' basic ability in historical study and source criticism.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to:

- develop an awareness of ancient and medieval European history

- understand the relationship between the past and the present

- acquire basic knowledge of historical study and the ability of source criticism

Modern British History
This course will be a survey of the history of Great Britain from the Revolution of 1688 to Brexit. Its main purpose is to help you understand from a historical perspective how Britain and the British came to be the way they are at present, including economy, society, politics, and culture. Britain today is a multi-national state that once included, though it does not now, all of the peoples of the British Isles. Therefore, the course will deal with the Scots, Irish, and Welsh, as well as the English. The main theme of the course will be the rise and fall of British power and influence: the expansion of English power within the British Isles, the formation of the United Kingdom of Great Britain, the transformation of a traditional society, the rise and decline of British industrial power, the development of a class society, and the rise and fall of Britain as a great power. Britain was the world’s first “modern” nation, and in the nineteenth century Britain was the greatest power on earth. But Britain now has receded from great power status, and the British (especially the English) are uncertain about their global role and even their national identity. In each development Britain has been (and is) an object lesson for other countries such as Japan and the United States.

Objectives:
By the end of this course students will have an understanding of the development of British history from 1688 to the present and will be able to articulate this change over time in terms of the following themes:

1. The formation of the British state and British national identity

2. The rise and decline of Britain as a great power

3. The rise and decline of Britain as an economic power

4. The development of a class society

5. The political system and the evolution of liberalism

6. Britain as an example and object lesson

[FULL FACE-TO-FACE COURSE]
This course is a survey of American history from the Age of Discovery to the current Trump Administration. Although a special emphasis will be placed upon the nineteenth century, when such historical landmarks as westward expansion, the Civil War, and Reconstruction occurred, the course offers a general narrative of the major themes and events of American history. Examining American history from its origins as a British colony to its emergence as the world’s superpower enables us to acquire knowledge of other parts of the world as well. This investigation into the entire American history might make us understand whether or not what President Trump has been doing is an aberration or part of American conservatism.

Objectives:
The purpose of this course is twofold: first, to make better sense of the world by learning the history of the country under whose influence most of us live; second, to benefit from the experiences of the people in the past in order for us to make sensible decisions for the future.

Given the fact that nobody seems able to avoid the influence of the United States, whether you like it or not, it is beneficial to understand how and why the world's first democratic nation has become such a dominant powerhouse in a short period of time.
This course examines some of the historical topics pertinent to the current United States, such as slavery (racism and wealth gap), the Civil War (political division, unified nation-statehood), Reconstruction (definition of American citizenship and equal protection of the law), and Jim Crow (inequality). The subject of slavery reminds us that the United States was established as a slaveholding nation, while it would not have become a consolidated capitalist nation without the abolition of slavery through the Civil War. Constitutional amendments enacted during Reconstruction, such as the 14th and 15th amendments laid the foundation for equality among people of color, women, and immigrants. And it was during the Jim Crow era when discrimination against non-white people, including Asians, gained legitimacy. As some scholars argue, Jim Crow, rather than slavery, has the lasting impact on American society of today.

By focusing on those topics, students will have a better grasp of other members of the country, such as Native Americans, and ideas of democracy, conservatism, and liberalism.

Objectives:
The goal of this course is to dispel widely-held but false ideas about some of the current issues by situating the selected topics within the history of the United States and that of the world as a whole.

This course explores various aspects of classical and early medieval Japan (circa 8th to 13th centuries) by listening to different voices recorded in historical and literary sources. The sessions will alternate in focus: first they will take up the history of a particular time or topic and then they will explore a related literary works. The course aims to expand our perspective and reshape our understanding of Japanese history as a complex and nonlinear process.

In addition to the lectures, the class will emphasize discussions based on a critical analysis of reading materials, including diverse literary texts in English translation. Students will be required to read, think, and share their views regularly throughout the semester.

As the participants usually comprise both local and international students with diverse regional and educational backgrounds, the course will be a good platform for you to meet new ideas and explore not only events in the past but also contemporary issues relevant to yourself. Students who just started to learn Japanese culture, including SP3/SP4 students, are by all means welcome, and no prior knowledge of Japanese history or literature is required to enroll. Please just note that you may (at least in the beginning) struggle with unfamiliar names, terms, and concepts, and will need to spend some extra time looking up those names and terms. Students who have previously studied Japanese history and classical literature are certainly also welcome. Those of you will be required to revisit your knowledge, especially if you have only studied the subject at Japanese elementary and/or secondary schools, and devise how to present your ideas in an academic fashion that makes sense in an international context.

Objectives:
1) Students acquire college-level knowledge of Japanese premodern history and classical literature.

2) Students grasp history as a complex and nonlinear process.

3) Students build skills in analyzing materials critically and expressing their analysis appropriately.

This course provides a survey of human activities and events in the Japanese islands up to the mid 19th century. Pivoting around the evolution of political structures, it aims to explore social, economic, religious, and cultural developments, with a particular focus on the regional context of East Asia, the relationship between capital cities and provinces, and the transformation of class and gender relationships.

The course will consist of readings, lectures, and discussion-based analyses of primary sources in English translation. It is not a class where you will just listen to the lectures and learn a series of facts that form a single narrative of Japanese history. Rather, students will need to read, think, and update their understanding regularly throughout the semester.

As the participants usually comprise both local and international students with diverse regional and educational backgrounds, the course will be a good platform for you to meet new ideas and explore not only events in the past but also contemporary issues relevant to yourself. Students who just started to learn Japanese culture, including SP3/SP4 students, are by all means welcome, and no prior knowledge of Japanese history is required to enroll. Please just note that you may (at least in the beginning) struggle with unfamiliar names, terms, and concepts, and you will need to spend some extra time looking up those names and terms. Students who have previously studied Japanese history are certainly also welcome. Those of you will be required to revisit your knowledge, especially if you have only studied the subject at Japanese elementary and/or secondary schools, and devise how to present your ideas in an academic fashion that makes sense in an international context.

Objectives:
1. Students grasp history as a complex and nonlinear process.

2. Students build skills in analyzing materials critically and expressing their analysis appropriately as a global citizen.

3. Students acquire college-level knowledge of Japanese premodern history.

This course serves as an introduction to the fundamental issues of modern Japanese history, emphasizing the interplay between international and domestic factors in Japan’s development. The lectures cover the period from the 1840s to the present.

As the historical interpretation of certain events—most notably World War II—remains a subject of significant public and academic debate, this course will explore a variety of competing narratives. Students will be encouraged to critically engage with these diverse perspectives, examining how national memory and political contexts influence the way history is written and remembered.

Objectives:
One primary goal of this course is to acquaint students with the broad historical framework of modern Japan. To this end, lectures will encompass social and cultural history alongside political and economic developments.

Furthermore, the course aims to empower students to understand contemporary events and issues by situating them within their specific historical context.

Before there were computers, there were algorithms.

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the modern study of computer algorithms.

The students will use Python language as a tool to learn many algorithms in depth.

The students are expected to have knowledge in mathematics, especially algebra.

The students are expected to have basic knowledge and experience in Python, which will be used to demonstrate class content.

Objectives:
The students are able to understand and utilize the various search and sorting algorithms.

IMPORTANT: This course will be conducted face-to-face. In addition, this instructor (Ishikawa) will extend slightly beyond a purely introductory level. While it remains a required course, the content will go beyond what is typically expected at the basic level. The goal is to provide a rigorous foundation for students genuinely interested in data science and who intend to develop deeper expertise in this field during their university studies.

This course offers an introductory, literacy-level approach to data science and is designed for students with no prior background in programming or calculus. However, students are expected to have completed either GE122 Introductory Statistics A or GE123 Introductory Statistics B.

Students will develop a foundational understanding of data science, focusing on key concepts, tools, and practical applications. The course covers essential techniques for data collection, data cleaning, and visualization, enabling students to extract insights from diverse datasets.

Core machine learning methods—including regression, classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction—will be introduced, with Python incorporated for hands-on practice. Students will also explore more advanced topics such as natural language processing, image and audio processing, and introductory concepts in reinforcement learning and deep learning.

In addition, the course addresses ethical issues in data science, including algorithmic bias, data privacy, and related social and institutional concerns.

Objectives:
In this course, students will:

• Develop a foundational understanding of data science, including its scope, applications, and core tools.

• Acquire techniques for data collection, cleaning, and preparation to ensure data quality and reliability.

• Learn methods for effective data visualization to communicate insights from diverse datasets.

• Study key machine learning techniques, such as regression, classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction.

• Gain hands-on experience using Python to implement data science methods and models.

• Explore advanced topics, including natural language processing, image and audio processing.

• Examine ethical considerations in data science, such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and related social issues.
