This is an intermediate-level course on data science that will focus on machine learning methods and algorithms using Python. We begin by introducing the big picture of machine learning using various examples. We shall learn techniques of how to do data visualization for various types of data, a very important subfield of machine learning. Other major topics will include: decision tree learning, learning linear separators, logistic regression , generalization and overfitting, model selection and regularization, linear regression, ensemble learning, unsupervised learning, neural network models and principal component analysis. The students will learn how to do prediction and classification tasks using artificial neural networks and deep neural network models, a through treatment of deep learning will be given in an advanced course “Advanced Data Science”. Finally, the students will learn how to interpret the results of accurate but black-box machine learning algorithms.

Objectives:
In this course, students will:

* Understand the basics of machine learning and how to apply it to various problems in liberal arts and humanities.

* Learn principles and methods of data visualization for various types of data.

* Learn predictions using decision trees.

* Learn linear and logistic regression.

* Learn about the problem of generalization and how to overcome the problem of overfitting.

* Learn about the importance and methods of model selection and various ways of doing regularization, including LASSO and cross-validation.

* Learn about the basics of artificial neural networks and deep neural network models.

* Learn about the importance and methods of ensemble learning.

* Learn about methods of reducing dimensionality using principal component analysis.

* Learn how to interpret the results of accurate but black-box machine learning algorithms.

IMPORTANT: This course will be taught Face-To-Face.

This is an advanced-level course on Data Science. The course will focus on deep learning, which has witnessed great success over the past decade. Image processing and natural language processing are two of the most successful fields of deep learning. Some of the most successful applications of deep learning in image processing include object detection, image segmentation, and image classification. In natural language processing, deep learning has been used to develop applications such as machine translation, text classification, automatic summarization and question answering.

The course will begin with an overview of the PyTorch library, a standard library used for deep learning. Students will then study linear algebra and calculus from numerical perspectives. After a gentle introduction of neural network models using the familiar linear and softmax regression, the concept of multilayer perceptrons and the essential technique of backward propagation will be introduced. Various ways to regularize deep neural networks will be studied, such as putting norm penalties or allowing dropout, and students will learn how to do optimization for training these regularized deep neural networks.

In the latter portion of this course, the students will learn convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image analysis and learn neural network models for natural language processing (NLP). The students will learn the state-of-the-art transformer models for NLP. Students will learn how to use and fine-tune pretrained large language models including BERT, T5 and GPT models.

An integral component of this course is project-based learning, where students will engage in two major group projects. The first project will revolve around the application of multilayer perceptrons in tasks involving regression and classification. In the second project students will explore the use of modern deep neural network models in either image analysis or NLP challenges.

Objectives:
In this course, students will:

* Learn the basics of (deep) neural network models.

* Learn how to do regularization for deep neural networks.

* Learn practical methods for implementing deep neural networks, such as selecting performance metrics and hyperparameters.

* Learn the basics of convolutional neural networks (CNN), and image classification using CNN.

* Learn how to use Modern advanced CNN

* Learn the basics of recurrent neural networks (RNN) and language models

* Learn the state-of-the-art transformer models for natural language processing

* Learn how to fine-tune pretrained large language models including BERT, T5 and GPT models, to perform sentiment analysis, text classification, automatic summarization and question answering, etc.

* Learn how to efficiently collect, preprocess, and analyze data. Develop the ability to effectively communicate results through collaborative group discussions and teamwork.

This seminar offers a critical look at data science, data analysis, and big data in particular. There is increasing concern over biased algorithms and how these affect fairness. The social impact of such algorithmic approaches is explored critically from an NLP and DH perspective.
Large datasets are becoming the norm in many fields, and people tend to accept that numbers do not lie. However, there are many ways how dehumanizing data can lead to a skewed or biased outcome. In this seminar, we will explore skewed data, bias in machine learning algorithms, and how to present data “ethically”. We discuss concepts such as actuarial fairness and algorithmic fairness. Basic programming skills are required.

In the fall semester we participate in a SemEval task learning hands-on NLP methods.

Objectives:
After successful completion of this course, students will be able to explain the core ethical issues with big data and machine learning as well as understand how biases hide in data and what the implications for downstream applications are. Students will also understand why open science is important and be able to explain what digital research ethics are.

IMPORTANT: This course will be taught Face-To-Face.
This seminar is designed for students who are interested in data science, a relatively new field of study that combines aspects of computer science and statistics to extract valuable insights from data. Data science is sometimes defined as the practice of collecting, cleaning, and analyzing data to draw conclusions and make decisions. Data science is important to all of us because it allows us to make better decisions by turning data into insights. Recent achievements of data science include the development of new ways to analyze social media data and predictive models that can be used for things like detecting credit card fraud or identifying cancerous tumors. Additionally, data science has been used to develop recommendation systems for book, movie and music streaming services.

In this seminar, we will take a practical approach to learning data science through extensive examples using the popular programming language Python. Students interested in both theory and applications in data science, with or without much previous exposure to Python, are welcomed to join this seminar. The first half of the seminar (Vol.1 to Vol. 6) focuses on learning Python. We will gently dive into data science by introducing Python and the convenient tool of Jupyter Notebook. Students with relatively lesser previous exposure to Python are expected to do more self-study on learning Python programming in order to catch up with others. Students will learn how to use the most important libraries, namely, NumPy and Pandas, the former being the basic for scientific computation and the latter for manipulation of data. Students will also learn basics of data visualization using the standard library Matplotlib. The second half of the seminar (Vol.7 to Vol. 14) focuses on learning of basic machine learning algorithms. Vol. 7 introduces the basic problems of machine learning and the basic library Scikit-Learn for implementing most of the machine learning algorithms to be learned later on. Students will learn basic concepts of a couple of core machine learning algorithms and how to implement them. These core algorithms include, but not limited to, naive Bayes for classification, linear regression for prediction, support vector machines for classification, decision trees for classification and prediction, principal component analysis for dimension reduction, k-means algorithm for clustering, and Gaussian mixture models for clustering and density estimation.
Students who possess a sufficient background in data science and proficiency in Python programming may directly commence their thesis research on topics within the field of data science.

Objectives:
In this seminar, students will obtain basic knowledge in Python which will be sufficient for implementing most of the core machine learning algorithms. Students will also learn some selected machine learning algorithms that are important for a wide range of problems in industry and academia.

In particular, students will:

* Learn how to use Jupyter Notebook for data science.

* Learn how to use NumPy for basic scientific computation.

* Learn how to use Pandas for data manipulation.

* Learn how to use Matplotlib for plotting and data visualization.

* Learn what machine learning is and how to use Scikit-Learn for implementing machine learning algorithms.

* Learn naive Bayes for classification.

* Learn linear regression for prediction.

* Learn support vector machines for classification.

* Learn decision trees for classification and prediction.

* Learn principal component analysis for dimension reduction.

* Learn k-means algorithm for clustering.

* Learn Gaussian mixture models for clustering and density estimation.

In this class students will learn how to define and interpret key humanitarian concepts such as human rights, human security and the responsibility to protect. Students will also learn how to define democracy, and study trends in democratization over the last 100 years. Students will learn about the content of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the United Nations Charter in some detail. We will also consider the strengths and weaknesses of the UN Security Council, and discuss the possibility of UN reform.

Which countries have the best records for respecting human rights, and which countries are the worst abusers of human rights? To address this question, we will look at two of the most respected measures of human rights, the Freedom House surveys of civil and political rights, and the reporting processes of the UN human rights treaty system, and look at how these processes are used to identify human rights abuses in countries such as Japan and Thailand.

We will consider the possibility, as many authors have suggested, that there is a positive and mutually re-enforcing relationship between peace, human rights, and democracy. Looking at previous patterns of democratization, we try to understand why something called the ‘Third Wave’ of democratization took place, and why the momentum behind global democratization has stalled. We evaluate the concept of human security, which some believe is a more helpful concept than that of human rights. Finally, we introduce the issue of humanitarian intervention and the responsibility to protect, through a case study of the Rwanda genocide.

Objectives:
Students will become familiar with the following documents, case studies and concepts:

- The United Nations Charter

- The Universal Declaration of Human Rights

- The UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights

- The annual Freedom in the World Surveys

- The death penalty and criminal justice in Japan

- Forced labour in Thailand

- The Rwanda Genocide

- Universal human rights

- Processes of democratization

- Democratic peace theory

- Human Security

- The Responsibility to Protect

This course is an advanced class, aimed at senior students, and offers what might be called an ‘advanced introduction’ to the European Union (EU), including its history, institutions, decision-making processes and policies.
An honest appraisal of the strengths and weaknesses of the EU is offered. The EU has been referred to as the most successful peace experiment in history, and the most successful international organization in history. The bases for both of these claims are examined. However the EU is also experiencing several interlocking and enduring crises, which some claim are a threat to the very future of the organization. These crisis include; the migration crisis, the Ukraine crisis, a ‘democratic deficit’, and Brexit. Each of these crises will be considered in some detail.
We also consider some of the key aspects of the EU’s international relations, with a focus on the role of the EU in the Asia-Pacific. We will study the EU’s relations with key state actors such as Japan, China, Russia, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam, and also analyse how the EU has tried to promote several human rights norms in the region, using a variety of norm diffusion methods. We will also look at the EU’s attempts to engage with other governance projects in the region, including ASEAN, the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative, and the Free and Open Indo-Pacific promoted by the US, India and Australia, as well as Japan.

Objectives:
Students will acquire a comprehensive understanding of the ‘domestic’ political dimensions of the European integration project. This includes:

- the historical context in which the European integration project emerged

- the major institutions of the EU

- the major treaties of the EU

- the main decision-making processes of the EU

- EU enlargement policy

- the challenges and crises that the EU is currently experiencing

Students will also receive a comprehensive and nuanced explanation of what type of international power the European Union is, and the ways in which it tries to engage with other international actors. There will be a particular emphasis on the EU as an actor in the Asia-Pacific, including analyses of:

-EU-Japan relations

-EU-China relations

-EU-ASEAN relations

-EU-Thailand relations

-EU-Vietnam relations

Finally, we will analyze human rights case studies involving issues such as:

-the death penalty

-criminal justice

-forced labour

-human trafficking

In this class we study the theory and practice of humanitarian intervention. Is it ever justifiable to intervene in the domestic affairs of another sovereign state? If so, when, and for what reasons?

We consider the possibility that a norm of humanitarian intervention has emerged in international society since the end of the Cold War, by examining case studies of most of the major intervention cases that have arisen in the last twenty years. Case studies include Iraq 1991, Somalia, Rwanda, Bosnia, Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq 2003, Darfur, Libya, Syria.

Objectives:
Students will acquire a comprehensive understanding of each of the specific cases listed above, and develop the capacity to evaluate the legality, legitimacy and effectiveness of humanitarian intervention. We will study the UN Charter in detail, and consider the extent to which the ‘responsibility to protect’, an influential concept that has been endorsed by the UN, can guide us in our future debates about when to intervene in other sovereign states for human protection purposes.

The principal aim of this course is to provide for the students an introduction of African studies, especially in Southern African Countries. While the African continent has significant legal, political and economic challenges, students are rarely introduced to the attempts of African states to set up structures to confront those challenges through regional integration. This course will introduce students to the various legal, political and economic regional integration initiatives in the Southern African region which has become an emerging region.
Under the powerful influence of South Africa’s significantly accelerating growth, the economic fortunes of Southern Africa as a whole should experience a major boost from 2010. With the region’s dominant economic power finally shaking off some of the heavy burdens of its inherited domestic problems and beginning to forge ahead much more convincingly, most countries in its closest orbit can expect to see positive gains in terms of improved trade and investment flows.
However, because Southern Africa is yet some way from being a truly cohesive economic bloc, a few contradictory and negative influences are still at work. These are seen most notably in Zimbabwe’s long-running political and economic meltdown; in Angola’s poor economic management in the midst of its latest oil revenue windfall; and in the persistence of drought and rural distress in Malawi. Most importantly, the overall trends are positive, and at least nine countries have been notching up growth rates in excess of 6％ a year. These include the familiar strong performers, like Botswana and Mauritius, as well as the best practitioners of fundamental economic reform like Mozambique and Zambia. The highest growth rate, Mozambique’s 7％ in 2020, may seem to be in a league of its own but in reality, reflected no more than the buoyancy of the natural gas sector.
From the copper of Zambia to Angola’s oil and Namibia’s uranium, many counties in the region are dependent on the export of unprocessed commodities. Looking for lessons on what works? Botswana and South Africa have been successful in attracting value-added processing.
The Tripartite Free Trade Area(TFTA) is a new continental integration project between the SADC, COMESA, and the EAC, expected to be operational by 2021 or 2022.
Now the COVID-19 affects the region, especially South Africa. As of August 2021, South Africa has the highest number of COVID-19 cases in Africa, but with a relatively low death rate.

In that connection, students will learn a lot about the region. This unique lecture at Waseda University started in 2008. In this lecture, each Ambassadors and Embassy officials from the SADC (Southern African Development Community) (http://www.sadc.int/) group will make a presentation on the variety of SADC regions, in terms of the Economy and Politics and the relationship between Japan and the SADC region during this class. In Japan, there are actually 12 embassies of SADC (Angola, Botswana, Democratic Republic of Congo, Lesotho, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe) (For a moment Mauritius, Seychelles, Eswatini(Former Swaziland) and Comores do not have Embassy in Japan). This SADC group is the biggest diplomatic group among the African Diplomatic Corps in Tokyo. The course will focus on the geopolitical area of southern Africa, and the issues that such regions face as they plan to seek to integrate their local economies.

Objectives:
Acquire knowledge about the political and economic situations of the SADC countries.

The European Union (EU) of today is the result of a process that began 73 years ago with the creation of the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) in 1952.
The principal aim of this course is to provide for the students an overview of the causes, the process and the current situation of European political and economic integration. The political and economic integration of each European nation-state into the European Union (EU) is one of the most complicated political enterprises unfolding in the world.

In fact, Europe is in the middle of a great transformation. The European Union is a dynamic ever-changing supranational institution composed of 28 European nation-states on July 2013. However, British people voted for the Brexit through a referendum held on 23 June 2016. That was a great earthquake for the EU as well as for the International Community. The UK intended to invoke Article50 of the Treaty of Lisbon, the formal procedure for withdrawing.

Brexit is officially done: More than four years after the British people voted in a referendum, the UK officially left the European Union on the 31st January 2020. After months of negotiations, the UK and the European Union finally agreed on a deal that will define their future relationship, which comes into effect at 23.00GMT on 31 December 2020. The year 2020 was the year of the COVID-19 also. The COVID-19 and its spread in Europe have had significant effects on some major EU members countries and on European Union institutions. Transmission of COVID-19 is still widespread in the EU/EEA even though most countries are experiencing stable or decreasing case rates. However, absolute numbers remain high, with increasing case rates among older age groups and increasing death rates in several countries. But the EU demonstrated its great solidarity face to this monumental crisis. EU should ride out this pandemic crisis with this European solidarity.

Macron took the power in 2017 and the Presidential election will be held in 2021 in France. Merkel left as a German Chancellor in December 2021. Social Democrat Olaf Scholz(SPD) became Germany's new chancellor on 8th December 2021.The Merkel era is over, but will this new government be very different?
What is the fate of the EU? The political and cultural diversity of the 27 Member States makes the EU a fascinating subject to study. But this diversity also adds to its complexity. Many important events will happen in Europe in 2025. This course aims to familiarize students with the history and institutions of the EU, issues and challenges of the EU, the significance of the EU for Europe, Ukrainian issue, and the Japan-EU relations.

In addition, the instructor will try to organize a meeting with the European Diplomatic Corps in Tokyo and another one with a representative of MOFA during this course so that we can learn what policymakers are thinking.

Acquire the knowledge about the history of European Integration and the complexity of the institutional system of EU

Africa is often perceived by the average Japanese as a continent of conflict and contagion, as the “dark continent,” chaotic and mysterious, or as a continent with wild animals and plants living throughout. In other words, Africa is a continent very far from Japan and Asia, both geographically and psychologically. Hopefully, through this course, students will find a different, more complex reality, a reality where people and countries, like the rest of the world, are struggling with war and peace, authoritarianism and democracy, colonial legacies and current dilemmas, and a reality that calls into question some of the most fundamental beliefs and theories about international relations.
In that connection, this course will try to provide an overview of the politics of sub-Saharan Africa and will examine the social, political, and economic systems in several countries in sub-Saharan Africa. We will also examine major problems facing African states and their citizens. The lectures and discussions will focus on the historical and social legacies that have shaped modern sub-Saharan Africa, and the current social, political, and economic circumstances in that region. We will explore early post-independence Africa, the liberation movements, the authoritarian regimes of the late 1960s to the early 1980s, and some important current social, political, and economic issues. We will examine how the governments and people in sub-Saharan Africa have responded to these issues and attempt to offer possible routes to a brighter political and economic future. We will try to understand the specificities of the current conflicts in Africa and we will consider how to bring these conflicts to an end and prevent their recurrence.
Now the COVID-19 affects the region, especially South Africa. As of August 2021, South Africa has the highest number of COVID-19 cases in Africa, but with a relatively low death rate. COVID-19 death rates have been low and the share of recoveries high in Africa despite earlier warnings from experts that the virus would overrun weak health systems in most countries and kill millions. However, Africa is still needing assistance to bear on the COVID-19 pandemic. Africa is still needing the COVID-19 vaccines also. The rate of vaccination in the whole of Africa is less than 1% as of August 2021. The principal aim of this course is to introduce students to the study of contemporary sub-Saharan African politics and issues. It will expose students to the great diversity of peoples, ideas, cultures, and economic and political systems in this region of the world. In addition, the course will familiarize students with the contemporary social, political, and economic issues being debated by analysts of sub-Saharan African politics. The course will help students develop a broader knowledge of how politics affect the millions of people living in the region. The Instructor will organize a special lecture with African Diplomatic Corps (ADC) in Tokyo within this lecture with the realm of possibility. Lastly, Japan is organizing its important policy forum on Africa, TICAD (Tokyo International Conference on African Development) since 1993. TICAD Ⅵ was held in Nairobi in 2016. TICAD 7 was held in Japan in 2019. TICAD 8 was held in Africa (Tunisia) in 2022. The instructor will explain the role of Japan in African development. TICAD 9 wiil be held in Yokohama in 2025.

Objectives:
Acquire the general knowledges about the African Studies, especially African Politics.

The course aims to build foundational skills in listening, speaking, reading, and writing, while also fostering an initial awareness of the Chinese-speaking societies and cultures.

Through sustained language practice, students will also begin to develop critical awareness of how language and culture interact in communication.

This course is designed for students who have completed the Chinese I course or who possess an equivalent level of proficiency. Each lesson includes dialogues and communicative activities, such as role-plays, grammar exercises, reading and listening tasks, covering a wide range of practical language functions (e.g., asking questions, accepting or refusing requests, and talking about oneself). The course also develops students’ lexical, grammatical, and phonetic knowledge. Students are expected to participate actively in class and to use Chinese as much as possible throughout the course.

Objectives:
By the end of the semester, students will be able to communicate in a wider range of everyday situations using Chinese. The course aims to help students master essential grammar and develop intermediate-level language proficiency. Particular emphasis will be placed on the development of accurate pronunciation throughout the course.

Objectives:
At the end of the semester, students should be able to cope with daily life using Chinese expressions in a greater variety of situations.

Stress will be placed particularly on teaching correct pronunciation.

This course is designed for students who have completed Chinese I and Chinese II. The course is taught by two instructors and consists of a “Reading and Writing class” and a “Listening and Speaking class”.
In the Reading class, students will develop their reading comprehension skills using materials at approximately the HSK Level 4 standard. In the Speaking class, listening materials are provided particularly for students who need additional support in listening comprehension. Regular oral presentations are incorporated to enhance speaking proficiency. In preparation for future study abroad opportunities, practice exercises for the HSK examination will also be included.

Objectives:
The course aims to develop students’ beginner to intermediate Chinese proficiency by improving the four language skills of reading, writing, speaking, and listening. Students are expected to work toward passing Level 3 of the Chinese Proficiency Test (中国語検定) and HSK Levels 4. Alongside language learning, students will deepen their understanding of Chinese culture and society.

This is an opportunity for non-native Chinese speakers to apply the basic language skills you have acquired over the past 1 to 2 years.

Even if you are unsure about your basic academic ability, you can improve while taking the course.

You have a lot of work to do during class, so you are going to use your own computer all the time.

Objectives:
(1) Reading contemporary articles in Chinese precisely.

(2) To express yourself in Chinese.

(3) Using computers and the Internet as your assistant.

This is an intermediate course for students who have completed either Intensive Chinese Ⅰ, or Chinese Ⅱ, or equivalent. This course is suitable for student planning to study abroad in a Chinese speaking country. There will be 4 classes per week, for reading, translating, speaking, listening and writing respectively.

3 textbooks will be used for reading, writing, and speaking classes and additional materials will be distributed for listening classes.

Students have to write Chinese essays almost every week.

This course is demanding.

Strong efforts and commitment are required.

Objectives:
The aim of this course is to help students acquire intermediate-level Chinese abilities, ready to read articles and journals in Chinese and discuss about wide range of topics in Chinese.

This is an intensive course designed for students preparing to transfer to a university in a Chinese-speaking country. It is intended for students who have completed Intensive Chinese I and II, as well as senior-level students who have attained an equivalent level of proficiency. Students who have previously studied in China and wish to further refine their Mandarin skills are also welcome to enroll.

The course aims to develop students’ overall academic Chinese competence through activities such as speed reading, intensive reading, discussion, and report writing based on a range of authentic Chinese-language materials. Depending on the instructor’s design, Chinese newspapers and other current materials may be introduced to support these learning objectives.

Through extensive reading and discussion of authentic texts, students will strengthen their ability to comprehend university-level lectures in Chinese and enhance their capacity to explain social and cultural topics related to Japan in Mandarin.

Objectives:
Foster the abilities of speed-reading and discussion of current issues and making reports on them in Chinese.

This course focuses on acquiring good discussion and presentation skills, which are essential for studying at SILS. It also provides general support for understanding various topics covered in introductory lectures at SILS, as well as an introduction to the various facilities available to students at Waseda (libraries, writing center, etc.) Please see the topics to be studied in this course, which are listed on the schedule.

Objectives:
The aim of this course is to help students to familiarize themselves with the topics covered in introductory lectures at SILS, and learn about the various facilities and services available to students at Waseda University. This course will also help students improve their TOEFL scores (especially for listening and speaking) as we work on understanding academic lectures and work with English vocabulary and structure. It is also expected that students will acquire good research skills and presentation skills needed to study in the university setting and to prepare for study abroad.

This course introduces students to the basics of English academic writing. Students will begin by learning how to write a coherent paragraph and then apply the skill to writing a five-paragraph essay. They will learn how to create an effective thesis statement, topic sentences, introduction and conclusion, as well as how to organize supporting sentences logically. The course will also focus on other essential skills for academic writing, such as paraphrasing, summarizing and citation. Practice for the TOEFL writing component is also incorporated in the course.

*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.

Objectives:
・Students will learn skills to identify basic components of paragraphs and essays, and will become able to use them to write essays.

・Students will learn basic rules of citation (in-text citation and works cited), and will be able to use them in their essays.

・Students will expand their grammar and vocabulary to express their opinions more accurately in English.

In this course students will focus on gaining an in-depth understanding of the form and function of different academic essay genres; in particular, the argumentative essay. Emphasis is placed on writing effective thesis statements, introductions and conclusions, and on developing paragraphs. Students will also learn effective citation, paraphrasing and summarizing skills. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing style, vocabulary and background knowledge.

*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.

Objectives:
・Students will gain a deeper understanding of academic essays, and will learn to write an effective argumentative essay that adheres to expected conventions.

・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.

・Students will practice skills to use information from outside sources (in-text citations and reference list entries) so that they can support their opinions more effectively in writing.

・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from their instructor and peers.

In this course students will focus on developing advanced essay-writing skills from understanding essay prompts to making better decisions about sentence construction. Emphasis is placed on taking a position in an argumentative essay, researching, evaluating sources, developing cohesive body paragraphs, logically developing ideas throughout the essay, and writing effective introductions and conclusions. Students will also learn essential skills in citation, paraphrasing and summarizing, and how to integrate sources into their writing. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and with subtle changes in emphasis and nuance, and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing styles, vocabulary, and background knowledge.

*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.

Objectives:
・Students will understand advanced academic essay requirements, and will learn to take an appropriate position, and argue and support it in an argumentative essay.

・Students will practice skills for using information from outside sources (source evaluation, in-text citation and reference lists) so that they can support their arguments more clearly and logically in writing.

・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.

・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from the instructor and peers.

This class will help students acquire techniques to create and present effective speeches. Speeches come in many kinds. Nevertheless, all good speeches have some common traits. By analyzing well-regarded examples, students will learn skills and strategies for creating and delivering talks that persuade audiences to feel and think. The lecturer will draw upon her experience as a TV anchor and storyteller to guide students toward advanced delivery and presentation skills. Classes will be conducted face-to-face.

Objectives:
This course is intended to help students become proficient in creating and delivering speeches that have lasting impact. By examining actual well-known speeches, they will learn both content and delivery aspects of the craft. During the semester, students will be required to create and deliver two presentations. They also will engage in question-and-answer sessions to prepare for professional careers. Participation in this class will lead to improvement in comprehension and presentation skills in English.

This course is for students who have a score of TOEFL ITP 550 or higher. This course is for those students who wish to use and develop their English speaking and leadership skills through formal discussion and presentation. In this course, you should expect to: “talk” to/with and at an audience without memorizing speeches; field and answer questions about a position on a given topic; understand the complexity of some contemporary issues; present information using sound educational pedagogy: and lead a 30-minute class using technologies and through Socratic dialogue. This is NOT a course to practice speech competitions or debate. Students should be expected to involve their peers in discussion through their topics.This course is about students developing their skills through practice.

Objectives:
Throughout my association with SILS, I have found that many students already have the verbal competencies to give a presentation. Often confidence, knowledge of topics, and opportunities are lacking. This course is also linked to educational practice. By the end of this course you should feel more confident to lead group discussions and make formal presentations, with and without the use of technology. You should expect to do the talking.

※in-person ONLY
This course is for students who have a score of TOEFL ITP 550 or higher. This course is for those students who wish to use and develop their English speaking and leadership skills through formal discussion and presentation. In this course, you should expect to:
“talk” to/with and at an audience without memorizing speeches
field and answer questions about a position on a given topic
understand the complexity of some contemporary issues
present information using sound educational pedagogy
understand how to be the “devil’s advocate” through Socratic dialogue

Objectives:
Throughout my association with SILS, I have found that many students already have the verbal competencies to give a presentation. Often “confidence” and “knowledge of topics” are the two weak areas. This gives the impression that students have some language deficiency. By the end of this course you should feel more confident to lead group discussions and make formal presentations, with and without the use of technology. You should expect to practice and do most of the talking.

This course is about students developing their skills through practice.

Our lives are made up of the stories we tell aboutthem. Being able to communicate our experiences effectively helps us to connectwith other people, form wider communities, and gain greater understanding ofourselves and others. This course will explore the nature of storytellingthrough the development and polishing of an autobiographical story. The processof the course will focus on the development and structuring of a narrative,along with work on finding the language to make the story reach an audience andmove them.

Objectives:
The general purpose of this course is to develop your writing skills in the form of autobiographical narrative. I hope that you will learn how to take incidents from your life and through your writing, share your experiences with others and entertain and move them by making them more aware of your world and their own lives. I would like students in this course to gain a greater understanding of themselves and their lives through crafting a story that can be shared with others.

This is a one-semester twice-a-week course for beginners. The textbook used for this class is published in France (Inspire 1, see: https://www.hachettefle.com/collections/inspire) and is essentially based on the principles of the communicative approaches. At the end of the semester, students should have learned enough vocabulary to manage to communicate in daily life, using simple French expressions (Target: Level A1 in the CFRL)

The main objective of this course is to prepare students to a successful year of study in France or in a French-speaking country.It is divided into two parts: Academic Studies and French for Academic Purposes. Academic Studies will cover topics necessary for students to integrate fully and beneficially in the country they choose for studying abroad. It will cover stimulating and profitable areas of interest both from an intellectual and a practical level. French for Academic Purposes will focus on specific demands and requirements of the French educational system and will teach skills and techniques necessary to succeed in higher education studies.

In this class, students will also improve their French skills thanks to DELF and Futsuken (仏検) practical exercises

Objectives:
This course is for students planning to study a French-speaking university in the near future. It is recommended to take this course along other French courses. This course will also be beneficial to students who already have a good level (A2+ or B1) and are willing to study the language, and students who have an interest in French society and culture. Finally, it is open to students from of all faculties.

This course is an integrated language-culture content course (CLIL) in English and in French to help students (on a linguistic and sociocultural level) improve both their understanding of French society and their oral skills in pronunciation and conversation. It is primarily aimed at students who already have an A1 level in French (Level 1 in SILS already completed), but it can be of interest to students with various levels of proficiency (from A1 to B1). The course will be partly taught in English and partly in French: half of the course will be devoted to French language learning practice (pronunciation, dialogue comprehension and memorization) with the multimedia TUFS Language Modules (https://www.coelang.tufs.ac.jp/mt/fr/index_en.html), and half will be devoted to linguistic and cultural analyses and discussions.

Objectives:
The objective of the course is to provide an introduction to the French sound system, sociocultural insight into French society, and opportunities to practice French conversation around specific speech acts to students who are interested in French studies.

This course explores cinema as a means of language acquisition and cultural learning. Through the analysis of films in their original version, students will:

- Strengthen their command of French vocabulary in real-life contexts.

- Improve their listening comprehension by engaging with native speakers’ natural speech patterns.

- Develop their ability to express ideas in French through film-based activities.

- Deepen their understanding of French culture by exploring societal and cultural themes through cinema.

Each session revolves around the study of a film or an excerpt, allowing students to progressively develop their language skills, refine their comprehension, and expand their vocabulary. The exploration of various cinematic genres will provide them with an enriched perspective on the cultural and social realities of France, while reinforcing their linguistic proficiency.

*The class will be conducted mostly in French, but some documents and movie subtitles will be in English.

**This class is for students who have a B1 level in French, i.e. students who have studied /are studying Level 3 in French and are preparing for study-abroad in a French-speaking area, but it can also be useful for students coming back from study-abroad or who have a higher level in French.

Objectives:
- Improve their comprehension of spoken French through film dialogues.

- Acquire vocabulary and common expressions in context.

- Express their impressions about a film in a simple and natural way.

- Discover cultural and social aspects of French cinema.

For historical reasons, French was considered the main language of diplomacy and is still today the official and/or working language of several international organisations such as WTO, UN, OECD, NATO, ICJ, FIFA, IOC, etc. French is therefore a requisite for the ones who intend to work in such places. This course is a CLIL class (Content and Language Integrated Learning), which means French and English will be used in class to help you not only improve your French skills but also develop your knowledge about diplomacy and international institutions where French is used as a communication tool, through different classroom activities such as discussion, presentation, conversation, aural (video and audio material) & reading comprehension tasks. The course is intended for students with a B1 level in French in the CEFR levels.The professor in charge of this class is a professional expert in preparing diplomats to go and work in the francophone world (he is the Special Chief Instructor for French at the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs - MOFA): a remarkable opportunity for students to know more about this field and career with first-hand information and training.

Objectives:
Besides discovering international organisations where French is used and giving you insights into diplomacy in the 21st century, the main objective of this course is to help you develop specific and useful French skills for your future career as a diplomat or as an active member of the international community.

Supported by an extensive international network of embassies and consulates, France ranks third in the world in terms of its representation and activity abroad. In this course, we will cover international issues and affairs connected to France on all continents (Semester 1 will focus on Europe, Africa and the Americas while semester 2 will concentrate on Asia, Oceania, the polar regions, space, etc.) and learn about its diplomatic relations and actions.Conducted both in French and English, this class will aim to improve general and professional French skills needed in a multicultural and international working environment and become more familiar with France’s foreign policy across the world. Discussion, presentation, conversation, aural (video and audio material) & reading comprehension tasks will be some of the different classroom activities.

2. Understanding and defining the place and role of France in the concert of nations.

Whenever cross-cultural communication occurs, the exchange of messages can soon become the cause of miscommunication and misunderstanding, creating funny and embarrassing moments at times. But when it comes to a message expressing the stance of one or more countries on an international issue, like in a joint communiqué for instance, its accurate translation is then of paramount importance. And although each language has its own particularities and uniqueness, it is the job of translators and interpreters to convey the exact, or at least, the most appropriate and meaningful message to each side so that communication can be facilitated and positions understood. In this course, we will work on different texts, speeches, communiqués and writings from the diplomatic domain. This class will be taught in French and in English, and we will try to apply a methodology to switch from one language to the other. This CLIL class (Content and Language Integrated Learning) will help you to get a glimpse of translation techniques and strategies while studying linguistic structures easily reusable in many professional situations.
The course is intended for students with a B1-B2 level in French in the CEFR levels.
The professor in charge of this class is a professional expert in preparing diplomats to go and work in the francophone world (he is the Special Chief Instructor for French at the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs - MOFA): a remarkable opportunity for students to know more about this field and career with first-hand information and training.

Objectives:
This course is an introduction to the problematic of translation and aims to give you linguistic tools and strategies to be able to render a message from one language into another in the most accurate way. We will start by acquiring a translation methodology to help us dealing first with short and varied articles (daily press briefings from embassies, news and short statements from government and international organisations, etc.) and then delve into longer and more complex texts or speeches.

Whenever cross-cultural communication occurs, the exchange of messages can soon become the cause of miscommunication and misunderstanding, creating funny and embarrassing moments at times. But when it comes to the message from a high-ranking official about the foreign policy of his or her country, the accuracy and clarity of the translation/interpretation is crucial. Translators and interpreters need to acquire and develop techniques to help facilitate communication. Although this course can be considered to build on the level 1 course, it is open to any student with the required language level and the will to know more about intercultural and linguistic communication. We will work on different documents from the diplomatic domain and even though this class will be mainly taught in French and English, we will also use the Japanese language, be it in an oral or written form. Translation and interpretation classes will alternate every other week. This CLIL class (Content and Language Integrated Learning) will help you to acquire better translation and interpretation techniques and strategies while studying linguistic structures and pattern easily reusable in a real life.
The course is intended for students with a B2-C1 level in French in the CEFR levels.
The professor in charge of this class is a professional expert in preparing diplomats to go and work in the francophone world (he is the Special Chief Instructor for French at the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs - MOFA): a remarkable opportunity for students to know more about this field and career with first-hand information and training.

Objectives:

This course instils thefundamental knowledge of Russian as a foreign language. The purpose of thiscourse is to help students acquire the basics of Russian grammar necessary for thecomprehension of sentence structures and develop conversational skills in arange of predictable everyday situations.

Objectives:
Course Objectives

By the end of the semester, students will:

• Acquire essential elements of Russian grammar at beginner level.

• Build a working vocabulary of approximately 900–1,000 lexical items.

• Master around 30 units of speech etiquette for everyday social interaction.

• Develop the ability to establish and maintain social contacts in standard everyday situations, such as making acquaintances and exchanging biographical information, stating profession and occupation, discussing hobbies and leisure activities, exchanging holiday greetings (public, national, family, or personal), expressing wishes and desires, giving, receiving, and responding to presents, extending, accepting, or declining invitations, arranging meetings (location, time, etc.), sharing contact details (address, telephone number, etc.), reading transport schedules and public signs, commenting on events (concerts, lectures, etc.), and reading menus and ordering meals.

Expected Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

• Listening and Speaking Skills: understand basic instructions and engage in simple factual conversations on predictable topics.

• Reading Skills: comprehend a range of basic notices and instructions in everyday contexts.

• Writing Skills: Produce short notes and messages on familiar or predictable matters with basic accuracy.

This course is the intermediate level of “Russian as a foreign language” for students who have learnt the primary level of the language in the previous semester. The students in this semester will continue to build on their proficiency in Russian grammar and conversation skills by using the same textbook that was used in autumn semester.
The lessons are taught in Russian, English and Japanese. The teaching level in the class will mostly be based on the students’ current grammar level and it will advance as they make progress.

Objectives:
The textbook consists of 21 chapters and the chapters that were not covered in the previous semester will be taught in this semester. By the end of the semester, the students will be expected to learn approximately 900 Russian words and all key concepts of Russian grammar, enabling them to express themselves clearly and fluently in Russian.

This course is a continuation of Russian I and is designed to further develop students’ foundational knowledge of Russian as a foreign language. It focuses on strengthening grammatical competence, expanding active vocabulary, and enhancing communicative skills across a wider range of everyday situations. Particular emphasis is placed on improving speaking and listening abilities, while also consolidating reading and writing skills, in order to enable students to participate more confidently in routine social and academic interactions.

Objectives:
Course Objectives

By the end of the semester, students will:

• Consolidate and extend their knowledge of Russian grammar at the elementary level.

• Expand their active vocabulary to approximately 1,300 lexical units.

• Master a wider range of speech etiquette for everyday social interaction.

• Strengthen listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills in Russian for practical communication.

• Develop confidence in initiating and sustaining dialogues in common social and academic contexts.

• Gain familiarity with cultural aspects of Russian society relevant to everyday interaction.

Expected Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

• Reading: Read short, simple texts drawn from a variety of everyday and adapted sources.

• Listening: Comprehend key information in audio and video materials on familiar topics, including references to place, time, and cause.

• Speaking: Initiate and maintain dialogues in predictable situations (friends, family, studies, work, hometown, health, weather, leisure activities).

• Writing: Produce short texts such as personal letters, memos, and greeting cards with basic accuracy.

• Interpretation: Summarise and present the main content of short texts in oral or written form.

• Cross‑cultural competence: Understand and respond appropriately to basic socio‑cultural conventions in everyday communication.

Spanish Intensive II is a second-semester intensive Spanish language course (Level 3 and 4) designed to enable students to develop and improve skills in understanding, speaking, reading, and writing Spanish, while increasing their awareness of the Spanish-speaking world. This course serves as a bridge where students' native language(s) and culture(s) and the target (Spanish) language and culture meet. Students will cross the bridge and be familiar with the Spanish-speaking world. Through this course, students will not only develop their Spanish language skills, but also acquire critical thinking skills by examining differences and similarities between the two (or more) languages and cultures. Students will be exposed to a variety of cultural aspects of the Spanish-speaking world through reading materials. This is a demanding course. The ultimate goal of Spanish Intensive II is to acquire effective and intelligent communication, critical thinking, and the appreciation and understanding of the Spanish-speaking world as well as an awareness of cultural and linguistic diversity in the world. This course is highly recommended to those who are to study abroad in a Spanish-speaking country and who have finished Intensive Spanish I or Spanish Level 2. It is an intensive course that meets 4 times per week. The language proficiency and level expected at the end of semester will be intermediate. Strong efforts and commitment are required.

Objectives:
Objective 1: Knowledge of the Spanish Language

In this course, you will improve your language skills acquired in the previous course(s). In order to best accomplish this, you and your professor will undertake activities carried out from the very first completely in the target language, that is, in Spanish.

Objective 2: Knowledge about the Cultures of Spain and Latin America

In addition to this paramount goal of learning the common (although varied!) language of the Spanish-speaking countries, you will also be exposed to different aspects of the cultures of Spain and Latin America through readings, songs, videos, and other materials.

Objective 3: Cultural Comparison and Critical Thinking

Because learning about another culture necessarily takes place through the prism of one’s own, this course encourages reflection about our daily lives and potential similarities and differences between our own and Latin American and Spanish cultures. In so doing, it promotes an awareness of the importance of point of view or personal experience in the interpretation and/or understanding of the world. Cultural comparison and communicating across cultures are fundamental skills that will open doors for your future.

Objective 4: Effective and Intelligent Communication

Learning another language involves creativity and a willingness to make mistakes in getting your message across. In this course, you will become adept at finding ways to say things that you need to say with the tools you have at hand. You will gain confidence and become a more effective communicator over-all as you bring into play the many –both verbal and non-verbal—elements of language use that perhaps (because you know it soooo well) you don’t make use of in English. Pausing to think about how to say something in another language can make us more careful, effective, and attentive communicators in our own. Please note that diligent study and active class participation are absolutely essential for making progress toward these first four objectives. The more you attempt to speak only Spanish, the more you will learn and the easier it will become.

Objective 5: Connecting with Other Disciplines

By working on basic communication skills, Spanish Intensive II will help you achieve success in your other courses. You will also find that many of the topics that will be discussed might come up in other classes. For example, a discussion of family or of poverty and migration in a sociology or anthropology class or a discussion of important political figures in a history or political science course. Continued study in Spanish will enable you to read and research sources written in Spanish and can provide you with important perspectives not available in English.

Objective 6: Preparing for Study Abroad

Significant engagement with and learning in the areas discussed in Objectives 1 – 5 will provide you with the building blocks that you will need for a successful semester or year of study in another country, whether it is Spanish-speaking or not. If you are serious about learning Spanish, there is no substitute for an extended stay in Spain or Latin America.

This course offers an overview of some of the most important Spanish-language texts that illustrate how Japan was portrayed in Spain and Latin America from the late nineteenth century through the first half of the twentieth century. Classes will focus on the analysis and critical interpretation of these texts within their broader cultural, political, and social contexts. We will explore how portrayals of Japan in the Spanish-speaking world took shape and evolved over time, and identify the key figures involved in shaping these representations. We will study both well-known works by Spanish and Latin American authors, such as Vicente Blasco Ibáñez and José Juan Tablada, and lesser-known texts, particularly those by women travelers.

Objectives:
The primary aim of this course is to provide the students with the analytical tools necessary to interpret key texts written in Spanish that convey diverse representations of Japan from the late nineteenth century to the 1950s,and to understand the cultural, political, and social factors that influenced their production. In addition, the course also aims to foster intercultural communication in Spanish through reading, discussion, and critical analysis, so that students can express their ideas clearly and confidently.

The course offers an introduction to some of the most influential literary movements in the Spanish-speaking world from the late nineteenth century to the 1970s. Through the analysis of literary excerpts in Spanish, alongside other forms of artistic expression such as painting and music, we will explore major literary trends in relation to broader artistic traditions in Spain and Latin America. We will also examine how cultural production in the Spanish-speaking world responded to wider social, political, and historical factors. We will address the work of both well-known writers and artists, such as Federico García Lorca and Salvador Dalí, as well as lesser-known creators whose contributions have often been overlooked.

Objectives:
The goal of this course is to help students identify and reflect on some of the major literary movements in the Spanish-speaking world from the late nineteenth century to the 1970s, and to interpret selected texts within their broader artistic, historical, and cultural contexts. The course also aims to develop strategies for successful intercultural communication in Spanish through reading, discussion, and critical analysis, so that students can express themselves clearly and confidently.

This course aims to explore some static and dynamic aspects of the legal system in a globalized world and to examine the function and application of international law in the settlement of disputes between actors (including states).
Students will learn the rules of law which are applied to current events in the world with a view to broadly understanding history, world politics, and other related fields of study.

To understand basic ideas of public international law under the idea of the Rule of Law in the international community.

This seminar will, through discussion, provide students with necessary knowledge and view-points to understand the structure and function of international law in time of cyberspace and AI. The course will also take a critical look at the theoretical and practical aspects of territorial and maritime dispute settlement under international law (with special reference to cyberspace/AI) from the perspective of other disciplines such as geopolitical science, geography, economics, history, and philosophy.
In accordance with the selected topics, the class will be divided into several working groups, and students will prepare for brief research papers for class discussion. Students of this seminar should have basic knowledge of both international relations and international law, so that they will explore the subjects more deeply and fully.
