The course will also take a critical look at the theoretical and practical aspects of the dispute settlement under international law from the perspective of other disciplines such as environmental and geopolitical science, geography, economics, and history.
In accordance with the selected topics, the class will be divided into several working groups, and students will prepare for brief research papers for class discussion. Students of this seminar should have basic knowledge of both international relations and international law, so that they will explore the subjects more deeply and fully.
This course will be basically held in class (face2face), if the COVID-19 situation is much more ameliorated and/or over. Please wait for further notices.

Objectives:
Students will learn to know and analyse important points concerning the concept of cyberspace/AI under international law and international relations, so that they will get ready to write a graduation thesis.

Laws have deeply affected the lives of minority groups in the U.S., and have been a source of both empowerment and deprivation. This course will look at some of the laws and legal issues surrounding minorities, with attention to historical, political and social contexts. The groups that will be covered are 1) African Americans, 2) Asian Americans, 3) Hispanics, 4) women, and 5) LGBTs. (Weeks 2 - 5 focuses on African Americans, Weeks 7 - 11 on immigrant minorities, and Weeks 13 - 14 on gender and sexual orientation)
From time to time, the situation in Japan will be taken up for a comparative discussion. Student input on the situation in other countries are also welcome.

Objectives:
Students will:

1) Be able to assess the role of law in defining the status and influencing the lives of minority groups in U.S. society,

2) Be able to analyze the factors behind changes in the law, and the mutual effects between law and society,

3) Be able to compare the case of the U.S. with the legal status of minorities in other countries.

This seminar will examine rights, politics, and society in a comparative perspective, especially focusing on diversity issues. Students are expected to build upon their study abroad experience in pursuing a research topic within this general theme. (Particular emphasis will be given to minority rights / diversity issues, but the research topic can focus on other rights issues based on consultation with the instructor.)

In addition to student presentations, the seminar will feature occasional events such as guest speakers, joint activities with other seminars, and/or a weekend excursion (if circumstances allow.)

Objectives:
Students will:

1) Be able to assess the interaction between law, politics and society on contemporary issues surrounding minority rights and diversity.

2) Be able to apply key ideas and concepts in the field to their own research.

3) Be able to articulate their analyses in a full-length academic thesis as well as present them as a structured academic presentation.

4) Be able to provide constructive, informed comments on other person's papers and presentations and to collaborate towards a shared understanding of important social issues.

This course will examine fundamental issues of constitutional law in postwar Japan.

The Constitution of Japan establishes important principles regarding human rights, pacifism, separation of powers, democracy, and judicial review.

However, the meaning of each item has evolved over time, and has often been a subject of political and social conflicts inside and outside of Japan.

We will examine these important issues with both the domestic and international context in mind.

*The instructor for this course, along with the content, has been changed from the previous year.

Objectives:
The goal of this course is to understand the basic constitutional framework in Japan, including its basic principles, structure of government, and guarantee of fundamental rights.

Students are expected to be able to：

1) discuss the basic ideas and conflicts behind the provisions;

2) discuss the significance of major Supreme Court cases in each field; and

3) state their views on major constitutional issues with the understanding of this background.

A significant phenomenon in U.S. law, society and politics is the active role of courts over many issues that divide the country, and the attention paid to judges,
especially U.S. Supreme Court justices, who differ in their orientations and can sway the outcome of issues that come to the Court.

This course will look into such important roles that the judicial branch in the U.S. and its judges have played in the evolution of the U.S. Constitution.

We will first look into theoretical considerations behind the role of the judiciary. Then we will look at how the U.S courts have performed this role, organized around three major themes: 1) the extent to which the ideology of the judges affect their decision-making; 2) the effectiveness of courts in bringing about social change; and 3) the tensions between the judiciary and the political branches.

We will examine the above items through cases that have divided U.S. society and politics-- such as abortion rights, same-sex marriage, gun regulation, racial and gender equality, and the President's power over immigration.

Objectives:
Students will:

1) Understand key ideas surrounding the role of the judiciary (especially in the U.S.), and to apply it to contemporary debate and discussion.

2) Acquire an advanced knowledge of how the U.S. Constitution is applied in practice, being able to understand the nuances of Supreme Court opinions and the historical/ social/ political context behind those opinions.

3) Be able to analyze the tendency of the Court and its justices from era to era, and apply this to the current Court.

4) Be able to assess and articulate the role of the Court within society and in the governance of a nation.

5) Be able to articulate their thoughts and engage in discussion with their peers on the above items.

This course provides an introduction to the field of psycholinguistics, exploring the intricate relationship between language and the human mind. Students will examine topics such as language acquisition, language processing, bilingualism, and the neural basis of language. Through a combination of theoretical discussions, empirical studies, and practical applications, students will gain insights into how psychology and linguistics intersect in the study of language.

Objectives:
- Students will become familiar with models of language processing, cognitive processes involved in comprehension and production, and experimental methodologies used to study language processing.

- Students will acquire the knowledge and skills to examine and compare various theories of language acquisition, understanding how individuals acquire language skills from early childhood through different developmental stages.

- Students will become familiar with the cognitive advantages and challenges associated with bilingualism and multilingualism, including the effects on language control, cognitive flexibility, and brain function.

Mode of Delivery: Face-to-Face

Sociolinguistics is a field of linguistics which examines the relationship between language and society, as they mutually influence each other. This course introduces basic concepts of sociolinguistics and explores both micro and macro sociolinguistic studies, reviewing various cases from the micro interpersonal interaction levels to the macro institutional and societal levels. Topics covered include language and power, thought and representation, ethnography of speaking, language and gender, language change, regional and social variation, multilingualism, language attitudes as well as language policy and language planning issues in various social contexts from around the world. Although concepts of both micro and macro sociolinguistics are introduced, an emphasis will be placed on language policy and language planning issues.

Objectives:
To understand basic concepts of both micro and macro sociolinguistics.

This course is for intermediate students of English Linguistics. It will provide them with the basic knowledge of English Language Teaching in secondary education in Japan from a practical point of view. Those students who wish to register for this course are expected to have attended at least one or two of the introductory courses of linguistics offered at SILS, such as Introduction to Applications of Linguistics and Introduction to English Linguistics. On the basis of the knowledge they have acquired from these introductory courses, this course is to offer them both the theoretical and practical knowledge of English Language Teaching. We will investigate how our knowledge of English (not only structural but also communicative) can be used to improve learners' abilities to use English.

The course covers a fourteen-week period and is organized into two sections: English Language Teaching and Pragmatics.

Objectives:
The student will acquire a basic understanding of some of the most important themes and issues with English Language Teaching in Japan.

Welcome to Introduction to Second Language Acquisition (SLA), a key interdisciplinary discipline within Applied Linguistics. This course provides a comprehensive foundation in SLA while encouraging critical examination of language teaching and learning experiences through current theories and research.

Through evidence-based approaches, we will examine key questions in language learning:

- How does age affect second language acquisition?

- What is the role of input, interaction and output in second language development?

- To what extent are individual differences (e.g., aptitude, motivation) important in second language development?

- What does it mean to become a bilingual/multilingual user?

- How does study abroad impact second language proficiency?

- What is the optimal teaching methods for Japanese English learners?

Students will explore these questions through various activities focusing on real-world language teaching and learning contexts. The course examines current SLA research findings and their applications to language pedagogy and learning practices.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, you will be expected to:

(1) Understand key concepts and theories underpinning SLA research.

(2) Assess the applicability and limitations of SLA research findings in practical language teaching and learning contexts.

(3) Apply SLA theories to reflect critically on personal and observed language learning experiences.

※Full face to face
This course will cover the field of interpreting comprehensively to understand the Japanese interpreting industry. The class is designed so that the students will be exposed to the history and current state of the market. The course will also give opportunity to students to understand major theories of interpreting, how they are applied in training, and finally how to enter and survive on the interpreting market.

The class content will be informed by the discussion that takes place in the class, so it will be very important for each student to contribute to the discussion. In this way, each person’s concerns and interests will be addressed in the content of the following classes.

※This class will be taught by a faculty member who possesses professional experience and will be taught based on the working experience.

Objectives:
The aim of the course is to provide students with an understanding of the interpreting industry in Japan so that they can analyze developments and events in the field. The course will also offer deep cultural and societal insight into the socioeconomic fabric within which the industry developed so that the students may themselves identify some of the key turning points of Japan's advancement into the international community and analyze how language played a significant role in Japan's globalization.

Mode of Delivery: Face-to-Face

The main goal of this course is to provide the participants with an opportunity to examine contemporary sociolinguistic issues. This course focuses mainly on macro sociolinguistic studies to present various issues in language policy and language planning from around the world. Topics covered in this course include language and ethnicity/migration, language and class, language and identity, language and conflicts, language and politics, multilingualism and education, language change and standardization, language maintenance, and literacy issues. The discipline of language policy and planning covers more than language itself; it has political, economic, social and cultural dimensions. We will examine the development of standard languages in the construction of national communities and identities, bilingualism and multilingualism, language attitudes in nationalism and globalization, language rights and endangered languages.

Objectives:
To critically review the concepts of language policy and planning.

This advanced course bridges theoretical understanding of Second Language Acquisition (SLA) with practical applications in English language teaching, specifically focused on the Japanese educational context. Students will explore the relationship between SLA research and effective pedagogical practices across second language skills (e.g., grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, reading, listening, writing, and speaking).

This course is particularly valuable for students pursuing careers in English language education across Japanese educational sectors (elementary, junior high, senior high schools, universities, and private education). Students will gain practical experience in applying SLA theories to real classroom contexts, with special attention to the unique challenges and opportunities in Japanese educational settings.

While the primary language of instruction is English, this course is provided in a bilingual format, incorporating both English and Japanese. Some readings will be in Japanese, so students need to be comfortable reading academic Japanese to get the most out of the course.

* Prior to taking this advanced course, students are strongly recommended to take Applied Linguistics (intermediate course) and/or the intermediate seminar, taught by the lecturer (Suzuki), to build a basic foundation in SLA.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

- Critically analyze and apply key principles and theories of second language acquisition to teaching contexts

- Design and develop effective, research-based English language teaching materials

- Plan and deliver effective English lessons for diverse learner groups in Japanese educational settings

- Evaluate and adapt teaching approaches based on SLA principles

This seminar is for those students who wish to study the grammatical and lexical aspects of the English language from its earliest stage. Since acquiring a good reading knowledge of historical documents is essential to this area of study, we shall start with learning the basics of Old English, including its spelling, pronunciation, syntax, paradigms, and lexicon. For this purpose we shall use an introductory textbook that contains not only a useful reference grammar of Old English but also a good selection of Old English verse and prose with detailed textual annotations. Together with this weekly reading knowledge class (i.e. translation exercises from Old English to Modern English), each student will be asked to conduct a research for their graduation work that will be supervised regularly throughout the semester. Towards the end of the semester, a research in progress report (1,200 words approx.) and an oral presentation (for 20 minutes in class) will be assigned to each student.

Objectives:
The student will acquire a good reading knowledge of medieval English texts and how to analyse them philologically. By reading linguistic writings widely they can develop their own interests in linguistic research in preparation for writing their graduation thesis.

The main focus of this course is learning the fundamental theories of language acquisition. Understanding these theories is essential for grasping the discipline, and they will also be necessary for students to identify topics for their graduation projects in the fourth year. The course consists of lectures and practical sessions. Students are expected to participate actively in seminars by analysing data, solving problems, and discussing ideas. Although the focus is on second language acquisition, the course will also cover some issues related to first and third language acquisition. This seminar is intended for students who are considering conducting research on any aspect of language acquisition for their graduation project, regardless of the language.

Objectives:
Students will learn the important theories and basic knowledge necessary for researching language acquisition in first, second and third languages, enabling them to conduct research for their graduation projects.

This course focuses on teaching students how to plan and conduct linguistic research and analyse data. Many students conduct research without a concrete plan and do not know what to do with the data they obtain. Therefore, during the first half of the semester, we will learn statistical methods for:

(1) planning and conducting graduation research;

(2) analysing obtained data; and

(3) understanding the results. In the second half of the semester, you will present your research plan, after which we will discuss how you can best organise and conduct your research, and analyse your data.

Objectives:
Students will learn the linguistic knowledge and statistical analysis methods necessary for conducting research in the fields of language acquisition and theoretical linguistics, so that they will be able to conduct research for graduation projects.

This course is designed to prepare and assist students in conducting research and writing academic papers on issues related to linguistic meaning: how it is influenced by structure, and, in turn, how linguistic structures are (under-)determined by meanings.

Basic principles of academic research will be reviewed. After the introductory weeks, students will be required to give oral presentations on the topic which they have chosen. They will then proceed to develop the outline and start writing a draft of their thesis. It is hoped that the draft will be finished by the end of the semester.

Seminars will be conducted in English and Japanese, and how they are conducted will be discussed at the beginning of the semester.

Objectives:
Students should find a suitable topic for their theses and start preparing a draft of their thesis.

They should be able to find the issues that they could discuss and find solutions for.

They need to be able to find relevant previous research on the same topic (e.g. journal articles and books) and see if they could provide better explanations to the same problem.

IIn this advanced course, students will gain a theoretical understanding of some aspects of lexicology, including lexical semantics (the study of word meaning), word frequency, and word collocation patterns. We will then see how this applies to the creation of materials for language teaching and language study, including dictionaries, thesauruses, and study materials. We will also briefly consider issues related to translation.

This class meets two times per week. In most class sessions, there will be short lectures combined with discussion in small groups and practice using on-line tools such as vocabulary profilers, dictionaries, corpora, and language-teaching web sites. Between classes, students will be asked to complete short reading assignments or to do further practice with the on-line tools to prepare for class discussion. Finally, students will do a final project which involves one of the following: a critical review of some of the on-line tools introduced in class, the use of these tools to investigate a some aspect of lexical meaning, or the use of the on-line tools to create teaching materials.

In order to access these tools, it is recommended that students bring a lap top computer (preferred) or tablet (also possible) to class.

During the semester, students will write several short assignments in which they reflect on their use of the on-line tools. There will also be some assignments in which students will find or create their own materials and share them with their classmates.

The class will mainly focus on materials related to the teaching and study of English, but there will be opportunities to investigate materials related to Japanese and other languages of interest to the students.

Objectives:
The students will learn about linguistic theories and research results related to words and vocabulary, and then see how these theories are applied in actual materials use for reference and language teaching and study.

Students will also learn about many online resources useful for language teaching and study, and develop their critical thinking ability in evaluating these resources.

In this seminar, students will explore ways in which linguistic theory and knowledge can be applied to actual situations; the main focus will be on second language learning and teaching, but we will also discuss other applications. such as in translation, lexicography, and advertising.

The seminar is conducted in English, but it is open to students interested in applications to ANY language. That is, it is not only for students who want to teach English, but also those who would like to teach Japanese, Korean or another language as a foreign language. The theories and methods to be discussed in class are applicable to a wide range of teaching situations.

It is expected that students in this seminar will already have taken some classes in linguistics or applied linguistics. This seminar is not appropriate for students with no previous background in linguistics or applied linguistics.

In addition to work in class, students are strongly encouraged to do some volunteer work or paid work related to their interest, for example, as a volunteer assistant in language classes at Waseda or as a private tutor.

Below are some of the graduation thesis topics of students who have taken this seminar in past years.

Topics related to the teaching of second or foreign languages:
* The portrayal of English in Japanese junior high school textbooks (Is English portrayed as a lingua franca? Or as a language used only by native speakers?)
* Policies related to English education in elementary schools in Japan and other Asian countries
* University students’ English vocabulary learning strategies
* Using loans word in the teaching of English or Japanese
* Student motivation and Japanese language study at Waseda
* The usefulness of linguistic knowledge of phonetics in study of a foreign language
* Computer-mediated communication and English education
* Japanese language education for linguistic minority (e.g. Brazilian-Japanese) children in Japan
* Japanese language education for foreign workers (e.g., nurses from Indonesia) or for refugees (from Myanmar)
* Kanji-learning strategies of students of Japanese from non-kanji language backgrounds

Topics from other areas of linguistics and applied linguistics:
* Attitudes toward the use of Taiwanese dialect in the media in Taiwan
* Attitudes toward the use of Shanghai dialect in Shanghai
* Metaphors and thought in Japanese and English
* Attempts to revive the Ainu language
* Translation of Japanese poetry into English
* Translation of English children’s literature into Japanese
* Translation of Korean literature into English
* Linguistic issues in the portrayal of characters in animated movies

Objectives:
The objective of this seminar is to deepen knowledge of linguistics and applied linguistics, in order to prepare for writing the graduation thesis.

This course will immerse students with the critical elements of interpreting skills which are listening comprehension, information processing, analysis, retention, note-taking, appropriate word choices and rendering skills. Students will build on these skills and practice consecutive interpreting in areas of international relations, political science, environmental studies and economics.
Students will be called upon randomly during each class to respond to relevant questions or to perform in front of their peers to receive peer evaluation from their classmates. Accuracy, precision and fidelity of rendering will be assessed by the instructor.

This course is not a language teaching course and assumes fluent speaking ability in both English and Japanese. It also assumes prior studies or courses in the practice of interpreting. (This class is not an introductory course in interpreting.)※This class will be taught by a faculty member who possesses working experience and will be taught based on the working experience.

Objectives:
Students will acquire consecutive interpreting skills between English and Japanese with special attention given to clarity in meaning and accuracy in word choice.

This course will immerse students with the critical elements of interpreting skills which are listening comprehension, information processing, analysis, retention, note-taking, appropriate word choices and rendering skills. We will build on those skills and practice consecutive interpreting in areas of international relations, political science, environmental studies and economics.
Students will be called upon randomly during each class to respond to relevant questions or to perform in front of their peers to receive peer evaluation from their classmates. Accuracy, precision and fidelity of rendering will be assessed by the instructor.

This course is not a language teaching course and assumes fluent speaking ability in both English and Japanese.

Objectives:
Students will acquire consecutive interpreting skills between English and Japanese with special attention given to clarity in meaning and accuracy in word choices.

Inthis advanced seminar, students will learn to carry out psycholinguisticexperiments using various experimental techniques. The course will covermethods such as reading time, reaction time, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging.Additionally, students will learn to conduct statistical analyses and reporttheir results in a scientific format. This seminar is designed to be intensiveand demanding. It requires a high level of commitment and focus; therefore,only students who are genuinely dedicated to learning and conductingpsycholinguistic experiments should enroll. While prior completion ofIntroduction to Psycholinguistics is preferred, it is not a prerequisite.

Objectives:
By the end of this seminar, students will be able to:

1. Design and conduct psycholinguistic experiments using various experimental techniques.

2. Analyze experimental data using appropriate statistical methods.

3. Report experimental findings in a scientific format, both in oral presentation and in writing.

4. Critically evaluate psycholinguistic research literature.

Mode of Delivery: Face-to-Face
This advanced seminar will examine various language issues related to the process of globalization such as the role language plays in globalization processes and the effects on language that globalization brings about. Topics include language and economic development, language and nationalism and democracy, language and the media, language and technology, language and education, language and the demographic/social changes caused by migration, language and ethnic identity, standardization and diversity, and language and inequality. This seminar is targeted not only for those who are interested in the sociolinguistic discipline per se (e.g., language planning and policy) but also for those who are seeking a deeper understanding of cross-disciplinary fields such as economics, political science, sociology, and education. Students from diverse backgrounds are encouraged to actively participate in class activities and discussions and to engage in academic research towards completing a senior thesis.

Objectives:
To conduct an original research project and complete a senior thesis.

The goal of this advanced seminar is to conduct empiricalresearch in Second Language Acquisition (SLA) and Language Teaching (LT).Students will delve into key issues surrounding SLA and LT research.

Students will explore fundamental research questions in SLA,including but not limited to: (a) How can we enhance instruction and learning?(e.g., vocabulary/grammar/pronunciation/pragmatics), (b) Is there a best agefor second language learning?, (c)What individual difference factors (e.g.,motivation, aptitude, non-cognitive abilities) predict high-level proficiencyof multiple languages?, etc.

This course is particularly valuable for students pursuingcareers in English language education in Japanese educational settings.However, the course welcomes students interested in foreign language learningand education beyond English, including those focused on bilingualism andmultilingualism.

While English is the primary language of instruction, thiscourse follows a bilingual format, incorporating both English and Japanese.Some readings will be in Japanese, so students must be comfortable readingacademic Japanese to get the most out of the course (see “Note / URL” sectionfor more details).

IMPORTANT:

- This intensive, research-oriented seminar demands rigorouscommitment. Due to its advanced nature and hands-on research requirements,enrollment is limited to students who demonstrate genuine interest in SLA andLT and are prepared to engage in research activities.

- This seminar is NOT appropriate for students withoutprevious background in second language acquisition and applied linguistics. Studentsare recommended to take preparatory courses with the lecturer (Suzuki): AppliedLinguistics (intermediate course), the intermediate seminar, and/or SelectedTopics in Language Education and Second Language Acquisition (advancedlecture).

Objectives:
This seminar aims to help students develop the ability to plan and implement a research project in SLA and language education. By the end of this course, students are expected to develop the ability to:

a) formulate relevant research questions that address SLA and language teaching issues,

b) develop an appropriate and feasible research design,

c) implement the research plan, and

d) write up a graduation thesis.

In this course, we will look at the importance of games for learning foreign languages on different levels:

- We will discuss theoretical aspects of games and play and their use in education.

- We will test instructional games and evaluate their effects on language skills.

- We will design a game together that is intended to improve the skills of learners of German.

In the first part of the course, students are familiarized with central concepts of game theory and game design and learn about the significance of games in education. In the second part, we want to jointly develop an educational game on a linguistic phenomenon of the German language, which in its procedural rhetoric depicts relevant aspects of the subject matter. The students will work in groups on mechanics, rules, character design, sound effects, music and level design and thus contribute to the development of the game.

In the course of the semester, students will also be encouraged to review their own gaming biography, reflect on their methods of foreign language learning and critically question processes of the gamification of education in general.

In-depth computer knowledge or coding skills are not a prerequisite for participation. However, students should be willing to familiarize themselves with software and tools. Because the game we want to develop in the course of the semester will be designed to represent an aspect of the German language, some knowledge of German and/or participation in the German language program at SILS are prerequisites for admission to the seminar. Students of German I are also welcome.

The course will be conducted in English.

Objectives:
Upon completion of this course, the students will have...

- gained knowledge of the function of games in society and for learning.

- acquired conceptual skills of game design and critical design analysis.

- explored fundamental concepts of game designs (rules, mechanics, emergence).

- gained the experience of creating a playable game using an established design process.

- reflected critically on the ideologies of game designers (as covert conceptions of the learning process and of learners) as well as the ideology behind the gamification of education.

- improved their German skills by closely studying those aspects of German that the collaboratively developed game is based on

This course examines the interrelations between language and society in the German-speaking countries, focusing on how language patterns and language attitudes both reflect and reshape social structure and cultural institutions. We will investigate this nexus from a variety of perspectives, engaging with literature drawn from cultural sociology, political science, linguistic anthropology, and sociolinguistics. Students will be introduced to key theoretical concepts to the scientific study of language and society and encouraged to assess critically research carried out in the German-speaking countries.

A selection of core features of the contemporary societies and cultures in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland -- lifestyles, identities, political cultures, migration, and xenophobia among others -- will be paired with research into related linguistic phenomena such as language ideologies, politeness, pluricentricity, political framing, and multilingualism.

The course aims not only to provide insights into the interrelation of culture, society and language, but also to improve the language skills of the participants. Although mainly taught in English, as a Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) course, we will get acquainted with basic scientific concepts in German and become familiar with the structures of German as a language of science. The course is therefore ideal for students planning to study abroad in Germany. However, students who are interested in the German-speaking countries and want to improve their language skills are also welcome.

Objectives:
On successful completion of this course students should:

- be able to understand core scientific terminology in German in the field of the sociology of language

- be familiar with frequent grammatical structures in German scientific texts

- be familiar with various research methods and their limits

- be able to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of relevant theories conceptualizing the interface of language and society

- be familiar with some major themes in contemporary social, political and cultural aspects of the German speaking countries

Linguistics is a scientific study of human language. People depend on language so heavily in their everyday lives that most of them would find life without it unimaginable. And yet, they don’t really know how language works or, for that matter, how they acquired their mother tongue in the first place. Indeed, first language acquisition poses an intriguing puzzle. Every normal child easily accomplishes it within a few years without any special training (so the task must be very simple), but even linguists with many years of training can't duplicate this "simple" feat. There are many mysteries like this about human language, which is why the field of linguistics is fascinating and linguistic research has been very active.

Against this backdrop, this course will explain the workings of human language by introducing important theoretical concepts from modern linguistics. More specifically, it will introduce core subfields of linguistics, i.e., phonetics/phonology, morphology/syntax, and semantics/pragmatics. It will thus provide a solid foundation for intermediate-level linguistics courses (and beyond), which will equip students with necessary tools for investigating language and language-related matters. The course will also serve as a good preparation for any discipline that applies knowledge of linguistics.

CO202 (Introduction to Applications of Linguistics) a companion course that deals with applied linguistics, sociolinguistics and historical linguistics, is offered in the spring semester. Students who are interested in linguistics are strongly encouraged to take this course as well.

Note: If you have already received credit for CO201 under the name "Introduction to Language Studies", you may NOT register for this class.

Objectives:
Basic understanding of core subfields of English linguistics, plus ability to discern purely linguistic matters from ones that are not.

Face to face
We all know that animals (and even insects) can communicate with each other, but our way of communication is fundamentally different in that it is greatly facilitated by language, whose structure seems species-specific. This course concentrates on this part of human language with special reference to its syntax, a set of rules that govern the way the words in a sentence come together.

The underlying assumption behind the paragraph above is that all human languages in the world are rule-governed and structurally the same at an abstract level, and, in this respect, they contrast sharply with other modes of communication employed by bees, bats, dolphins, etc, which all seem to lack systematic structure that allows users to create an infinite number of novel language expressions. This course thus aims to discover principles that govern this essential aspect of human language and tries to tackle issues such as how child language acquisition takes place and how surface differences among languages may be explained by the notion of parameter.

In more practical terms, this course critically reviews and revises school English grammar (i.e., prescriptive grammar), and in so doing, it will equip students with skills necessary to tackle real linguistic issues, including those related to English language education (which has been a big problem in countries like Japan).

Objectives:
Understanding of fundamental ideas of generative syntax.

This course will study English phonetics and phonology, dealing with segmental and prosodic aspects of the language. Lectures will focus on the typical characteristics of the sound systems of English in relation to phonetic and phonological theories. The course will focus mainly on theory, but practical pronunciation training will also be included, whenever appropriate, in order to help understanding of the theories. The course is aimed at students who are interested in teaching English as a foreign language. Students will be encouraged to participate during the classes.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to identify speech sounds in English, to understand and describe these sounds using International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and to explain features and characteristics of English pronunciation for both learning and teaching.

This course will study Japanese phonetics and phonology, focusing on segmental and prosodic aspects of the language. You will learn about the typical characteristics of Japanese sound systems in relation to phonetic and phonological theories. While the course will focus mainly on theory, but practical pronunciation training will also be included wherever appropriate to help you understand the concepts and theories. While Japanese language ability is not essential for this course, some knowledge of the language will help you to understand the theoretical points and examples. Therefore, I encourage students to learn to read Hiragana and Katakana.

Objectives:
Students will be able to understand the sound system of the Japanese language, analyse Japanese pronunciation and explain learner pronunciation difficulties. They will also be able to teach correct pronunciation effectively.

Linguistic expressions typically convey more than one kind of ‘meaning’. This course focuses on how different kinds of meanings are conveyed and how they interact and/or are controlled by other factors, drawing examples mainly from English and Japanese.
Basic concepts to be covered include:
--word, phrase, sentence [review]--natural language and logical language meanings
--logical symbols and formula
--valence and thematic roles
--lexical (or sense) reations
--contextual information
--implicature, presupposition, speech act theories and illocutionary acts
--politeness
--discourse

Objectives:
-- understanding basic concepts in theoretical linguistics

-- being capable of explaining how utterances can convey meanings

-- being capable of distinguishing and explaining different types of 'meaning'

-- being capable of noticing subtle differences in meanings as a result

-- being capable of analyzing new linguistic data using the concepts learnt

This course focuses on words in Japanese and English -- how these words are made, where new words come from, how the meanings and sounds of words change over time, and how individual words fit into the overall system of a language. That is, this course will introduce the basics of morphology-- the way words are built from parts such as roots and affixes. It will also consider some of the other interesting aspects of words, including etymology (the history of words), patterns of semantic change, phonological aspects of words (such as stress in English and pitch accent and rendaku in Japanese), and recent trends in word creation, including as the rise of blends, acronyms and use of characters in electronic communication.

This class meets twice per week in first period on Mondays and Fridays. Most classes will start with a short lecture which introduces concepts and online tools or which reviews work done in class during the previous session. Then a large portion of class time will involve students working together in groups to discuss ideas and to analyze data. Sometimes groups will be assigned by the teacher, and other times they will be self-selected.

This class should be of interest to students who are studying English or Japanese as a foreign language and who would like a deeper understanding of the structure of it, as well as students who are interested in teaching either Japanese or English.

Objectives:
In this class, students will

- learn to apply theory through exercises done in class and as homework.

- become familiar with resources for studying vocabulary, including online dictionaries and corpora.

- work in groups to find and analyze linguistic examples in the language used around them.

- learn linguistic conventions for writing about words.

[Course Delivery Method] : Face-to-Face

This course focuses on matters that are truly linguistic. After separating linguistic problems from those that should be studied in other fields like sociology, anthropology, psychology, culture, pedagogy, history, religion, etc., the course introduces students to genuinely scientific study of human language. By the time students successfully complete the course, they will have developed an attitude of a scientist, rather than that of a prescriptive grammarian.

More specifically, using Radford’s textbook (Radford 2009), the course provides a concise and clear introduction to current work in syntactic theory, drawing on the key concepts of Chomsky’s Minimalist Program. By looking at data mainly from English, it will also introduce students to quite a few linguistic mysteries found not only in present-day English but also in languages like Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Belfast English, Elizabethan English, etc. Analytical skills gained in this course will be a solid foundation for conducting research in the following linguistics-related fields: child language, language acquisition, computational linguistics, machine translation, sign language, pidgin and creole, comparative linguistics, historical linguistics, language and thought, speech therapy, textbook writing, etc.

In more practical terms, this course critically reviews and revises school English grammar (i.e., prescriptive grammar), and in so doing, it will equip students with skills necessary to tackle real linguistic issues, including those related to English language education (which has been a big problem in countries like Japan).

Objectives:
Basic understanding of human language structure

[Course Delivery Method] : Face-to-Face
This three-semester-long seminar provides an approachable introduction to scientific research of human language. The history of language science is rather short, and there are still quite a few mysteries about human language, which any normal individual uses every day. In this seminar, students will be trained to be beginning linguists who can actually conduct decent research in this young but very systematic and exciting field.

In the first semester, students study linguistics as cognitive science, using Patterns in the Mind (Jackendoff 1994) as textbook. Questions that are asked in class include: “Do babies imitate their parents when they try to acquire language?” “Can we think without language?” “What happens to babies if they are raised by wild animals?” “What happens to one’s language if the right and left hemispheres of one’s brain are severed?” “What do language, vision, and music have in common?” “Can babies develop their own language?” “What is the language DNA?” “What happens when two people that don’t have a common language have to work together?”

In the second semester, students will read academic papers and critically review them. Then, they will engage in comparative studies of English and Japanese (or some other language, depending on students’interest). By the end of the semester, students will write and submit a term paper, which they can choose to develop further as graduation thesis in the third semester. Alternatively, students may also choose a different topic; in that case, they are expected to find another topic by the end of the summer break.

As for thesis topic, following the spirit of liberal arts, this seminar allows students to select virtually any topic of linguistic science; students may choose a topic from general linguistics, morphology, syntax, linguistics as cognitive science, English education, textbook writing, bilingualism, historical linguistics, comparative linguistics, language acquisition, etc. (as long as it is something that can be studied scientifically).

In the third semester, each student will work on his/her topic for graduation thesis individually. Students are expected to meet with the instructor frequently so that they can submit decent theses in time for graduation.

By actively participating in this seminar, students will be able to conduct quality linguistic research by thoroughly utilizing theoretical tools. If you wish to graduate with a sense of accomplishment, this seminar is for you.

Objectives:
Acquisition of ability to distinguish genuinely linguistic matters from ones that are not.

Development of linguistic research skills

This course will introduce theories of acoustic and auditory phonetics, and demonstrate basic techniques for computational analysis of speech sounds. The course will cover the anatomy and physiology of the speech and auditory organs, physics of speech, speech production and perception, and basic theories of speech recognition and synthesis. The classes will consist of both lectures and also practical sessions where the students will conduct speech analysis. No previous knowledge of computation or programming is necessary, but students need to be able to use basic software such as Word, Excel, etc.

Objectives:
Students will learn about the system of speech production and perception, and also how to plan and carry out experiments and analyse speech data for phonetic and phonological study.

This course will examine the key principles of phonetic and phonological theory. It will begin with a review of classical taxonomic phonology, before moving on to modern phonological theories. Students will also practise producing the speech sounds of languages spoken around the world based on the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). Although examples will mainly be presented from English and Japanese to help students understand the theories, examples from various other languages will also be used to further explain the theoretical concepts. Students are expected to have a basic knowledge of phonetics and phonology.

Objectives:
On this course, students will learn about current phonetic and phonological theories to help them understand relevant academic papers. They will also learn how to analyse real-world language data and interpret the results using these theories.

Put crudely, pragmatics is the study of meaning of linguistic expressions in context (linguistic and otherwise). Speakers of any language need to grasp different kinds of meaning other than the so-called “literal” one (i.e. propositional meaning) in order to express what they wish to convey. This is necessary also in order to clearly understand what other people have said or written. Most of the time, people perform this task without much effort, but explicating how it is done is no simple task. This course explores how meaning interacts with structure.

Issues to be discussed include meanings of the predicate (including thematic roles), functions of nominal expressions (including deixis), politeness, and viewpoint. The special focus will be on expressive meanings. Some of these issues are universally found whilst others are salient only in certain languages.

If the majority of students have not taken a pragmatics course, the first few classes will be spent discussing basic concepts in syntax and morphology so that they can later explore multifaceted aspects of "meaning" and also to apply them for analyses of actual language use.

Objectives:
Students should have understood basic concepts in theoretical linguistics when the course starts as this is an ADVANCED-level course. The minimum basics will be reviewed in the first four weeks but the students are expected to self-study if their knowledge is insufficient.

Students should be able to apply this knowledge in order to analyze natural language data and have a better understanding of utterance meaning by the end of the semester. In particular, they should be

-- capable of understanding and distinguishing different types of meanings

-- capable of providing convincing explanations as to how utterances can convey such meanings

-- capable of using the basic concepts to explain more complex data

In this course basic notions in studying literature and literary works are introduced. The course will draw on a wide variety of literary references specifically devoted to this subject, with particular attention paid to structures and techniques of literary works in the world. We will also look at how so-called ‘classics’ can be defined according to traditional western criteria. In addition, we will discuss the extent to which these inner values have been lost or left intact by the fundamental changes in the socio-historical contexts．【Special Notice】The description above is for non-COVID years; as far as the pandemic alerts are active, the class will be held by On-Demand style and class organization will be given in the first class of the semester. Objectives:
The goal of this course is to reconsider the distinctive features of literary works in a wide range of cultural contexts as well as in terms of political, social, and post-colonial approaches. Literature is also about personal perception and understanding, about communication, about imagination; therefore, unlike many other academic subjects, literature studies still demand a personal response from its audience...

Human civiilation develped within the 10,000-year period known as the Holocene during which the processes that regulate the stability and resilience of the Earth system were remarkably stable. Now, however, human behavior has begun to push such processes beyond their ability to recover, threatening to destabalize them with catastrophic consequences. Although like many institutions around the world, Japanese universites refuse to acknowldge this crisis, as students educate themselves, they increasingly realize that they are facing an unprecedented climate and ecological emergency that will not be solved by better technology. One goal of this course is to create space for young people to share their concerns for the future.

Japanese Translation for the purposes of this course does not presuppose only linguistic translation, but includes as well the social and cultural appropriation of Western-centered modernity, which involved radically new ways of organizing knowledge. The creation of the modern nation-state requires the “invention of tradition,” made possible through the reformulation of older cultural productions. From the Meiji period onward, literature may thus be read as a double translation of Western modernity and pre-Meiji cultural forms. Literary translation plays a central role in the construction of modern Japanese language (kokugo) and modern national literature. We will deconstruct the idea of national culture as we embark on close readings of Japanese modern literature.
This is a student-centered course in which students consider relations among language, culture, gender, race/ethnicity, power, nation and empire. Students interested in participating enthusiastically in a classroom community that emphasizes ethical and social engagement are especially welcome.

Objectives:
This course should give students a greater understanding of Japanese history, Japanese literature, and postcolonial and gender theory. The class is designed to help students rethink institutions and systems of knowledge created within modernity. Engaged students are also given guided opportunities to develop skills in critical reading, writing, self-expression, analytical reasoning, social engagement, communication and community building.

Students should：

・achieve a greater understanding of Japanese cultural and social history

・begin to comprehend the post-colonial critique of modernity, including the history of European violence, the violence underlying the creation and maintenance of every modern nation and the use of ‘discourse’as a mechanism of control

・understand basic post-colonial theory and become familiar with some basic terms

・gain experience in close, critical readings of complex and ambiguous Japanese literary texts

・gain experience in articulating ideas succinctly and coherently

・began to understand the historical construction of modern knowledge and be able to critically deconstruct it

・connect academic and social knowledge with personal experience in a manner that leads to introspection and social engagement

・learn how to engage in active listening in order to imaginatively understand the viewpoints of others with contrasting backgrounds, social positions and opinions

・engage dynamically with others to create knowledge and classroom community

・recognize the ethical component of knowledge, communication and action and consider the personal responsibility that accompanies it

・learn how to accurately summarize theoretical, academic texts

・write with conviction and clarity of purpose

・understand the value of editing and rewriting

In this introductory course, we will examine classic English novels. We will focus on novels by Jane Austen, Charlotte Brontë, Emily Brontë, Anne Brontë, Charles Dickens, Elizabeth Gaskell and Thomas Hardy, examining how these novels explore complex themes of love and marriage. Alongside textual analysis, we will watch clips from various film and TV adaptations of these novels in order to further understand the richness and complexity of these literary masterpieces and to explore how and why they continue to resonate with and fascinate us today.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to be able to:

・Understand the richness and complexity of English novels.

・Situate English novels in their social and cultural contexts.

・Explore how English novels reflect and critique the societal norms of their time.

・Analyse how film and TV adaptations interpret and reimagine English novels for contemporary audiences.

a. Face-to-Face (F2F)
This class is designed to provide students with a broad-based survey and foundational knowledge of acting and directing, aimed at enhancing their appreciation and understanding of practical theatrical experience. Various aspects of acting and directing will be covered, including—but not limited to—classical, modern, and avant-garde performance theories and methodologies. Classes will be conducted in an in-person format but may be switched to an online (remote) format in the event of COVID-19 restrictions or other unavoidable circumstances.

Objectives:
By the end of this class, students will be able to:

2.Recognize the types and genres of drama and performance, along with their conventions.

3.Understand diverse approaches to acting and directing in relation to the audience, the script, and the stage environment.

a. Face-to-Face (F2F)This course introduces and explores the variety and richness of the performing arts of the world, to illustrate the diversity of human expression. Areas covered include the ritualistic roots of performance, Japanese and Western theatre, dance, and opera, as well as contemporary performing arts. The general goals in this course are (1) to develop an awareness of, and interest in, various aspects of theatre and (2) to encourage an appreciation of theatrical performance and dramatic literature within diverse social and cultural contexts.Classes will be conducted based on "in-person format". Objectives:
In this course, the students will (1) develop an awareness of, and interest in, various aspects of theatre and (2) acquire knowledge for deeper appreciation of theatrical performance and dramatic literature within diverse social and cultural contexts.

In translation practices, students have to show advanced Japanese language skills; just being a native Japanese speaker is not enough to do translation. When you register, you need to know your Japanese language proficiency; if language skill is not enough, you should realize you will not be able to get grades you expect. This course will focus on practices in translating short English texts (up to two pages) from various genres into Japanese. Translation consists in reproducing the reception language to the closest natural equivalent of the source-language message, first in terms of meaning and secondly in terms of style. Though style is secondary to contents, it is nevertheless important. We should not translate poetry as though it were prose, nor essay as though it were expository material. A translation should preserve somewhat the beauty of style and the flowing cadences of the original. Therefore, the important thing is to be able to build a Japanese translation so that those who have not read the English original(poems, proses, and essays)might enjoy. To do so, many skills and considerable background knowledge should be accumulated. In this course, the following points will be dealt with: skills such as how to consult dictionaries, to write persuasive Japanese, to interpret literary texts, and to acquire a great deal of knowledge of British and American culture, society and literature. Through classroom discussions, we will find ways to improve translated versions that students might create. For this purpose, regular attendance, participation and adequate reading/writing (understanding) proficiencies in Japanese are required.

Objectives:
The aim of this course is for the student to be able to create an accurate and reliable Japanese version on the basis of the translation rules they might learn each week; Students will learn various ‘styles’.

Translating literary texts should be more about the creative imagination than it is about the rule-governed text analysis. The translator should be more like a poet or a novelist than like a machine translation system.

a. Face-to-Face (F2F)Mime/Pantomime is one of the oldest forms of human communication and, at the same time, one of the most essential tools for stage expression. The goal of this class is to explore the history, theories and practice of mimes, pantomimes and other physically-oriented/ non-verbal performances of each era, with the consideration of their cultural, societal background context. Our study will include comments of people, impressions of critics, or the sometimes vehement attacks of Christian authority on these activities. By doing so, we will explore not only the art of physical expression but the social context in which a certain art form was created, modified, developed and prospered.
Classes will be conducted based on "in-person format". It might be changed to "online (remote) format" depending upon the COVID19.status.

Objectives:
At the end of class, the students will be provided not only with broad knowledge of the art of physical expression but the social context in which a certain art form was created, modified, developed and practiced. The students will also learn to handle some of the actual modern mime techniques with solid theoretical backups.

In this course, we will focus on understanding and analyzing the main changes and important aspects of American culture, society, politics, and history, through reading important texts of American literature; in terms of U. S. influence on Japanese society, some parts of the focus will be on how Japanese academic have analyzed American cultural and literary topic and the assigned readings will include Japanese academic writings. Throughout the course, we will try to review the history of American literature in particular by reading a text, mainly a short story in one section, sometimes an excerpt from a longer text. In the first half of the semester, we will read texts written before 1900 and in the latter half, we will target on stories published after 1900. The analysis of each text, along with history and social context, will help understanding several aspects of American society and culture. The course will be conducted in the combination of the lecture parts given in advance through Moodle, group-works and discussions and writing essays. Group-works and discussions, and essay writing will be assigned in the classroom; there is a possibility of doing research works at the library; the class readings might include not only prose writings but also letters, diaries and several official documents written by American influential writers from the 17th century to the 20th century, making use of DVDs, music CDs and films. In the classes, students are expected to prepare for the class readings in English each time; therefore, the participants should be interested in reading literary works and criticisms both in Japanese and English. Besides, we will make use of DVDs in order to help/deepen students’ understanding of literary texts and American social issues. As an important part of preparation for classroom tasks, students are supposed to download and print out each section's main text by themselves, to bring each own material for discussions. Considering impacts on brains by the usage of electronic devices such as phones, pads, PCs, no electronic devices are allowed to use during the discussions and task works in the classroom. Note-taking by traditional paper notebooks and pens/pencils is recommended for preparation.

Objectives:
The goal of this course is to enhance students knowledge on American literature along with historical and cultural backgrounds of the U.S. Students are expected to enrich their critical analysis methods through literary interpretation. Close reading skills also help such analytical methods so as to deepen each one’s interpretation.

Students with an interest in fine art, art history, photography, visual/material culture (including design, advertising, crafts, fashion), or museum studies will get support to pursue their interests in this seminar. Students present on topics related to the arts (contemporary, modern, or premodern) or to their reception and exhibition. These presentations are investigations of potential themes for the senior thesis, synopses of final thesis drafts, and reports to the class on exhibitions, artists, etc.

Time is set aside to visit museums or galleries, to discuss thesis projects, and to workshop employment or graduate-school opportunities and strategies.

Classes will be conducted in person only.

To view, think, talk, and write about art and visual culture.

To connect student interests with career objectives.

It is said that all humans have an innate desire to imitate and copy their environment—a concept known as the “dramatic instinct.” When this instinct is fully engaged, drama becomes a highly effective and natural means of learning. Through processes such as imitation, interpretation, imagination, and role-playing, much of a child’s learning in language, logical thinking, movement, and social behavior takes place.

“Drama in Education” is also a dynamic learning experience that caters to a broad range of students with diverse intelligences and prepares them for effective and responsible participation in society. It is now recognized as a crucial subject that supplements the limitations of conventional IQ-based learning.

Course Organization
During the first four weeks, you will be exposed to a wide range of readings as well as various drama techniques and methodologies to prepare you for the design, implementation, and evaluation of drama activities. After these initial four weeks, each group will report on an assigned drama practitioner and conduct a drama activity based on a lesson plan your group has created. The entire class will then reflect on the activity at the end of the session. (For detailed information on projects, please refer to “Project Procedures.”) Additionally, each group will report on Dr. Shoyo Tsubouchi’s work on child drama activities, based on the assigned paper.

Objectives:
The goal of this class is to acquaint students with the basic history, philosophy, methodologies, and practices of Drama in Education. Through the study of the history, philosophy, and work of various practitioners, we will explore the potential of drama as a tool for diverse learning. Alongside theoretical study, students will engage in hands-on exercises and techniques related to “Educational Drama.”

By the end of the class,

1) Students will learn to structure creative learning experiences based on dramatics.

2)Students will become familiar with the variety and richness of dramatic literature for youth.

3)Students will acquire a broad knowledge of the history and philosophy of educational drama.

In this advanced course, we will explore Shakespeare’s plays alongside their film adaptations, examining not only the rich and complex worlds of Shakespeare’s texts but also the dynamic and exciting interaction between literature and its visual adaptations. Through analysis of Shakespeare’s plays and film screenings, we will discuss how Shakespeare’s plays were shaped by the cultural and social contexts of his time and how Shakespearean adaptations have also been shaped by the cultural and social contexts of the time of their production and reception. By focusing, for example, on critical debates surrounding feminism, gender and race, we will explore how film adaptations of Shakespeare’s plays have been deeply influenced by our shifting perspectives on these themes and by the emerging cultural and social movements of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Each week, we will focus on one Shakespearean play and its significant film adaptations and discuss the nuanced and often innovative ways in which Shakespeare’s timeless texts have been read by scholars, readers, theatre practitioners and filmmakers and reimagined through adaptation.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to be able to:

・Conduct a critical analysis of English literary texts from multiple perspectives

・Understand the richness and complexity of Shakespeare’s drama

・Examine the intricate and exciting interaction between English literary texts and film adaptations

In this advanced seminar, we will explore William Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet through close reading/dramatic reading, discussion and critical analysis. You will be divided into small groups to read and discuss, sharing your thoughts on the scene(s) and the characters. The instructor will also provide critical analysis of the play and encourage you to develop your own interpretations. When time permits, we will also watch TV and film adaptations of the play to enrich our understanding of the enduring relevance of Shakespeare’s text.

This seminar is built around active participation and designed to be collaborative and lively—a safe space where students can test out ideas, ask questions and experience Shakespeare’s play from multiple angles.

Alongside the readings and discussions, you will also learn how to write an academic essay to effectively communicate your interpretation of the text. In the latter half of the course, you are encouraged to think about your forthcoming graduation thesis project by coming up with possible topics you would like to work on.

Please also read my section in the “Advanced Seminar Course List and Information, Fall 2026.”

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to be able to:

・Analyse texts from multiple perspectives.

・Recite and perform theatrical texts with confidence and an understanding of their dramatic and poetic elements.

・Lay out their own arguments effectively.

・Provide meaningful comments and questions on the arguments of others.

This is a topic-based survey class of American Literature; in this course, we will focus on understanding and analyzing the main changes and important aspects of American culture, society, politics, and history by exposing students to the works of various kinds of American literature authors; our readings will include not only prose writings but also letters, diaries and several official documents written by American influential writers from the 15th century to the 19th century, from time to time making use of rare photographs, musical CDs, and films. Students are expected to be interested in basics of modern literary theory which are widely associated in American literary studies. As we challenge the process of creating the notions such as “America,” “American History/Literature,” “race,” “class,” and “borders,” our readings will sometimes go beyond narrowly-defined “American” texts. Through these readings and analyses, students will learn various cultural aspects to approach social issues seen in American society, past and present. This course will be conducted in a mixed style of lecture/seminar, and research works at out main library; therefore, participants will be assigned to make presentations, discussion, research and other activities. In the library survey sessions, students are expected to write and submit 2-3 page long paper each time during the class hours.

Objectives:
The goal of this course is to enhance students’ abilities in reading and interpreting American literary texts and improve their research skills in the library; by so doing, students will be exposed to the invisible, less-known aspects of the American society. Each student will gain basic knowledge of American literary works and well-known, canonical authors through video lectures and each one's research projects.

The following list is provisional only, but the general pattern will be that one class will be devoted to a text or texts on a particular theory or approach to translation This will then be followed by a class in which we will discuss a specific translated text. In this way, we will work our way through a selection of writings about translation, some very well-known and others less so, and in the following lesson, examine some specific examples of translation that seem to relate either directly or indirectly to the theoretical text. This ought to allow us to consider how the theories of translation that we have been reading might apply in practice. Since the language that everyone in class must have in common will be English, the theoretical texts will be read in that language, although naturally, some of these will themselves be translations. The sample texts of actual translation will also normally be those of works translated into or out of English, but where appropriate, Japanese translations will also be supplied since Japanese is likely to be the second most commonly understood language in the class. Objectives:
To understand the crucial role of translation as a cultural and social practice and to become familiar with the major issues in translation theory and comparative literature.

In this course, we will learn the basics of major literary theories. Each lecture will focus on a specific theoretical approach to texts and cultural phenomena, such as psychoanalytic criticism, feminist criticism, gender and queer criticism, new historicism and postcolonial criticism. By engaging with diverse critical frameworks, we will aim to deepen our appreciation for the richness and complexity of literature and other cultural forms.

Objectives:
By the end of this course, students are expected to be able to:

・Explain the basics of major literary theories.

・Apply critical frameworks to the analysis of literary texts and cultural phenomena.

・Examine how literature and other cultural forms reflect and shape social and ideological issues.

The course will examine the rich variety of capitalisms, and of other economic systems, across time and place. We will explore the historical development of the business firm, its particular economic advantages and social impacts, and the technological, political, creative, financial and societal forces that are transforming the landscape of contemporary enterprise. The course will examine how governance of the private institution of the firm is patterned by the structures of public governance within which it situated, how they have evolved mutually over time, and how there has been systematic variance in market systems, governance and enterprise outcomes across countries. It will offer a multidisciplinary and historical feel for the development of enterprise & market systems and will complement prior studies in business, politics, history and related fields. It also explores large contemporary issues - such as aging societies, inequality, digitisation, locational clustering - through the prism of the varied 'adaptive efficiency' of firms and societies, so is of general career relevance too.

Objectives:
Intended learning outcomes:

+ familiarity with key concepts in contemporary corporate governance.

+ an understanding of the historical and contemporary relationships between the worlds of business, politics, and their societal contexts

+ familiarity with relevant examples from a number of countries and regions.

+ engagemnent with theories of the origins of national and regional particularity in business and economic systems.

+ some awareness of the relative effectiveness of particular business systems.

+ understanding of common criticisms and defences of private and state enterprise and regulation.

+ engagement with contemporary discussions about key issues facing market economies, including aging populations, Ai & automation, spatial clustering of economic activities, agility, creativity and innovation systems.

+ some analytical capacity to navigate the complexity of particular industry and firm case studies, from corporate and public governance perspectives.

This course is designed to provide basic skills in calculus, which are useful in fields such as biological, physical and social sciences. The graph theory provides a basis for computationalsciences, financial engineering, chemistry, and epidemiology, among manyothers. A main reason for the importance of the theory is that it is useful toremove non-essential information from huge information given in the form ofcomplex data so that the system is represented in a simple form. By the end of the course, students should understand basic objects in the graph theory including graphs, paths, cycles, trees, connectivity, Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs, and planar graphs, as wel as some important algorithms.

The purpose of this course is to provide basic set operations in set theory and how to prove propositions in formal manners. Set theory is the fundamental theory of any modern mathematics. The lecture focuses on set operations and links to the proofs. Proofs are regarded as construction to formal/systematic operations. Students study systematic operations in set theory and apply such operations to extended mathematical proofs.

The lecture intends to teach how to prove statements logically or in formal ways. We start linear functions. However, instead of high-school math, we study the essential meaning of the components, and how to generalize them. The students will realize that ‘1 < 2’ involves many concepts.

In that sense, there is few requirement of math knowledge. Rather, students will study how to get an insight into the true nature of mathematical components, and then will realize that what you have already studied is not trivial, but realizations of the abstract concepts.

Linear algebra is a branch of mathematics. A majorconcern in the field is the study of vectors, matrices, and systems oflinearequations. ・Students should be able to apply these concepts and techniques to solve linear algebra problems.

・In particular, students should master the diagonalisation of square matrices and how to apply it to various cases.

This course will cover fundamental concepts and techniques in calculus, which are useful in broad fields of natural and social sciences. Following the textbook, students will learn inverse functions and techniques of integration for functions of one real variable. In the next part of the course, they will learn applications of integration as well as the fundamentals of sequences and series, and differential calculus for functions of several real variables.

Objectives:
The main objective is for students to develop fundamental skills to perform operations in calculus, focusing on working with functions and computing integrals. Aside from calculations, another objective is for students to become comfortable with calculus as a mathematical theory with formal definitions, which will be the focus of the part of the course on sequences and series. There will also be an emphasis on applications, and students are expected to use techniques from calculus in the mathematical modelling and analysis of natural and social phenomena.

This course is designed to study differential equations, which are essential to understand the physical sciences, economics, and the social and biological sciences.
